examples.professional: The engineering team modeled soil denudation after the burn to predict where the slope might slide.
examples.analytical: The denudation of the ridge exposed layers that record millions of years of sediment deposition.

nuance.analogy: Denudation is like peeling paint off an old wall until only the bare plaster shows.
nuance.etymology: From Latin denudatio, from denudare, to make bare, from de- and nudus, naked.
common_mistakes: Confusing denudation with denunciation, which means public condemnation.
Using denudation as a casual word for a simple cut; everyday speech says stripping or clearing.

senses.definition: (poetic) Chiefly in the form descend into (or within) oneself: to mentally enter a state of (deep) meditation or thought; to retire.
senses.example: Before answering, she would descend into herself for a long moment of silent reflection.
senses.label: poetic

senses.definition: Senses relating to moving from a higher to a lower position.
senses.example: they descended the river in boats

senses.definition: Of a flight of stairs, a road, etc.: to lead down (a hill, a slope, etc.).
senses.example: They took the steep path that descends the hill down to the beach.

senses.definition: To physically move or pass from a higher to a lower place or position; to come or go down in any way, such as by climbing, falling, flowing, walking, etc. to move downwards; to fall, to sink.
senses.example: Cryptorchidism is the failure of one or both testes to descend into the scrotum.

senses.definition: Of a zodiac sign: to move away from the zenith towards the horizon; to sink; also, of a planet: to move to a place where it has less astrological significance.
senses.example: In the old almanac, Virgo was said to descend toward the horizon each evening in autumn.

senses.definition: To slope or stretch downwards.
senses.example: The garden path began to descend gently toward the river, lined with willows on both sides.

senses.definition: To come or go down, or reduce, in intensity or some other quality.
senses.example: By midnight, the temperature had begun to descend, and the wind finally stopped blowing.

senses.definition: Of a physical thing (such as a cloud or storm) or a (generally negative) immaterial thing (such as darkness, gloom, or silence): to settle upon and start to affect a person or place.
senses.example: A heavy silence seemed to descend on the room after the verdict was read aloud.

senses.definition: In speech or writing: to proceed from one matter to another; especially, to pass from more general or important to specific or less important matters to be considered.
senses.example: Let us descend from these abstract theories to the practical problems facing rural clinics.

senses.definition: Chiefly followed by into or to: of a situation: to become worse; to decline, to deteriorate.
senses.example: The meeting descended into chaos.

senses.definition: Chiefly followed by on or upon: to make an attack or incursion, from or as if from a vantage ground; to come suddenly and with violence.
senses.example: Raiders descended on the village at dawn, burning houses and seizing the harvest.

senses.definition: Chiefly followed by on or upon: to arrive suddenly or unexpectedly, especially in a manner that causes disruption or inconvenience.
senses.example: My neighbor descended upon me just as I was walking out the door.

senses.definition: To come down to a humbler or less fortunate, or a worse or less virtuous, rank or state; to abase or lower oneself; to condescend or stoop to something.
senses.example: He descended from his high estate.

senses.definition: Of a sequence or series: to proceed from higher to lower values.
senses.example: In a decreasing sequence, each term is smaller than the one before, so values descend.

senses.definition: Senses relating to passing down from a source to another thing.
senses.example: The beggar may descend from a prince.

senses.definition: Of a characteristic: to be transmitted from a parent to a child.
senses.example: Eye color may descend from parents to children through complex patterns of inherited genes.

senses.definition: Chiefly followed by from or (obsolete) of: to come down or derive from an ancestor or ancestral stock, or a source; to originate, to stem.
senses.example: The beggar may descend from a prince.

senses.definition: To pass from a higher to a lower part of (something, such as a flight of stairs or a slope); to go down along or upon.
senses.example: they descended the river in boats

senses.definition: Of a celestial body: to move away from the zenith towards the horizon; to sink; also, to move towards the south.
senses.example: Each night the bright star would descend toward the southern horizon before dawn.

senses.definition: Of a body part: to move downwards, especially during development of the embryo; specifically, of the testes of a mammal: to move downwards from the abdominal cavity into the scrotum.
senses.example: Cryptorchidism is the failure of one or both testes to descend into the scrotum.

senses.definition: To pass from a higher to a lower note or tone; to fall in pitch.
senses.example: Her voice would descend to a low murmur at the end of every lullaby.

senses.definition: Of property, a right, etc.: to pass down to a generation, a person, etc. by inheritance.
senses.example: The crown descends to the heir of the previous monarch.

senses.definition: (historical) To alight from a carriage, a horse, etc. also, to disembark from a vessel; to land.
senses.example: The travelers descended from their carriage at the inn and stretched their stiff legs.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: Synonym of descent (“instance of descending; sloping incline or passage; way down; decline, etc.”).
senses.example: The steep descend through the canyon took nearly three hours on the rocky trail.

core.definition: To move or go downward from a higher place to a lower one, such as down stairs or a hill.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SEND, the second syllable, and the first is a weak schwa. Pronounce the final d clearly rather than dropping it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is more formal and dignified than 'go down'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use descend in formal, literary, and religious contexts, while in everyday talk 'go down' or 'come down' is more natural. The phrase 'descend into' is used figuratively for a deep mood or condition, as in 'descend into chaos'. In ordinary life, you'd more often say 'we walked down the trail'.

distinctions.note: Go down is everyday and flexible, while descend is more formal and suggests a gradual or dignified movement.
Fall suggests a sudden or uncontrolled drop, while descend suggests a deliberate or gradual movement downward.

examples.everyday: We had to descend the steep trail slowly because it had been raining.
examples.professional: The stock price began to descend after the earnings report came out.
examples.analytical: In Plato's allegory of the cave, the philosopher must descend back into the darkness to free the others.

nuance.analogy: To descend is like a lift going down one floor at a time, under control.
nuance.etymology: From Latin descendere, from de- 'down' plus scandere 'to climb'.
common_mistakes: Using descend with a preposition like 'to' in the wrong place; say 'descend the stairs' without 'from' or 'to'.
Saying 'descend down', which is redundant.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek katabainō means 'to go down'. Genesis 11:5 (RSV) says the LORD came down to see the city and the tower of Babel. John 1:51 describes angels ascending and descending upon the Son of man. Ephesians 4:9 says Christ descended into the lower parts of the earth before ascending far above the heavens.

senses.definition: Moving or sloping downwards.
Ordered such that each element is less than or equal to the previous element.
senses.example: Please arrange these numbers in a descending order.

senses.definition: Causing a sequence to follow a descending order.
senses.example: We used a descending sort.

senses.definition: Becoming lower in pitch.
senses.example: The descending notes of the cello faded gently into silence at the end of the piece.

senses.definition: A descent.
senses.example: continual ascendings and descendings

core.definition: Moving or sloping downward, or arranged from highest to lowest value.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, SEN, and the vowel is short like the 'e' in 'bed'. The final -ing is a clear 'ing' sound, with no 'ink' ending.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes direction or order without any judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use descending for stairs, slopes, elevators, and above all for ordering data: 'sort in descending order' means largest first. In everyday talk, 'going down' is more natural than 'descending' for stairs or hills. In data work, 'descending' is the standard word in spreadsheets, code and reports.

distinctions.note: Decreasing describes values getting smaller over time; descending describes an arrangement of items from largest to smallest.
Downward is a general direction word; descending adds the idea of a sequence or steady movement down.

examples.everyday: Can you list the restaurants by rating, in descending order, so the best one is first?
examples.professional: Sort the query results in descending order by revenue so the top accounts show up first.
examples.analytical: A sequence is strictly descending when each term is less than the one before it, so the proof must establish strict inequality at every step.

nuance.analogy: Like a list of finalists ranked from the top score down to the lowest.
nuance.etymology: From Latin descendere, 'to climb down', from de- 'down' plus scandere, 'to climb'.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as 'decending' by dropping the s.
Confusing 'descending order' with 'decreasing order' in code; both can work, but 'descending' is the usual term in SQL and spreadsheets.

senses.definition: A specification of an object or process, referring to requirements to be satisfied and thus conditions to be met for them to solve a problem.
senses.example: The design specifies that the server must handle ten thousand requests per second without failing.

senses.definition: A plan (with more or less detail) for the structure and functions of an artifact, building or system.
senses.example: The initial design of the park was rejected for being too expensive.

senses.definition: A pattern, as an element of a work of art or architecture.
senses.example: We're working on some new designs for our range of summer shirts

senses.definition: The composition of a work of art.
Intention or plot.
senses.example: We have designs on winning the league next season.

senses.definition: The shape or appearance given to an object, especially one that is intended to make it more attractive.
senses.example: I love the clean design of this lamp, with its brushed steel base and soft curve.

senses.definition: The art of designing.
senses.example: Danish furniture design is world-famous.

senses.definition: To plan and carry out (a picture, work of art, construction etc.).
senses.example: comments designed to chip away at my self-esteem

senses.definition: To assign, appoint (something to someone); to designate.
senses.example: The board designed her as interim director until a permanent search could finish.

senses.definition: To manifest requirements to be satisfied by an object or process for them to solve a problem.
senses.example: Good engineers design systems so that failures are contained, not spread.

core.definition: A plan or specification for an object, building, system, or process, showing its structure, features, and how it will work.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, ZINE. The g is silent, so the word ends with a clear 'n' sound. Do not say 'dih-ZIG-n'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. 'Good design' is a strong compliment, while a 'design flaw' is a negative judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'design' constantly, in everyday talk about clothes, furniture, websites, and products, and in technical settings about systems and engineering. As a noun, it can mean the plan, the finished appearance, or a pattern on a surface. In professional talk, people often say 'system design' or 'design review' to refer to the planning stage of a project.

distinctions.note: A blueprint is a detailed technical drawing used to build something; a design is broader and can include the concept, requirements, and overall structure.
Style is the characteristic look or manner of something; design is the deliberate planning behind its form and function.

examples.everyday: I really like the design of this lamp, because it fits the room and doesn't take up much space.
examples.professional: Let's review the system design before we start coding so we don't have to rework the database later.
examples.analytical: Paley's argument from design claims that the order of nature implies a designer, though critics question whether that inference is justified by the evidence.

nuance.analogy: Like a recipe that lists both the ingredients and the steps, a design specifies both what something is made of and how it works.
nuance.etymology: From Italian disegno, from Latin designare, 'to mark out, designate'.
common_mistakes: Using 'design' as a verb with a preposition, as in 'design for the house'; say 'design the house'.
Confusing the noun 'design' (the plan) with the activity 'designing' in sentences about the process.

design.etymology: From Middle English *designen*, from Old French *designer*, from Latin *designō* (“to mark out, point out, describe, design, contrive”), from *de-* (or *dis-*) + *signō* (“to mark”), from *signum* (“mark”).

senses.definition: A function that runs when an object is no longer required, used to release any resources that it was using.
One who destructs.
senses.example: Fire is a destructor of wood, but it also cleanses the forest floor.

senses.definition: A furnace or oven for the burning or carbonizing of refuse.
senses.example: The city's destructor burns hospital waste and garbage at extremely high temperatures.

senses.definition: A taxonomic descriptor, a specific epithet, for naming species that are destructive in some manner.
senses.example: The epithet destructor was chosen for the beetle because it devastates stored timber.

core.definition: In programming, a special method that runs automatically when an object is no longer needed, to release the resources it used.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on STRUK, and the final -or is a reduced vowel close to 'er', with the r pronounced in American speech. Do not say it with a long 'oor' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: In American software engineering, destructor is used mainly in C++ and similar languages, and programmers often say destructor when discussing object cleanup. Outside programming, the word is rare and would sound odd. In everyday talk, the word means nothing special to most Americans.

distinctions.note: A constructor sets up an object when it is created, while a destructor cleans up when it is destroyed.
A garbage collector automatically frees unused memory in many languages, whereas a destructor is a specific method the programmer or language runs for cleanup.

examples.everyday: I'm not sure what a destructor does, so I'll ask the team after lunch.
examples.professional: Make sure the destructor closes the database connection so we don't leak resources in production.
examples.analytical: The lifecycle of a C++ object is symmetric: the constructor establishes its invariants, and the destructor restores the environment it found.

nuance.analogy: A destructor is like a cleanup crew that comes in after a party and puts everything back where it belongs.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin destructor, one who pulls down, from destruere, to pull down.
common_mistakes: Confusing destructor with destroyer, which is a warship or a person who ruins something.
Using it outside programming as if it were a common word for a demolition worker.

senses.definition: A loss of synchronization of brain waves.
The loss or absence of synchronization; asynchronism.

core.definition: The loss of synchronization, when things that moved together, such as brain waves or devices, fall out of step.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on ZAY, with a lighter secondary stress on the first syllable. The middle -ro- and -ni- are reduced to 'ruh' and 'nuh', and the ending is 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a process or state of losing coordination, without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use desynchronization in neuroscience, computing, networking and engineering to describe loss of timing or phase. In everyday speech people say out of sync or off. The word is precise and technical, so using it in ordinary conversation may sound overly formal.

distinctions.note: Asynchrony describes the state of not being synchronous, while desynchronization describes the process or event of losing synchronization.
Jitter is a small, rapid variation in timing, while desynchronization is a more lasting loss of alignment.

examples.everyday: After the power glitch, our smart lights had some desynchronization, so one room lags half a second behind the others.
examples.professional: The desynchronization between the two sensor clocks explains the drift in our time-stamped logs.
examples.analytical: Event-related desynchronization in the alpha band is often read as cortical activation rather than mere inhibition.

nuance.analogy: Desynchronization is like a marching band where some musicians fall behind the beat, and the parade no longer looks unified.
nuance.etymology: From de- (removal) plus synchronization, from Greek syn (together) and chronos (time).
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on the first syllable, as in 'DEE-sink-ruh-nay-shun'; the main stress falls on ZAY.
Misspelling it as 'desynchronisation' in American writing; the American spelling is desynchronization.

senses.definition: Causing damage or harm.
senses.example: Smoking tobacco can be detrimental to your health.

senses.definition: Anything harmful.
senses.example: Constant overtime was the detrimental that finally wore down the whole team.

core.definition: Causing damage or harm to something, especially in a way that weakens or makes it worse.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, MEN. The first syllable is 'det' with a clear t, and the final -al is a reduced syllable that sounds like 'tul'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a harmful effect, often on health, progress, or reputation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use detrimental in workplace emails, reports, news, and health discussions, especially with 'to' or 'for', as in detrimental to morale. In casual talk people more often say 'bad for' or 'harmful'. It sounds professional and measured, so it is a good choice for meetings and formal writing.

distinctions.note: Harmful is more general and everyday; detrimental is more formal and suggests a loss of value or advantage.
Damaging often suggests physical or direct harm; detrimental often describes gradual or indirect harm.
Injurious is formal and legal in tone; detrimental is more common in business and general speech.

examples.everyday: Eating fast food every day can be detrimental to your energy.
examples.professional: Frequent last-minute schedule changes are detrimental to team morale and delivery quality.
examples.analytical: Such a policy is detrimental to public trust because it rewards silence over honest disagreement.

nuance.analogy: A detrimental factor is like a crack in a foundation: it may not break the house at once, but it steadily weakens everything above it.
nuance.etymology: From detriment, from Latin detrimentum, damage, plus the suffix -al.
common_mistakes: Saying 'detrimental for' when 'detrimental to' is the standard preposition.
Pronouncing the stress on the first syllable, giving 'DET-ruh-men-tul'; the main stress is on MEN.

detrimental.etymology: From Medieval Latin **dētrīmentālis*, from Latin *dētrīmentum* (“harm”), from *dēterō* (“to rub off, wear”), from *dē-* (“down, away”) + *terō* (“to rub or grab”).

senses.definition: A type of syllogism of the form "if A is true then B is true; if C is true then D is true; either A or C is true; therefore either B or D is true".
senses.example: The logician's dilemma: if he is honest, he is guilty; if he lies, he is caught.

senses.definition: Offering to an opponent a choice between two (equally unfavorable) alternatives.
senses.example: Her debate tactic was a dilemma: either admit the error or defend an indefensible claim.

senses.definition: A circumstance in which a choice must be made between two or more alternatives that seem equally undesirable.
senses.example: Facing a dilemma, I had to choose between paying rent or paying my car loan.

senses.definition: Any difficult circumstance or problem.
senses.example: Finding affordable childcare has become a dilemma for many working families.

core.definition: A situation in which you must choose between two or more options that all seem unpleasant or unfavorable.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on LEM, the second syllable. The final syllable is a reduced schwa, like 'uh', not a full 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It signals a hard choice with no good option, but it is not necessarily dramatic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say I have a dilemma in everyday conversation, for example when deciding between two good restaurants. Strictly, a dilemma means both options are unpleasant, so reserve it for real trade-offs. Common replies include What are your options? or Which one do you lean toward?

distinctions.note: A problem can have a clear solution, while a dilemma forces a choice between two difficult options.
Predicament is a broader term for any difficult situation, while dilemma focuses specifically on a choice.

examples.everyday: I have a dilemma: I can either go to my cousin's wedding or stay home and finish the taxes.
examples.professional: We face a dilemma: ship the feature on schedule with known bugs, or delay the launch and miss the marketing date.
examples.analytical: Kant's ethics places the moral agent in a dilemma when duty to truth appears to conflict with duty to protect the innocent.

nuance.analogy: Like standing at a fork in a road where both paths are muddy.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin dilemma, from Greek dilemma, a double proposition, from di- two and lemma, premise or assumption.
common_mistakes: Using dilemma for any ordinary problem with a clear answer.
Stressing the first syllable instead of LEM.

dilemma.etymology: First attested 1523, from Late Latin *dilemma*, from Ancient Greek *δίλημμα* (“ambiguous proposition”), from *δι-* (“having two of”) + *λῆμμα* (“premise, proposition”), equivalent to *di-* + *lemma*.

senses.definition: One who directs; the person in charge of managing a department or directorate (e.g. director of engineering), project, or production (as in a show or film, e.g. film director).
A member of a board of directors.
senses.example: The bank's newest director joined the board after a decade in finance.

senses.definition: A counselor, confessor, or spiritual guide.
senses.example: After years of struggle, he finally sought a spiritual director at the seminary.

senses.definition: That which directs or orientates something.
senses.example: Clear goals serve as the director of every decision our team makes.

senses.definition: A component of a Yagi–Uda antenna.
senses.example: The director sits in front of the driven element to boost the antenna's forward gain.

senses.definition: A device that displays graphical information concerning the targets of a weapons system in real time.
senses.example: The radar operator watched the director display track the incoming missile in real time.

senses.definition: The common axis of symmetry of the molecules of a liquid crystal.
senses.example: In a nematic phase, the director points along the average orientation of the molecules.

core.definition: A person who manages or leads a department, project, or production, such as a film director or director of engineering.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, REK. Keep the r sound clear and make the final syllable a light, reduced 'ter' rather than 'tor'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it signals authority and responsibility. It is used for almost any leader of a department or project, so the exact role is usually named with it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use director for the head of a department, a creative lead in film or theater, or a board member, and the job title is often given as director of something (director of marketing). In a casual conversation you can ask someone what they direct, but in a meeting you would normally use a specific title. The word can also mean a spiritual adviser in Catholic and Orthodox settings, though that sense is less common in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: A manager runs daily operations and people, while a director sets strategy and oversees several managers or a whole function.
A supervisor oversees a small group of workers directly, a lower and more hands-on role than a director.
A chair presides over a board or committee meeting, while a director is a member of the board or leads an organization.

examples.everyday: My sister is a film director, so she is always traveling to shoot on location.
examples.professional: Dana was promoted to director of data engineering last month, so she now approves our hiring plans.
examples.analytical: The director of a modern institution must balance the authority of the office against the autonomy of the professionals who carry out its mission.

nuance.analogy: A director is like the conductor of an orchestra: many players do the work, but the conductor sets the tempo and keeps everyone together.
nuance.etymology: From Latin dirigere, to direct, from dis- apart plus regere to lead straight.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable of dirigere-style forms incorrectly; in director the stress is on REK, not on the final syllable.
Using director for a manager of daily work; in American offices a director usually sits one level higher.

director.etymology: Middle French *directeur* and its source Late Latin *dīrēctor*, from Latin *dīrēctus*.

senses.definition: A soiling or making dirty.

core.definition: The act or process of soiling something or making it dirty.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the vowel r-colored. The 'y' becomes a clear 'ee' sound before '-ing', so do not add an extra 'j' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, depending on whether the soiling is accidental or deliberate.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'dirtying' as a noun in daily speech; they say 'getting something dirty' or 'the dirt.' It is more natural as a gerund in a sentence, such as 'the dirtying of the lens.' It sounds slightly technical or literary as a noun.

distinctions.note: Soiling is a more formal or legal word for dirtying, often used for clothing or property.
Staining implies a mark that is hard to remove; dirtying is the general process of making something unclean.

examples.everyday: Kids' hands cause a constant dirtying of the walls, so we repaint every spring.
examples.professional: The dirtying of the sensor lens is a common cause of image errors in the pipeline.
examples.analytical: For medieval writers, the dirtying of the sacred vessel through worldly contact was a symbol of sin.

nuance.analogy: The dirtying of something is like rust forming on metal: it happens slowly, through contact, until the surface changes.
nuance.etymology: From 'dirty' (Middle English 'dritty') plus the suffix '-ing'.
common_mistakes: Using 'dirtying' as a common noun in everyday talk, where 'getting dirty' or 'the dirt' is more natural.
Confusing 'dirtying' with 'dirtiness'; dirtying is the act, dirtiness is the state.

senses.definition: A thin, flat, circular plate or similar object.
senses.example: A coin is a disc of metal.

senses.definition: Something resembling a disc.
senses.example: Venus's disc cut off light from the Sun.

senses.definition: A vinyl phonograph or gramophone record.
senses.example: Turn the disc over, after it has finished.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of flying disc; synonym of frisbee; generic name for the trademark Frisbee.
An intervertebral disc.
senses.example: The MRI showed a herniated disc pressing on the nerve in his lower back.

senses.definition: The flat surface of an organ, as a leaf, any flat, round growth.
senses.example: The flat disc of the sunflower attracted bees from across the entire field.

senses.definition: To harrow with a disc harrow.
senses.example: Before planting, the farmer disced the field twice to break up the hard soil.

senses.definition: To move towards, or operate at, zero blade pitch, orienting the propeller blades face-on to the oncoming airflow and maximizing the drag generated by the propeller.
senses.example: In the air, the asymmetric drag generated by a discing propeller can result in loss of control of the airplane.

core.definition: A thin, flat, round object, such as a CD or DVD, or a round flat part in machinery.

pronunciation.tip: Say it in one syllable with a short i and a clear final k. Do not add a vowel after the k, and do not confuse it with 'desk' (/dɛsk/), which has a short e.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word carries no emotional charge; it names a physical or technical object.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use disc for CDs, DVDs, brake discs, and a herniated or slipped disc in the spine, but they spell it disk for computer storage such as hard disk or floppy disk. In everyday talk, people usually say CD or DVD rather than disc by itself. The phrases disc jockey and disc golf also use disc.
word_family: disk (noun, US spelling for computer storage)

distinctions.note: In American English, disk is the standard spelling for computer storage, while disc is used for CDs, DVDs and physical round objects.
A plate is usually a flat dish or a flat sheet of metal, while a disc is specifically thin and round, often with a central part or hole.

examples.everyday: I burned our old vacation photos onto a disc so my mom could watch them on her TV.
examples.professional: The vendor sent the firmware update on a disc, but we install updates over the network now.
examples.analytical: In geometry, a disc is the region enclosed by a circle, including its interior rather than just its edge.

nuance.analogy: Like a coin or a pizza: thin, flat and round.
nuance.etymology: From Latin discus, a quoit or throwing plate, from Greek diskos.
common_mistakes: Spelling computer storage as disc; in American English, use disk for a hard disk or floppy disk.
Confusing disc with desk; the vowel in disc is a short i, while desk has a short e.

disc.etymology: From French *disque*, from Latin *discus*, from Ancient Greek *δίσκος* (“disk, quoit, platter”).

related: disk (noun, US spelling for computer storage)

senses.definition: In a disconcerting manner; upsettingly.

core.definition: In a way that unsettles or upsets someone, often because it is unexpected or hard to explain.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on -SUR-, and the -ing and -ly endings are light. The final -ly sounds like 'lee', with a clear, short vowel. Avoid stressing the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative; it describes something that unsettles without being alarming.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use disconcertingly to describe something strange or unsettling in a way that is hard to pin down: 'The room was disconcertingly quiet.' It appears more often in writing and news than in casual talk. In speech people might say really creepy or kind of weird instead.

distinctions.note: Unnervingly stresses fear or nerves; disconcertingly stresses surprise and disruption of expectations.
Disturbingly is stronger and more serious, often suggesting moral or emotional alarm.

examples.everyday: The guy at the counter was disconcertingly friendly, like he already knew me.
examples.professional: The latency numbers were disconcertingly low, so we reran the tests before trusting them.
examples.analytical: The narrator is disconcertingly calm about events that should horrify, which unsettles the reader's moral expectations.

nuance.analogy: Like a familiar song played in the wrong key: you recognize it, but something is off.
nuance.etymology: From disconcerting plus -ly, from disconcert.
common_mistakes: Using the adverb where an adjective is needed: say a disconcerting result, not a disconcertingly result.
Stressing the wrong syllable; the main stress is on -SUR-, not on the first syllable.

senses.definition: An inconsistency between facts or sentiments.
senses.example: They found a discrepancy between the first set of test results and the second, and they're still trying to figure out why.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being discrepant.
senses.example: There is a discrepancy between the sales figures in the report and the bank statements.

core.definition: A difference or mismatch between things that should agree, such as figures, reports or accounts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, SKREH. The middle -an- reduces to a weak 'uh' sound, so do not pronounce each vowel strongly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative: it signals a problem to be checked, not an accusation.
nuance.usage_note: In American offices, discrepancy is standard for numbers that do not match, as in 'There's a discrepancy in the invoice.' It sounds calm and professional, softer than 'error' or 'fraud,' so it works well in meetings. In casual talk people often say 'something doesn't add up.'

distinctions.note: A difference is any variation; a discrepancy is a difference that should not exist, such as between two totals that ought to match.
An error is a mistake; a discrepancy is an observed mismatch that may reveal an error and may not yet be explained.

examples.everyday: There's a discrepancy between my bank statement and my receipts, so I'm calling them today.
examples.professional: We found a discrepancy between the test results and the production logs, so I'm holding the release.
examples.analytical: The discrepancy between the two gospel accounts has provoked centuries of harmonizing attempts and of careful source criticism.

nuance.analogy: Like two clocks showing different times: you know one is wrong, and you must check which.
nuance.etymology: From Latin discrepare, to be discordant, from dis- plus crepare, to rattle or sound.
common_mistakes: Using discrepancy for a difference of opinion; it implies facts that should agree.
Using discrepancy with when comparing two things; the usual pattern is discrepancy between or discrepancy in.
patterns: [C, U] a discrepancy between X and Y

senses.definition: To convert (a continuous space) into an equivalent discrete space, often for the purposes of easier calculation.
senses.example: We discretize the time axis into one-minute intervals so the simulation runs faster.

senses.definition: To represent (any spectrum of reality) as a set of discrete categories or classes; to categorize (a spectral aspect of reality) by lumping together some of its finer distinctions.
senses.example: A rainbow truly contains thousands of color values but can usually be discretized by human sentience into bands of primary and secondary colors.

core.definition: To convert a continuous space, range or variable into a finite set of discrete values or categories, so it can be computed or classified.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable (DIS-kruh-tyz), unlike discrete (dih-SKREET), which stresses the second. Pronounce the r and reduce the middle vowel to a schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge; it describes a method, not a judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use discretize mainly in mathematics, statistics, engineering and data science, such as in numerical methods or machine learning. In casual talk people say 'round off' or 'put into groups' instead. In a meeting, saying you will discretize a variable signals that you are turning a numeric feature into bins or categories.

distinctions.note: Discrete is an adjective meaning separate and distinct; discretize is the verb for making something discrete.
Discreet means tactful or careful about privacy. It sounds the same as discrete in some pronunciations but has an entirely different meaning.
Quantize is common in signal processing and computing for mapping values onto fixed levels; discretize is the broader mathematical term.

examples.everyday: My daughter asked why the app shows height in whole inches, and I said it's basically discretizing the numbers, which made her roll her eyes.
examples.professional: Before we feed the income column into the decision tree, we'll discretize it into four bins.
examples.analytical: Any model that discretizes a continuous space discards information about the distances between its points, and that loss must be justified.

nuance.analogy: Like replacing a smooth dimmer switch with a three-position light switch: you lose the in-between settings but gain something simple to work with.
nuance.etymology: From discrete (Latin discretus, separated) plus the verb-forming suffix -ize.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as in discrete (dih-SKREET); the verb stresses the first syllable.
Confusing it with discreet, which means tactful or private.

senses.definition: To vomit or spew, to discharge.
senses.example: After the rough boat ride, the sailor began to disgorge his lunch over the rail.

senses.definition: To surrender (stolen goods or money, for example) unwillingly.
To remove traces of yeast from sparkling wine by the méthode champenoise.
senses.example: The winery will disgorge each bottle of its vintage sparkling wine after aging for three years.

core.definition: To pour out or discharge something forcefully, or to hand over something unwillingly, such as stolen money.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the single syllable -GORJ. The 'r' is pronounced clearly in General American, and the final sound is a soft 'j' like 'judge'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests forceful or unwilling release, often with an unpleasant image.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'disgorge' mainly in literary, journalistic, or formal writing. In everyday speech, people say 'throw up' for vomiting, or 'hand over' and 'give back' for returning money. The word is vivid, so use it carefully in conversation.

distinctions.note: Vomit is the everyday word for throwing up; disgorge is more literary and can describe any forceful discharge, not only sickness.
Emit means to release something such as light or gas; disgorge suggests a larger, more forceful outpouring.

examples.everyday: After he ate too much, he was sick and nearly disgorged everything at the table.
examples.professional: The court ordered the company to disgorge the profits it earned from the illegal contracts.
examples.analytical: The novel's narrator describes the city's subway tunnels disgorging crowds into the rainy morning streets.

nuance.analogy: Like a pipe that suddenly bursts and spills out everything inside, disgorge describes something pouring out with force.
nuance.etymology: From Old French desgorger, from des- (out) plus gorge (throat).
common_mistakes: Using 'disgorge' in casual conversation where 'throw up' or 'give back' would sound more natural.
Confusing 'disgorge' with 'digest' or 'absorb'; disgorge means to release, not to take in.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being disheveled.

core.definition: The state of being untidy or disordered, especially in one's hair, clothing or general appearance.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SHEV, the second syllable. The middle syllables reduce to weak vowels, and the final -ment is a quick 'muhnt'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative, depending on whether the disorder seems careless or charming.
nuance.usage_note: This noun is rare in American conversation. Americans usually say 'messy hair', 'rumpled look' or 'disheveled appearance' instead. You are more likely to find it in writing, such as descriptions in novels or formal reports.

distinctions.note: Disarray is a more general noun for disorder and can apply to plans or rooms, while dishevelment usually refers to a person's appearance.
Messiness is the common everyday noun; dishevelment is more formal and emphasizes the disordered look.

examples.professional: The dishevelment of the office after the move made it hard to find anything for a week.
examples.analytical: The novel's dishevelment of narrative time reflects the protagonist's psychological fragmentation.

nuance.analogy: Like a room after a party, when nothing is in its place.
nuance.etymology: From dishevel plus the noun ending -ment.
common_mistakes: Confusing the noun 'dishevelment' with the adjective 'disheveled'.
Using it in casual speech where 'messy look' sounds more natural to Americans.

senses.definition: Treatment with disinfectant materials in order to destroy harmful microorganisms.
senses.example: Proper hand washing and surface disinfection helped the clinic stop the outbreak.

core.definition: The process of killing harmful germs on surfaces, water, or objects, using chemicals, heat, or ultraviolet light.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the FEK syllable, and pronounce the final -tion as shun. The ih vowels in the first syllables are short and quick.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a process, often in health, public safety, or water treatment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use disinfection in healthcare, cleaning, water treatment, and public health news. In everyday talk people more often say cleaning or wiping things down, but disinfection is the standard term in official guidance. A natural sentence might be The hospital increased disinfection of door handles during flu season.

distinctions.note: Sanitation refers to keeping conditions clean and safe overall, often in sewage and food systems; disinfection is a specific step that kills microbes.
Sterilization kills all microorganisms, including spores; disinfection kills most but not necessarily all.

examples.everyday: After the flood, the city posted notices about boiling water and disinfection tablets.
examples.professional: Our facilities team scheduled deep disinfection of the break room every Friday.
examples.analytical: The debate over disinfection by-products shows how public health gains can carry unexpected chemical costs.

nuance.analogy: Like a final rinse after washing: it is the step that removes the remaining threat.
nuance.etymology: From disinfect, with the suffix -ion denoting a process or result.
common_mistakes: Using disinfection as a verb, instead of disinfect
Using a disinfection with an article in general statements when the uncountable form is intended
Confusing disinfection with sterilization in technical writing

senses.definition: A process by which anything disintegrates.
senses.example: The disintegration of the old wooden bridge began after decades of salt corrosion and neglect.

senses.definition: The condition of anything which has disintegrated.
senses.example: Engineers inspected the disintegration of the concrete pillars after the hurricane passed through town.

senses.definition: The radioactive decay of a single atom.
senses.example: The sample exhibited an activity of three disintegrations per second.

senses.definition: The wearing away or falling to pieces of rocks or strata, produced by atmospheric action, frost, ice, etc.
senses.example: Frost wedging contributed to the disintegration of the granite cliffs over thousands of years.

senses.definition: The process of radioactive decay.
senses.example: The sample exhibited an activity of three disintegrations per second.

core.definition: The process of breaking apart into smaller pieces, or of losing unity and cohesion until a whole no longer holds together.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on GRAY, the fourth syllable, and the middle syllables 'in-tuh' are quick and reduced. The -tion ending is pronounced 'shun', not 'tee-on'.

nuance.connotation: Negative in everyday and social uses, suggesting loss of order or collapse; neutral in physics and chemistry.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word for physical breakup, such as rock, ceramics, or an old structure, for social or political collapse, such as the disintegration of a marriage or an empire, and for nuclear decay in science. In casual conversation people usually say 'falling apart', which is more natural. The word sounds heavy and formal, so use it when the breakdown is serious.

distinctions.note: Decay suggests rot or gradual chemical change; disintegration emphasizes breaking into separate parts or losing unity.
Collapse is usually sudden; disintegration is often gradual, with the whole coming apart over time.
Breakdown often refers to a machine or a person's health; disintegration suggests a total loss of structure or cohesion.

examples.everyday: The old porch is in total disintegration after that storm, so please don't stand on it.
examples.professional: The sprint reviews showed a gradual disintegration of ownership after the reorganization, and nobody was sure who owned the service anymore.
examples.analytical: Many sociologists read the disintegration of shared norms as a symptom of rapid social change rather than a simple moral failure.

nuance.analogy: Like a sandcastle after the tide comes in: the grains are still there, but the shape they held is gone.
nuance.etymology: From disintegrate + -ion, from dis- (apart) + integrare 'make whole' (from integer 'whole').
common_mistakes: Putting the primary stress on the first or second syllable instead of GRAY.
Using disintegration for minor wear, such as a small scratch or stain; the word implies serious breakdown.

senses.definition: The act of disowning.
senses.example: Her father's disownment after the wedding left her estranged from the entire family for years.

core.definition: The formal act of rejecting a family member or refusing to acknowledge a connection to a person, group, or decision.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on OHN, and the final -ment is reduced to a weak syllable, pronounced ment. Do not add an extra vowel after the n, which can make the word sound like three syllables.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it describes a painful rejection or break in a relationship.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use disownment in casual conversation. They usually say was disowned or cut off. The noun appears more in formal writing, legal or family discussions, and literary contexts, and it describes the act or fact of disowning someone.

distinctions.note: Disinheritance is a legal removal from a will or estate; disownment is a personal or social rejection, which may or may not include legal action.
Disavowal is a public denial of responsibility or belief; disownment usually concerns a family or personal bond.

examples.professional: The company's disownment of the campaign came quickly after the ad went viral for the wrong reasons.
examples.analytical: Hegel would read the disownment of a child by a parent as a moment of alienation within the family, a rupture that both sides must struggle to overcome.

nuance.analogy: A disownment is like a door shut firmly from the inside: the connection still exists in memory, but the family no longer lets it through.
nuance.etymology: From disown and the suffix -ment, denoting an act or result.
common_mistakes: Using disownment as a verb, as in He disownment his son; the verb is disown.
Using disownment in everyday speech where disowned is more natural.

senses.definition: Not respectable, lacking repute; discreditable.
A person who is not reputable.
senses.example: Nobody trusted the disreputable who hung around the docks offering cheap watches.

core.definition: Having a bad reputation; not respectable or trustworthy in the eyes of others.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on -REP-, and the American r is clear before the vowel. Non-native speakers often stress the final syllable or drop the reduced vowels in the -table ending.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes someone or something with a poor reputation, and it can be used strongly or lightly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use disreputable for people, businesses, or places that are not trusted or respected, as in 'a disreputable lawyer'. In casual talk they might say shady or sketchy. It is a fairly strong word, so use it carefully when talking about real people.

distinctions.note: Shady is informal and suggests dishonesty or a questionable deal. Disreputable is more formal and refers to a general bad reputation.
Unreliable means not dependable in performance. Disreputable means not respected or trusted because of character or conduct.

examples.everyday: My neighbor warned me to stay away from that pawn shop because the owner has a disreputable history.
examples.professional: We should drop that vendor because their billing practices are disreputable and could expose us to legal risk.
examples.analytical: Many philosophers have defended the disreputable sophist, arguing that his reputation obscures his actual contributions to rhetoric.

nuance.analogy: A disreputable place is like a restaurant with a bad review on every site: people may still walk in, but they expect trouble.
nuance.etymology: From dis- (not) and reputable, from Latin reputare, to consider again.
common_mistakes: Confusing disreputable (bad reputation) with unreputable, which is not a standard English word.
Using the adjective as a noun without the article; say a disreputable person or the disreputable.

senses.definition: To disagree; to withhold assent. Construed with from (or, formerly, to).
senses.example: Several board members dissented from the decision to close the downtown branch.

senses.definition: To differ from, especially in opinion, beliefs, etc.
senses.example: Many theologians dissent on the question of whether scripture should be read literally.

senses.definition: Disagreement with the ideas, doctrines, decrees, etc. of a political party, government or religion.
senses.example: ethnopolitical dissent

senses.definition: An act of disagreeing with, or deviating from, the views and opinions of those holding authority.
senses.example: Her dissent against the new policy was quiet but firm and well documented.

senses.definition: A separate opinion filed in a case by judges who disagree with the outcome of the majority of the court in that case.
senses.example: The justice's dissent argued that the majority had misread the statute entirely.

senses.definition: A violation that arises when disagreement with an official call is expressed in an inappropriate manner such as foul language, rude gestures, or failure to comply.
senses.example: The umpire assessed a technical foul for dissent after the player shouted at him.

core.definition: Public disagreement with an official decision, policy, or the views of a group or authority.

pronunciation.tip: Noun stress is on the first syllable, DIS-sent. As a verb, it is dih-SENT, so the stress shifts to the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive in democratic contexts, since dissent is often seen as a healthy part of public life, but can be negative in authoritarian or workplace settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dissent for political disagreement, court opinions and public debate, such as 'a voice of dissent' or 'a dissent in the Supreme Court'. In everyday speech, you might say 'I disagree' or 'I'm not on board'. The word is widely respected in the US because the First Amendment protects dissent, but it can sound formal in casual office chat.

distinctions.note: Disagreement is a general word for not agreeing; dissent often implies a formal or public objection to an official decision or authority.
Opposition usually means an organized group actively working against something; dissent can be an individual or minority view.

examples.everyday: There was a lot of dissent at the neighborhood meeting about the new parking rules.
examples.professional: Two engineers filed written dissent before the architecture review was approved.
examples.analytical: The dissent argues that the majority misread the statute and ignored the original intent of the law.

nuance.analogy: Like a single note played against a choir: it stands out, and it shows that the song is not unanimous.
nuance.etymology: From Latin dissentire, 'to disagree', from dis- (apart) and sentire (to feel or think).
common_mistakes: Using the noun pronunciation for the verb: the verb is dih-SENT, with stress on the second syllable.
Using dissent to mean any small disagreement in casual talk; it sounds stiff and political.

dissent.etymology: From Middle English *dissenten*, from Latin *dissentiō* (“to differ in sentiments, disagree, be at odds, contradict, quarrel”), from *dis-* + *sentiō*.

senses.definition: The golden section.

core.definition: The golden ratio, about 1.618, in which the whole relates to the larger part as the larger part relates to the smaller.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on -POR- in proportion, and divine has a weaker secondary stress. The first syllable of proportion is a reduced 'pruh', not 'pro' or 'pra'. Link the two words smoothly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly mystical. The term suggests cosmic beauty, which some enthusiasts exaggerate, so scientific writers often prefer golden ratio.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say golden ratio or golden section in most technical and modern writing. Divine proportion is older and appears in art history, Renaissance studies, and popular writing about harmony. Use it when you want historical or mystical flavor, but in mathematics and design the golden ratio is the standard term.

distinctions.note: They are the same number; golden ratio is the modern standard term, while divine proportion is older and more mystical.
Aspect ratio is the width-to-height relation of an image or screen, which is a technical measurement, not a special number like the golden ratio.
The ratios of successive Fibonacci numbers approach the golden ratio, but the sequence itself is a different mathematical object.

collocations: the divine proportion of the rectangle

examples.everyday: My friend who studied architecture keeps talking about the divine proportion, but I mostly hear about the golden ratio.
examples.professional: The design team used the golden ratio, which some people still call the divine proportion, to set the layout grid.
examples.analytical: Pacioli's 1509 treatise presents the divine proportion as a sign of God's order in geometry and art.

nuance.analogy: Like a rectangle that, once you cut off a square, leaves another rectangle of the same shape: the pattern repeats at a smaller scale.
nuance.etymology: Named by Luca Pacioli in his 1509 book De divina proportione, from Latin divina (divine) and proportio (proportion).
common_mistakes: Using the plural divine proportions as if there were many; in technical use it is one ratio.
Treating the divine proportion as a fixed law of nature; many claims about its presence in art and biology are overstated.
Confusing it with aspect ratio, which is a screen or image measurement.

senses.definition: Someone who dodges (avoids something by quickly moving).
senses.example: Our best dodger ducked every snowball thrown at him during the recess game.

senses.definition: A person full of tricks or street smarts.
senses.example: That kid is a real dodger, so don't try to fool him with a fake story.

senses.definition: An advertising leaflet; a flyer.
senses.example: The grocery store slipped a dodger about weekend sales under our apartment door.

senses.definition: A frame-supported canvas over the companionway (entrance) of a sailboat providing the on-deck crew partial cover from the splashes of the seas that break against the hull of the boat.
senses.example: The crew stayed dry under the dodger while spray from the waves hit the hull.

senses.definition: Bread.
senses.example: Pass the dodger, would you? I need something to soak up this stew.

core.definition: A person who avoids something, especially a duty, payment, or responsibility, often by dishonest means.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final -er is a rhotic American 'r' sound that is reduced and often not fully pronounced, so it sounds like 'DAH-jer'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes someone who avoids obligations, often unethically. It can also be a neutral word for a quick-moving person in some contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use 'dodger' in phrases like 'tax dodger' or 'draft dodger' for people who evade obligations. In everyday speech you might hear 'a ticket dodger' for someone who avoids paying for transit. Be aware that 'Dodgers' also means the Los Angeles baseball team, so capitalization and context matter.

distinctions.note: 'Evader' is more formal and general, while 'dodger' is more informal and often used in compound phrases like 'tax dodger'.
'Tax evader' is the formal legal term, while 'tax dodger' is common in journalism and everyday speech.

examples.everyday: My neighbor calls him a tax dodger, but I think that's a bit harsh.
examples.professional: The compliance team flagged several vendors as potential tax dodgers during the audit.
examples.analytical: The label of 'dodger' carries a moral judgment that the bare act of avoiding a duty does not always justify.

nuance.analogy: Like a magician who slips past the audience's attention, a dodger avoids what everyone expects them to pay or do.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'dodger' (someone who avoids) with 'the Dodgers' (the baseball team), which requires a capital D and the plural.
Using 'dodger' for a physical avoider; in most contexts it refers to a person avoiding responsibility or payment.

senses.definition: Like a dolt; dull in intellect; stupid.

core.definition: Slow-witted, foolish, or dull in understanding; acting like a dolt.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The ending -ish is a short 'ish,' not 'eesh,' and the 'o' is the 'ah' of 'hot.'

nuance.connotation: Negative and insulting. It implies someone is stupid or clueless, so it can sound harsh when used about a person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'doltish' mostly in writing, criticism, or humorous speech. In everyday talk, 'dumb,' 'clueless,' or 'dim' is more common. Calling someone doltish directly is a strong insult, so use it with care.

distinctions.note: Stupid is the general, common word for lacking intelligence or good judgment. Doltish suggests a dull, slow, foolish quality and sounds more literary.
Obtuse is formal and means slow to understand or insensitive. Doltish is more insulting and suggests silliness.

examples.everyday: I felt pretty doltish for leaving my keys in the car again.
examples.professional: Skipping the code review was a doltish decision that caused the outage, and everyone knew it.
examples.analytical: Satire often exposes the doltish certainty of officials who mistake confidence for competence.

nuance.analogy: A doltish mind is like a dull knife: it cannot cut through the problem, no matter how hard it presses.
nuance.etymology: From dolt, from Middle English dold, 'stupefied,' the past participle of dullen (to dull), with the suffix -ish meaning 'like.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ending as 'eesh' instead of 'ish.'
Using 'doltish' as a playful word for minor mistakes, when it is a strong insult.

senses.definition: To be weakly or foolishly fond of somebody.
senses.example: Little Bill's parents just keep doting on him.

senses.definition: Decay in a tree.
senses.example: The arborist found dote spreading through the heartwood of the old maple.

senses.definition: Dowry.
senses.example: Her father set aside a generous dote for each daughter's marriage.

core.definition: To love someone in an excessive, almost foolish way; to be overly fond of a person or thing.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the long "oh" diphthong, and the word has one syllable. The final "t" is clear. Don't add an extra "uh" sound at the end.

nuance.connotation: Warm or teasing. It usually describes affection that looks excessive or indulgent, and it can sound slightly mocking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "dote" mostly in the phrase "dote on," often about grandparents with grandchildren or pet owners with their animals. It is warm and a bit old-fashioned, so it sounds natural in family conversation. In everyday speech you might also hear "spoil" or "adore."

distinctions.note: "Adore" is an enthusiastic word for strong love, while "dote" suggests affection so intense that it seems indulgent.
"Spoil" means to give too much and damage someone's character, while "dote" describes the feeling behind the indulgence.

examples.everyday: My grandmother totally doted on my little cousin, buying him a toy every time we visited.
examples.professional: Our manager doted on the new hires, so they had less accountability than the rest of the team.
examples.analytical: The narrator doted on the past, idealizing a childhood that the reader can see was far from perfect.

nuance.analogy: To dote is like wrapping a gift so many times that the wrapping becomes the main thing you notice.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English doten, "to be foolish," probably from Old Norse or Germanic roots related to "dotard."
common_mistakes: Saying "dote to" or "dote with" instead of "dote on."
Confusing "dote" with "dot," which is pronounced differently and has no connection to affection.

dote.etymology: The verb is derived from Middle English *doten*, from *doten* (“to be foolish”) or Middle Dutch *doten* (“to be silly”).

senses.definition: Robust, sturdy; strong and perhaps stout.
senses.example: The doughty old farmer hauled the heavy sacks onto the truck without any help.

senses.definition: Catachresis for dowdy.
senses.example: Her doughty brown suit made her look old-fashioned at the interview.

core.definition: Brave, strong and determined, especially in a sturdy, admirable way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the gh is silent. The ending is a light 'tee' sound, not 'ty'.

nuance.connotation: Positive, but old-fashioned and admiring.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use doughty in everyday speech; it appears in literature, history writing and sometimes about older people with hardy spirit. It sounds warm and a little old-fashioned, so use it to praise someone's courage or persistence. Do not confuse it with dowdy, which is a different and negative word.

distinctions.note: Dowdy means shabby and unfashionable in appearance, while doughty means brave and sturdy; the two are not interchangeable.
Brave is common and neutral, while doughty is literary and emphasizes sturdiness together with courage.

examples.everyday: My grandpa is a doughty old guy who still shovels his own driveway in January.
examples.professional: Our doughty team kept the project alive through three budget cuts and two reorganizations.
examples.analytical: The doughty resistance of small farmers reshaped the policy debate and forced the government to reconsider its assumptions.

nuance.analogy: Like an old oak tree that bends in a storm but keeps its roots deep and does not break.
nuance.etymology: From Old English dohtig, meaning strong or capable, from dugan, to be good for or to avail.
common_mistakes: Confusing doughty with dowdy, which has the opposite positive sense.
Confusing doughty with doughy, which describes soft, dough-like texture.

doughty.etymology: The adjective is derived from Middle English *doughty* (“brave, bold, valiant”), from Old English *dohtiġ*, *dyhtiġ* (“competent, good, strong, valiant”), from **duhtīg*.

senses.definition: A file transfer to a given computer or device from a remote one through a network connection.
senses.example: The download took longer than I expected.

senses.definition: A file that has been or is intended to be transferred in this way.
senses.example: I got the download but it wouldn't work on my computer.

senses.definition: To transfer data to a given computer from a remote one via a network.
senses.example: You can download a trial version of the program for thirty days to determine whether you want to purchase the full version.

senses.definition: Synonym of upload: to send data from a given computer to a remote one.
senses.example: She downloaded the final report to the client's server before the midnight deadline.

senses.definition: Synonym of copy: to transfer data to or from removable media.
senses.example: When I was your age, there were no flash drives. I needed to download photos to a CD-ROM.

senses.definition: Synonym of install: to load software forced.
senses.example: Our IT team had to download the printer driver onto each laptop by hand.

senses.definition: To load a gun (especially a muzzle-loader) with less propellant than its designed load.
senses.example: The old hunter always downloaded his muzzle-loader to reduce recoil on cold mornings.

senses.definition: To transfer jurisdiction and responsibility of a government asset or service to a lower level of government.
senses.example: The state agreed to download the rural road program to county governments.

senses.definition: To be downloaded.
senses.example: Don't close this window. Your messages are dowloading.

core.definition: To copy a file or program from the internet or another computer onto your own device.

pronunciation.tip: Stress DOWN with a lighter secondary stress on LOAD. The vowel in load is a long 'oh' sound, and the final d is clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a routine technical action with no positive or negative tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use download constantly for apps, movies, PDFs, and music: 'I downloaded the boarding pass.' It can also be a noun: 'That update is a big download.' Its opposite is upload, which sends files from your device to a server.

distinctions.note: Upload means sending a file from your device to another computer or server, while download means receiving a file onto your device.
Streaming plays content as it arrives without keeping a copy, while downloading saves a complete copy on your device.
Installing sets up downloaded software so it can run, and it usually comes after downloading.

examples.everyday: Can you download the map before we leave, in case we lose signal on the highway?
examples.professional: Please download the latest build from the shared drive before the sprint review on Thursday.
examples.analytical: Downloading a dataset is trivial, but verifying its provenance and licensing is the harder epistemic task.

nuance.analogy: Like taking a book off a library shelf and bringing a copy home to keep.
nuance.etymology: From down (toward the receiver) and load; the computing sense developed in late twentieth-century computing.
common_mistakes: Using download for sending files out; that action is upload.
Pronouncing the second syllable like 'loud' instead of 'lohd'.

senses.definition: The characteristic of being drab.
senses.example: The drabness of the office walls made the long afternoons feel even longer.

core.definition: The quality of being dull and colorless, or lacking interest and excitement.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final syllable is a reduced schwa, so say it as a short 'nuhs', not a strong 'ness' with a clear e.

nuance.connotation: Negative, describing a dull or colorless quality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use drabness mostly in writing and reviews to describe the dullness of a place, a design or a way of life, as in 'the drabness of the office'. It is more formal than saying it's so boring. In conversation, people usually say the place is drab or dreary rather than using the noun.

distinctions.note: Dullness is a general lack of interest, while drabness adds the sense of missing color or cheer in appearance.
Dreariness suggests gloom and depression, often from weather or circumstances, while drabness is about visual or cultural dullness.

examples.everyday: After a week of gray rain, I was tired of the drabness of the office.
examples.professional: The brand refresh was meant to fix the drabness of our product packaging.
examples.analytical: Her novel captures the drabness of postwar factory towns, where routine seems to erase individual color.

nuance.analogy: Drabness is like a room where someone turned off the lights and dimmed every color.
nuance.etymology: From drab (adjective) plus the suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Giving the final syllable a strong e sound; it is a reduced vowel.
Using drabness to describe someone's personality; it is clearer to say a person is dull.

senses.definition: To create (a hole) by removing material with a drill (tool).
senses.example: Drill a small hole to start the screw in the right direction.

senses.definition: To practice, especially in (or as in) a military context.
senses.example: They drilled daily to learn the routine exactly.

senses.definition: To cause to drill (practice); to train, especially in military arts.
senses.example: The sergeant was up by 6:00 every morning, drilling his troops.

senses.definition: To repeat an idea frequently in order to encourage someone to remember it.
senses.example: The instructor drilled into us the importance of reading the instructions.

senses.definition: To investigate or examine something in more detail or at a different level.
senses.example: Drill deeper and you may find the underlying assumptions faulty.

senses.definition: To throw, run, hit or kick with a lot of power.
senses.example: He drilled down the court and made a three-pointer.

senses.definition: To have sexual intercourse with; to penetrate.
To shoot; to kill by shooting.
senses.example: Deputies warned that they would drill any armed intruder who refused to drop the weapon.

senses.definition: To sow (seeds) by dribbling them along a furrow or in a row.
senses.example: Each spring, the farmer would drill corn seeds in neat rows behind the old tractor.

senses.definition: To cause to flow in drills or rills or by trickling; to drain by trickling.
senses.example: waters drilled through a sandy stratum

senses.definition: To hit someone with a pitch, especially in an intentional context.
senses.example: The reliever was ejected after he drilled the batter in the ribs with a fastball.

senses.definition: A tool or machine used to remove material so as to create a hole, typically by plunging a rotating cutting bit into a stationary workpiece.
senses.example: Wear safety glasses when operating an electric drill.

senses.definition: The portion of a drilling tool that drives the bit.
senses.example: Use a drill with a wire brush to remove any rust or buildup.

senses.definition: An activity done as an exercise or practice (especially a military exercise), particularly in preparation for some possible future event or occurrence.
senses.example: fire drill

senses.definition: A short and highly repeatable sports training exercise designed to hone a particular skill that may be useful in competition.
senses.example: At today's practice, the football team performed a variety of goalkeeping drills.

senses.definition: Any of several molluscs, of the genus Urosalpinx and others, especially the oyster drill (Urosalpinx cinerea), that make holes in the shells of their prey.
senses.example: Oyster farmers in the Chesapeake worry about drills, which bore neat round holes into shells.

senses.definition: An agricultural implement for making holes for sowing seed, and sometimes so formed as to contain seeds and drop them into the hole made.
senses.example: The farmer hitched the old seed drill to the tractor and rolled across the field.

senses.definition: A light furrow or channel made to put seed into, when sowing.
senses.example: Keep the drill straight and shallow so the seeds land at an even depth.

senses.definition: A row of seed sown in a furrow.
senses.example: Each drill of beans came up evenly, so the field looked perfectly planted from the road.

senses.definition: An Old World monkey of West Africa, Mandrillus leucophaeus, similar in appearance to the mandrill, but lacking the colorful face.
senses.example: The zoologist spotted a drill foraging near the river, its face plainer than a mandrill's.

senses.definition: A strong, durable cotton fabric with a strong bias (diagonal) in the weave.
senses.example: The tailor recommended heavy cotton drill for the work pants, since it holds up to daily wear.

senses.definition: A style of trap music with gritty, violent lyrics, originating on the South Side of Chicago.
senses.example: Drill has roots on Chicago's South Side, and its gritty lyrics reflect neighborhood life.

senses.definition: A single performance of drill music.
senses.example: The crowd went wild during the rapper's closing drill, which the fans had been waiting to hear.

core.definition: To make a hole in something by using a rotating tool called a drill, or to practice a skill through repetition.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a short i, like the i in 'kit,' so say dril, not dreel. The r is clearly pronounced at the start.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. As a practice word, it can sound strict or repetitive; as a tool word, it is simply practical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say drill a hole in the wall for home repairs, and drill for a practice exercise, such as a fire drill or a pronunciation drill. In a meeting, drill down means to examine data more closely, which is common in business. The noun drill is the tool, and the verb can mean repeated training in school or the military.

distinctions.note: Bore is more technical and often describes deep or large holes in rock, metal or the ground, while drill is the everyday word.
Practice is a general word for improving a skill, while drill suggests repeating the same exercise over and over.

examples.everyday: I need to drill a hole for the new shelf brackets, so can you hold the level?
examples.professional: Our geologists will drill three exploratory boreholes next month, and we will share the results before the board meeting.
examples.analytical: Rote repetition can drill a formula into memory, but it does not necessarily build the understanding needed to apply it.

nuance.analogy: Like a carpenter steadily working into a board, a drill makes progress by repeatedly pressing and turning into the same spot.
nuance.etymology: From Dutch drillen, meaning to bore or turn round.
common_mistakes: Saying dreel or dreal, which is not the standard American pronunciation; the vowel is short.
Confusing the verb sense of practicing with the tool sense when speaking about a fire drill or training.

drill.etymology: From Middle Dutch *drillen* (“bore, move in a circle”).

senses.definition: A set of two elements treated as one; a pair.
Two persons in an ongoing relationship; a dyadic relationship.
The relationship or interaction itself in reference to a couple.
A secondary unit of organization consisting of an aggregate of monads.
A tensor of order two and rank one.
Any set of two different pitch classes.
An element, atom, or radical having a valence of or combining power of two.
A chromosome structure, usually X- or V-shaped, consisting of two condensed sister chromatids joined by a centromere.

core.definition: A pair of two things or people treated as a single unit, or the relationship between the two.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the vowel in the second syllable is the short a of 'cat', not 'ed'. Non-native speakers often add an extra syllable or stress the second part.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word is descriptive and carries no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dyad mostly in sociology, psychology, philosophy and mathematics, not in everyday talk. In casual speech they would say 'pair', 'couple' or 'duo'. In research writing, a dyad usually means two people studied together, such as a parent and child or two coworkers.

distinctions.note: Pair is everyday and neutral, while dyad is technical and emphasizes the two as a structural unit studied as a system.
Couple usually means two people in a romantic or marital relationship, whereas dyad can refer to any two-member relationship or unit.

examples.everyday: My sister and I are a real dyad, so when one of us gets stressed, the other one knows right away.
examples.professional: In the team study, we analyzed each dyad of coworkers separately instead of looking only at the whole group.
examples.analytical: Simmel treats the dyad as a distinct social form, since either member can end the relationship and thereby dissolve the whole unit.

nuance.analogy: A dyad is like a two-person seesaw: the balance depends entirely on the two riders, and one leaving ends the game.
nuance.etymology: From Greek dyas, meaning 'two' or 'a pair'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'dyad' for any group of three or more people; a dyad always has exactly two members.
Pronouncing it with a long i and a stressed second syllable (dy-AD), which sounds unnatural to Americans.

dyad.etymology: From Ancient Greek *δυάς*, from *δύο* (“two”), from Proto-Indo-European **duwó*, **duwéh₃* (**dwóh₁*).

senses.definition: A boiling or bubbling up; an ebullition.
senses.example: The chemist watched the ebullience of the solution, noting how quickly the bubbles rose.

senses.definition: The quality of enthusiastic or lively expression of feelings and thoughts.

core.definition: Lively, enthusiastic energy and excitement in how someone expresses feelings or ideas.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on BUL, the middle syllable is short, and the ending sounds like 'yuns', not 'ee-ens'. Keep the first vowel reduced.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it describes admirable, infectious energy and high spirits.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ebullience mostly in writing or formal speech about a person's energy or a mood. In casual talk say enthusiasm or energy; ebullience sounds slightly elevated and literary.

distinctions.note: Enthusiasm is common and neutral, while ebullience is more vivid and suggests overflowing spirits.
Exuberance stresses joyful excess and lively physical energy; ebullience stresses bubbling, expressive high spirits.
Ebullition is the technical sense of boiling or bubbling up, especially of gases or liquids.

examples.everyday: Her ebullience at the party was contagious, and soon everyone was laughing with her.
examples.professional: The team lead's ebullience at the kickoff meeting got the whole group excited about the launch.
examples.analytical: Whitman's ebullience is a poetic celebration of the body and the self, expressed in long, rushing lines.

nuance.analogy: Like water coming to a boil, ebullience is energy bubbling up and spilling out.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ebullire, to bubble up or boil out, from e- out and bullire to boil.
common_mistakes: Confusing ebullience with ebullition, which in technical use means boiling or bubbling up
Stressing the last syllable instead of the middle one

senses.definition: Focused on ecological concerns.

core.definition: Focused on ecological concerns, putting nature, species or whole ecosystems at the center of values and decisions.
