senses.example: He had been visiting an area zoo when a monkey swung from its tree perch, swiped his glasses and hurled them into a hippo hole.

senses.definition: Any simian, including humans.
senses.example: Scientists observed the young monkey learning to crack nuts with a stone.

senses.definition: Any simian primate other than hominids; any monkey or ape.
senses.example: Chimpanzees are known to form bands to hunt and kill other monkeys.

senses.definition: A human considered to resemble monkeys in some way.
senses.example: Stop misbehaving, you cheeky little monkey!

senses.definition: A naughty or mischievous person, especially a child.
senses.example: Stop misbehaving, you cheeky little monkey!

senses.definition: The person in the motorcycle sidecar in sidecar racing.
senses.example: In sidecar racing, the monkey must hold on tight while the driver takes the corners.

senses.definition: Synonym of idiot: a person of minimal intelligence.
senses.example: Don't be a monkey; read the instructions before you plug in the router.

senses.definition: Synonym of uggo: an unattractive person, especially one whose face supposedly resembles a monkey's.
senses.example: Mean comments online called the model a monkey, which only proved how shallow those critics were.

senses.definition: Synonym of puppet: a person dancing to another's tune, a person controlled or directed by another.
senses.example: No, no, no, not you. I want to talk to the organ grinder, not the monkey.

senses.definition: A menial employee who does a repetitive job supposedly requiring minimal intelligence.
senses.example: code monkey

senses.definition: A black person.
The weight of a pile driver or drop hammer.
senses.example: The crew hoisted the monkey to the top of the pile driver before releasing it.

senses.definition: A fluid consisting of hydrochloric acid and zinc, used in the process of soldering.
senses.example: The plumber brushed a bit of monkey on the copper joint before applying the solder.

senses.definition: Synonym of five hundred, especially 500 pounds sterling or 500 dollars.
senses.example: He handed the bartender a monkey and told him to keep the change.

senses.definition: Synonym of face card.
senses.example: She laid down a monkey and a pair of tens to win the hand.

senses.definition: A person's temper, said to be "up" when they are angry.
senses.example: Stay calm, because your brother's monkey is up and he's ready to yell.

senses.definition: A drug habit; an addiction; a compulsion.
senses.example: Everybody's got something to hide except for me and my monkey.

senses.definition: A dance popularized by Major Lance in 1963, now usually only its upper-body dance move involving exaggerated drumming motions.
senses.example: At the wedding, everyone did the monkey during the chorus of the old soul song.

senses.definition: The vessel in which a mess receives its full allowance of grog.
senses.example: The sailors lined up at the monkey to receive their daily ration of grog.

senses.definition: (uncommon) A penis.
senses.label: uncommon

senses.definition: (historical) A small trading vessel of the sixteenth century.
senses.example: The merchant's small monkey sailed from Lisbon, loaded with salt and dried cod.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To meddle; to mess (with).
senses.example: Please don't monkey with the controls if you don't know what you're doing.

senses.definition: To mimic; to ape.
senses.example: The comedian monkeyed his boss's gestures so well that the whole office laughed.

core.definition: A long-tailed primate that is not an ape; in informal use, also a mischievous child, often said affectionately.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with the ng sound followed by a short 'uh' and a final 'ee' sound. Do not pronounce the o as in 'mon'; the vowel is the short u of 'hung'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for the animal. For people, it can be affectionate ('you little monkey') or negative when it means someone who acts like a fool.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use monkey in everyday phrases more than in its literal sense. Monkey around means to fool around or waste time, monkey with means to tamper with something, and monkey business means mischief or shady behavior. Using monkey for a person can be playful with children but insulting with adults, so be careful.

distinctions.note: Apes, such as chimpanzees and gorillas, have no tails and are generally larger; monkeys have tails and are a different group of primates.
Primate is the broad category that includes monkeys, apes and humans, while monkey is a narrower animal term.
Chimp is an informal short form for chimpanzee, which is an ape, not a monkey.

examples.everyday: Stop monkeying with the remote, or you're going to break it.
examples.professional: Please don't monkey with the production configuration without filing a ticket first.
examples.analytical: The essay uses the monkey not to dismiss the animal but to reflect on the thin line between mimicry and thought.

nuance.analogy: Monkeying with a machine you do not understand is like a child with a wrench: the tool is powerful, but the child may cause a breakdown.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; probably from a Low German or Romance source, first recorded in the 1500s.
common_mistakes: Using monkey as a neutral word for any ape; chimpanzees and gorillas are apes, not monkeys.
Using monkey with the wrong preposition, such as 'monkey on', instead of 'monkey with' or 'monkey around'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word qophim, usually rendered apes, appears in 1 Kings 10:22 and 2 Chronicles 9:21 (RSV) among the goods brought from Tarshish by Solomon's fleet. The passages mention the animals as trade goods without any moral point.

senses.definition: A fear of being alone.
Any phobia relating to a single specific thing, such as spiders or heights.

core.definition: An intense, irrational fear of being alone, or more broadly, a phobia about a single specific thing.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on FOH, as with other -phobia words like arachnophobia. Many learners wrongly stress the first syllable, MON-o-fobia, and the American 'a' in mono is a reduced 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes an anxiety condition and is clinical in tone.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare, mostly clinical or literary term. Americans would more often say they have a fear of being alone or talk about separation anxiety. The second sense, a phobia about one specific thing, is confusing and is rarely used, so use the word carefully.

distinctions.note: Agoraphobia is a fear of open or crowded spaces, while monophobia refers to fear of being alone.
Loneliness is a sad feeling, while monophobia is a clinical fear of solitude.

examples.everyday: My friend says she has a bit of monophobia, so she always keeps the TV on when she is home by herself.
examples.professional: The counselor noted that some clients with anxiety disorders report monophobia, which may affect how we schedule their sessions.
examples.analytical: The term monophobia, read as a fear of solitude, raises the question of whether such fear is a distinct disorder or a symptom of broader anxiety.

nuance.analogy: If arachnophobia is a fear of spiders, monophobia is the fear of being alone, like a fear of an empty room.
nuance.etymology: From Greek monos (alone) and phobos (fear).
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable instead of the 'foh' syllable.
Using monophobia to mean ordinary shyness or dislike of being alone, when it refers to a stronger fear.

senses.definition: In a monotonic manner, pertaining to the Greek system of diacritics which discards the breathings and employs a single accent to indicate stress.
senses.example: The modern Greek textbook was printed monotonically, dropping breathings and keeping only one accent.

senses.definition: In a monotonic manner, of a function that either never decreases or never increases as its independent variable increases.

core.definition: In a way that never decreases or never increases as its input grows, such as a monotonically increasing function.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on TAHN, with secondary stress on the first syllable. The vowel in 'mon' and 'ton' is the 'ah' of cot, and '-ically' is said as 'ik-lee', not 'eye-cal-ly'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use monotonically mainly in mathematics, statistics, economics and computer science, and rarely in casual speech. In everyday talk they would say 'always goes up' or 'never goes down'. The Greek-diacritics sense, a monotonic system of accents, belongs to classics and is found mainly in academic writing about ancient texts.

distinctions.note: Monotonically is a mathematical term about the direction of change, while monotonously means in a dull, repetitive way. Do not swap them.
A monotonic function may stay level in places, while strictly monotonically means it always moves in one direction and never stays flat.

examples.everyday: My cousin jokes that our family's grocery bill only goes up, so it grows monotonically.
examples.professional: Cumulative sign-ups increase monotonically across every quarter, so the trend is easy to forecast.
examples.analytical: A cumulative distribution function is monotonically non-decreasing, since adding more of the range can never lower the probability.

nuance.analogy: A monotonically rising staircase never has a step down: each stair is at least as high as the one before.
nuance.etymology: From Greek monotonos 'single-toned', from monos 'single' and tonos 'tone, tension'.
common_mistakes: Using it to mean boringly or repetitively; that meaning belongs to monotonously.
Stressing the first syllable, as in MAHN-uh-tahn-ik-lee; the primary stress is on TAHN.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of mons pubis.
An extraterrestrial mountain or volcano.
senses.example: Olympus Mons

core.definition: A mountain or large volcanic peak on a planet or moon, such as Olympus Mons on Mars.

pronunciation.tip: It is one stressed syllable. Use the 'ah' vowel of cot and end with a clear 'z' sound, and don't add an extra vowel like 'mo-nuhz'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term, though the anatomical sense can be sensitive in everyday conversation.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, mons is used almost only in planetary science and in medicine. In medical settings, Americans may say mons alone for the mons pubis, but in everyday talk they say 'pubic area' or 'mons pubis' in full. Do not use mons casually for a hill; say mountain or hill.

distinctions.note: Mountain is the everyday word for a large, high landform on Earth, while mons is a technical or planetary term, often used for features on other worlds.
Mons alone can mean the pubic mound in medical settings, while mons pubis is the full, more precise anatomical term.

examples.everyday: Have you seen the pictures of Olympus Mons? It's taller than Mount Everest.
examples.professional: The rover team mapped the lower slopes of the mons to plan a safe route for the traverse.
examples.analytical: Olympus Mons is a shield volcano whose flanks are far gentler than most mountains on Earth, which says much about gravity and lava on Mars.

nuance.analogy: A mons is a planet's version of a mountain, built up by lava rather than folded rock.
nuance.etymology: From Latin mōns, montis 'mountain', also the source of mount and montane.
common_mistakes: Using mons for an ordinary hill or mountain on Earth; say mountain.
Adding an extra syllable, as in MOH-nuhz; it is one syllable, MAHNZ.

senses.definition: Designating a marriage (or the wife involved) between a man of higher rank and a woman of lower rank, often having various legal repercussions (typically that such a wife has no claim on the husband's possessions or title). It was not an aspect of English law, but was common in other royal houses, especially in Germany.
senses.example: The prince's morganatic marriage meant his commoner wife could not inherit his title.

core.definition: Describing a marriage in which a man of higher rank marries a woman of lower rank, and she and their children have no claim to his title or property.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, 'NAT'. The 'g' is hard, as in 'go', and the final 'ic' is short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use morganatic mainly in history, royal studies, or legal discussions of European noble families. It is not used in U.S. law, which has no equivalent system of titles. In everyday talk, Americans would say the marriage was unequal in rank or that she had no claim to the title.

distinctions.note: A bigamous marriage is illegal because one spouse is already married; a morganatic marriage is legal but restricts the spouse's inheritance and title.

examples.everyday: People still gossip about the prince's morganatic marriage, since she never got his title.
examples.professional: The museum's exhibit on European royal families explained how a morganatic marriage affected inheritance.
examples.analytical: The morganatic marriage shows how dynastic law separated personal union from the transmission of rank and property.

nuance.analogy: A morganatic marriage is like a membership with a fine print: the spouse is part of the family in love, but not in title or property.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin matrimonium ad morganaticam, from German Morgengabe, a morning gift that a husband gave his bride.
common_mistakes: Assuming morganatic means illegal; the marriage was legal but restricted.
Using it for any unequal marriage in everyday American contexts, where it would sound too technical.

morganatic.etymology: From New Latin *morganāticus*, from the Medieval Latin phrase *mātrimōnium ad morganāticum*, from Proto-Germanic **murgnagebō* (“morning gift”).

senses.definition: A scientific study of form and structure, usually without regard to function. Especially:
senses.example: Morphology examines form and structure in biology without focusing on how things function.

senses.definition: The study of the internal structure of morphemes (words and their semantic building blocks).
Mathematical morphology.
The form and structure of something.
A description of the form and structure of something.
senses.example: The report includes a detailed morphology of the fossil's skull and jaw.

senses.definition: The study of the form and structure of animals and plants.
senses.example: Her doctoral thesis focused on the morphology of desert beetles and their shell structures.

senses.definition: The study of the structure of rocks and landforms.

core.definition: The study of the internal structure of words, meaning how smaller units called morphemes combine to create meaning.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, 'FOL'. The middle syllables are reduced to 'uh', and the 'ph' is pronounced as 'f'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: In American English, morphology is most often used in linguistics and language teaching. It also appears in biology, where it describes the form of organisms, and in image processing as mathematical morphology. In a meeting or everyday talk, it may confuse listeners unless the context is clear.

distinctions.note: Morphology concerns word structure; syntax concerns how words combine into sentences.
Phonology concerns sound systems; morphology concerns meaningful units within words.

examples.everyday: My daughter is studying morphology in her English class, learning how prefixes change word meaning.
examples.professional: Our NLP team uses morphology to break down user search terms into their root forms before matching them.
examples.analytical: A theory of morphology must explain why some languages create meaning through affixes while others rely on word order.

nuance.analogy: Morphology is like the Lego instructions for words: small pieces such as un-, break, and -able snap together into a new whole with its own meaning.
nuance.etymology: From Greek morphē, form, plus -logia, study of.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'MOR-fol-ogy'.
Confusing morphology with phonology, which studies sound patterns.

senses.definition: Acutely embarrassed.
Having undergone mortification (discipline of the bodily appetites etc.)
senses.example: The mortified brother fasted through Lent and slept on bare stone, seeking humility before God.

core.definition: Very embarrassed or ashamed, to the point of feeling humiliated in front of others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MOR. The final ed is pronounced as a single d after the diphthong, so the word ends in fide, not fied.

nuance.connotation: Negative, describing acute embarrassment. It is often used lightly, as in a mild joke about a small mistake.
nuance.usage_note: Americans commonly say I was mortified when something embarrassing happens, especially in front of others, and people often add a laugh. It is stronger than embarrassed. Mortified is also used for the religious sense of disciplined body, but that use is rare in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Embarrassed is the everyday word for a mild feeling of shame; mortified signals a much stronger reaction.
Ashamed refers to guilt about a moral failing, while mortified refers to social embarrassment in front of others.

examples.everyday: I was mortified when my phone rang loudly during the funeral.
examples.professional: She was mortified when she sent the wrong attachment to the whole client list.
examples.analytical: The narrator is mortified not by his sin itself but by the public exposure of his hypocrisy.

nuance.analogy: Being mortified is like having your zipper down in front of a crowded room: the feeling is sharp, immediate and hard to hide.
nuance.etymology: From the verb mortify, from Late Latin mortificare, 'to put to death'.
common_mistakes: Using mortified without a cause, as in I'm mortified about the weather; it needs an embarrassing event.
Saying mortified by to someone when you mean mortified in front of someone; American usage usually says in front of.

conversation.text: I was mortified when my phone rang during the funeral.
She was mortified to find out she had spinach in her teeth all day.
My son was mortified when I hugged him in front of his friends.

senses.definition: Filled with grief or sadness; being in a state in which one mourns.
senses.example: The mournful sound of the church bell drifted over the empty town.

senses.definition: Fit to inspire mourning; tragic.
senses.example: The mournful collapse of the old bridge closed the valley for two years.

core.definition: Full of sadness or grief, often in a way that is sad to hear or see.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a reduced 'fuhl' with the light American schwa. The first vowel is the 'aw' of 'law', and the r is clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Negative to sad. It describes a feeling or sound that conveys sorrow, often in a poetic or emotional way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'mournful' in writing, music descriptions, and poetic speech, such as 'a mournful song' or 'a mournful tone'. In everyday speech, people more often say 'sad' or 'gloomy'. It can sound slightly dramatic if used for ordinary disappointments.

distinctions.note: 'Sad' is a common, everyday word, while 'mournful' suggests a deeper, more lingering sorrow, often connected with loss.
'Sorrowful' is similar but more formal and often connected with religious or emotional suffering, while 'mournful' often describes sounds or moods.

examples.everyday: The mournful sound of the train whistle made me feel lonely on the late drive home.
examples.professional: The email had a mournful tone as it announced the end of the project after three years.
examples.analytical: The elegy's mournful refrain turns grief into a form of hope by naming the dead.

nuance.analogy: Like a cello playing a slow, low note that seems to carry a whole history of loss.
nuance.etymology: From 'mourn' with the suffix '-ful', meaning full of.
common_mistakes: Using 'mournful' for mild sadness; it implies deep sorrow.
Spelling it 'mourneful', which is not a standard word.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to more than one class (grouping or category).
To cause a character to belong to more than one character class.
senses.example: The game designer decided to multiclass the rogue so she could also cast healing spells.

senses.definition: A character belonging to more than one character class.
senses.example: As a multiclass, my paladin can now cast spells and also use stealth.

core.definition: Involving three or more possible categories, so a classifier must assign each input to exactly one of several labels.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the first syllable, MUL, and the second syllable tee is short and light. Class has a short a, like the a in cat, not the a in father.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term in data science.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use multiclass in data science and machine learning when talking about classification with more than two labels, such as sorting emails into five topics. The word is also used in gaming for multiclass characters, but in data science it is always about labels. Writers often say multiclass classification, and they use binary to mean two classes.

distinctions.note: Binary means exactly two classes, such as spam or not spam, while multiclass means three or more classes.
In multiclass each input has one label chosen from several options, while in multilabel an input can have several labels at once.

examples.everyday: My friend works on a model that sorts photos into several categories, so she calls it a multiclass problem.
examples.professional: Our fraud model is multiclass now, so we need to track precision separately for each risk tier.
examples.analytical: A multiclass setting forces us to ask whether the categories are truly exclusive, since overlapping labels can distort the evaluation.

nuance.analogy: Multiclass is like sorting mail into many bins rather than just two, where every letter must go into exactly one bin.
nuance.etymology: Multi- from Latin multus (many); class from Latin classis (a division or group).
common_mistakes: Using multiclass to mean many features; it refers to the number of labels or classes.
Saying multi-class with a pause; it is usually one word, multiclass.
Confusing multiclass with multilabel, where one input can carry several labels at once.

senses.definition: Of or relating to more than one source control repository.
senses.example: Our multirepo setup made it hard to keep shared libraries in sync across teams.

core.definition: Describing a software project organized across several separate source-code repositories instead of one shared repository.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the second syllable of repo, REE, with a lighter secondary stress on mul. Repo is short for repository, and many developers say it REE-poh, though some say REP-oh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is technical jargon with no positive or negative tone.
nuance.usage_note: Developers and engineering managers use multirepo in discussions about how to organize code, often in contrast with a monorepo. Americans say it casually in team meetings and online forums, but it is unfamiliar outside software. In everyday talk you would describe the same idea as 'each project has its own code folder online'.

distinctions.note: A monorepo keeps the code for many projects in one repository, while a multirepo setup keeps each project in its own repository.
Polyrepo is a close synonym that means the same thing; multirepo is more common in American engineering teams.

examples.everyday: Since our team split everything into separate projects, we call our setup a multirepo, which makes the code easier to manage.
examples.professional: Because our services ship on different schedules, we are keeping a multirepo structure instead of consolidating everything into a monorepo.
examples.analytical: A multirepo arrangement isolates dependencies and permissions, but it makes cross-project refactoring and coordinated versioning harder.

nuance.analogy: Like keeping each recipe in its own binder instead of putting all of them in one giant cookbook.
nuance.etymology: Multi- from Latin multus, 'many', and repo, a clipping of repository, from Latin repositorium, 'storehouse'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing repo like the word report, as REP-ort; repo ends in an ō sound and has no t.
Writing multi-repo with a hyphen or confusing it with monorepo, which is a different setup.

senses.definition: Unmissably good.
Anything unmissably good, such as a film or television program or a tourist attraction.
senses.example: The new museum exhibit is a must-see if you're visiting the city this summer.

core.definition: So good, interesting, or impressive that you should definitely see it before you miss it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MUST, and see is weaker. The two words link as one phrase, so say them quickly and do not add a pause.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It recommends something enthusiastically.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use must-see for movies, shows, tourist sights, exhibits, and events, both as an adjective and a noun. A natural reply to a recommendation is Thanks, I'll add it to my list. It sounds casual and friendly, so it is best in conversation rather than formal writing.

distinctions.note: Must-read refers to a book or article. Must-see refers to a show, film, sight, or event.
Recommended is neutral. Must-see is enthusiastic and strongly suggests it is worth your time.

examples.everyday: You have to watch that new show, it's a must-see.
examples.professional: The recorded keynote is a must-see for anyone on the data team.
examples.analytical: The 1960s film is a must-see for historians of cinematic realism because of its long takes.

nuance.analogy: Like a sign on a trail that says you cannot leave without seeing the waterfall.
nuance.etymology: Compound of must, from Old English motan, and see, from Old English seon.
common_mistakes: Saying must-see with equal stress on both words.
Writing must see without the hyphen when used as an adjective before a noun.

conversation.text: That movie is a must-see; it's amazing.
The Grand Canyon is a must-see if you're in Arizona.
Critics are calling it a must-see.

senses.definition: Pertaining to a nation or country, especially as a whole; affecting, shared by, or existing throughout all of a nation; the state.
senses.example: a national assembly · on the front page of every national newspaper

senses.definition: Belonging to or characteristic of a specific nation or country, as opposed to others.
senses.example: this is their national dish · our national tendency to laugh at the French

senses.definition: (rare) Nationalistic; patriotic.
senses.example: My uncle's national pride made him wave a flag at every backyard barbecue.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: A subject of a nation.
senses.example: The diplomats were advised not to interact with any foreign nationals except on official duty.

senses.definition: A tournament in which participants from all over the nation compete.
senses.example: After winning the regional tournament, the team advanced to the nationals.

senses.definition: A national newspaper.
senses.example: Her grandfather still gets a national delivered daily, even though he reads everything online.

senses.definition: Somebody born under the authority of a given country.
senses.example: Under the law, the child is a national of the country where she was born.

core.definition: Relating to a whole country or its people; shared by, affecting or existing throughout a country.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, the -tion sound becomes sh, and the final -al is a weak uhl. The middle syllable is a quick schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and factual; it is positive in phrases like national pride, but it can sound nationalistic depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use national constantly in everyday speech for news, parks, holidays and averages, usually with no political meaning. National is the normal opposite of local or regional. It is different from nationalist, which has a political sense, so do not use national to mean someone who loves their country too much.

distinctions.note: Nationwide stresses that something covers the whole country in its spread, while national can also describe what belongs to the country as a whole.
Federal refers specifically to the central government, while national refers to the whole country, its people or its scope.
International concerns relations between countries, while national concerns matters inside one country.

examples.everyday: Did you catch the national news tonight? The storm is hitting the whole East Coast.
examples.professional: Our rate is 4.2 percent, which is above the national average, so we need to explain the regional gap in the report.
examples.analytical: A national identity is not simply inherited at birth; it is built through schools, media and shared rituals over generations.

nuance.analogy: National is like a family photo: it shows the whole group at once, not just one room or one person.
nuance.etymology: From Latin nationalis, from natio, nation, from nasci, to be born.
common_mistakes: Confusing national with nationalist; national describes scope, while nationalist describes a political attitude.
Stressing the second syllable (nash-OO-nal); the main stress falls on the first syllable.

senses.definition: Legal membership of a particular nation or state, by origin, birth, naturalization, ownership, allegiance or otherwise.
senses.example: By living in the country for five years, you are entitled to get nationality.

senses.definition: A people sharing a common origin, culture and/or language, and possibly constituting a nation-state.
senses.example: Many nationalities were represented among the refugees who arrived at the border camp.

senses.definition: (rare) National, i.e. ethnic and/or cultural, character or identity.
senses.example: Her poetry expresses a strong sense of nationality, rooted in the landscape of her childhood.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (rare) Nationalism or patriotism.
senses.example: The speech appealed to nationality, urging voters to put the country above all else.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: The legal status of belonging to a particular country, such as the citizenship shown on your passport.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NAL, the first syllable is a light nash, and the final -ty is a quick tee, often flapped. The vowels in the middle syllables are reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and factual; it is used on forms and in official contexts, and in conversation it can sound personal if asked directly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nationality in forms, legal contexts and talk about travel, but many US forms say citizenship or country of citizenship instead. Asking someone's nationality in casual conversation can sound too personal, so people usually ask where someone is from. In everyday speech, nationality can also refer to a person's cultural or ethnic background.

distinctions.note: Citizenship is the formal legal status of belonging to a state, while nationality can also refer to cultural or ethnic identity.
Ethnicity refers to shared ancestry, culture and heritage, while nationality usually refers to legal membership in a nation.

examples.everyday: When the form asked for my nationality, I wasn't sure whether they wanted my citizenship or where my family comes from.
examples.professional: HR needs your country of citizenship, not nationality, for the work visa paperwork, so please update the form.
examples.analytical: Under international law, nationality is a legal bond, distinct from the cultural identity that people also call their nationality.

nuance.analogy: Nationality is like a membership card in a club: it records official membership, though it says little about your personality.
nuance.etymology: From nation, from Latin natio, plus the suffix -ality, forming an abstract noun.
common_mistakes: Asking someone their nationality in casual conversation, where Americans would ask where they are from.
Stressing the first syllable (NASH-uh-nal-ih-tee); the main stress falls on NAL.

nationality.etymology: From *national* + *-ity*, perhaps after French *nationalité*; ultimately from Latin *nātio* (“nation, people”).

senses.definition: In need; poor.
senses.example: Needy people want to give too, but have few material goods to offer.

senses.definition: Desiring constant affirmation; lacking self-confidence.
senses.example: It's emotionally exhausting to be around her because she's so needy.

core.definition: Lacking money, food, or other basic things; poor and in need of help from others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, and the final 'y' is a long 'ee' sound. Keep the first vowel short-to-medium, a clear 'ee' like 'need', not 'nay-dee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in charitable contexts such as 'the needy', but negative when describing a person who constantly seeks reassurance, as it can sound judgmental.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, 'the needy' is a common phrase for people who lack money or help, often in discussions of charity or government programs. Calling a person 'needy' about attention or approval is a critical, informal insult, so avoid it unless you mean that. Use 'in need' or 'poor' when speaking politely about a family's situation.

distinctions.note: 'Poor' describes a lack of money in general, while 'needy' focuses on the immediate need for help or assistance.
'Clingy' is a casual insult for someone who wants constant closeness; 'needy' is similar but more about emotional dependence.

examples.everyday: Our church runs a food pantry every Saturday for needy families in the neighborhood.
examples.professional: Our nonprofit prioritizes funding for needy students in the rural districts we serve.
examples.analytical: Psalm 72:12 describes God as one who delivers the needy when he calls, placing the needy at the center of a just king's responsibilities.

nuance.analogy: Being needy is like an empty bowl: it is waiting to be filled, and it cannot fill itself.
nuance.etymology: From 'need' plus the suffix '-y', meaning full of or characterized by need.
common_mistakes: Calling a friend 'needy' in polite conversation, which can sound unkind.
Using 'needy' for a temporary problem where 'in need' or 'short on money' is more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word is 'ebyon' (אֶבְיוֹן), meaning poor, needy, or destitute, and it is used repeatedly for those who depend on God's justice. Psalm 72:12 (RSV) says God delivers the needy when he cries for help, and Psalm 9:18 says the needy shall not always be forgotten. The prophets, such as Amos 8:4, condemn those who oppress the needy, showing that caring for them is a central demand of covenant faithfulness.

needy.etymology: From Middle English *nedy*, *nedi* (“necessitous”), from Old English *nēdiġ*, **nīediġ* "of need, obligated, compelled"; found in the derivative *nīediġnes* (“obligation”), from Proto-Germanic **naudigaz* (“of need, forced, compelled”), equivalent to…

senses.definition: Not taking sides in a conflict such as war; nonaligned.
Favoring neither the supporting nor opposing viewpoint of a topic of debate; unbiased.
senses.example: I am neutral regarding the issue of gay marriage.

senses.definition: Neither positive nor negative.
senses.example: The judge kept a neutral expression throughout the testimony, revealing nothing about her opinion.

senses.definition: Not biased; viewing situations objectively in a way that is neither positive nor negative.
senses.example: a neutral person

senses.definition: Neither beneficial nor harmful.
senses.example: Most doctors consider this supplement neutral for the heart, so it probably won't help or hurt.

senses.definition: Having no obvious color; gray.
senses.example: We chose neutral gray paint for the living room so it would suit any furniture.

senses.definition: Having an alignment that is situated between two notable possibilities, such as between good and evil, or between chaotic and lawful.
senses.example: My character is neutral, so she helps whoever offers the better bargain rather than picking a side.

senses.definition: Having no sex; neuter.
senses.example: In Latin class we learned that most nouns ending in -um are neutral in gender.

senses.definition: Neither positive nor negative; possessing no charge or equivalent positive and negative charge such that there is no imbalance.
senses.example: A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, so its net charge is zero.

senses.definition: Having a pH of or near 7, neither acidic nor alkaline.
senses.example: Pure water is neutral at room temperature, with a pH of about seven.

senses.definition: Of an alcoholic drink, having been fermented and distilled but with no additives.
senses.example: The bartender poured a neutral vodka, which is distilled and has no added flavors.

senses.definition: A nonaligned state, or a member of such a state.
senses.example: During the Cold War, the small country declared itself a neutral and refused to join either bloc.

senses.definition: A person who takes no side in a dispute.
senses.example: When the siblings fought, their grandmother acted as a neutral and refused to take anyone's side.

senses.definition: An individual or entity serving as an arbitrator or adjudicator.
senses.example: The contract called for a neutral to settle any dispute that the two companies could not resolve.

senses.definition: A neutral hue.
senses.example: Her wardrobe is mostly neutrals, such as beige, gray, and navy.

senses.definition: The position of a set of gears in which power cannot be transmitted to the drive mechanism.
senses.example: Put it in neutral, and we'll push it out of the garage.

senses.definition: An electrical terminal or conductor which has zero or close to zero voltage with respect to the ground.
senses.example: Connect the white wire to the neutral bar, and the black wire to the hot terminal.

core.definition: Not taking sides in an argument, conflict or disagreement; impartial and fair to everyone involved.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable: NOO-truhl. Say the tr quickly, and let the final -al be a light syllabic l with no separate vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing fairness; can sound evasive if someone refuses to commit to any position.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use neutral for not taking sides in arguments, politics, business and family disputes, and phrases like neutral party or neutral territory are common. In design and interiors, neutral colors such as beige and gray are an everyday idea. Overusing it can sound like you are dodging the question, so pair it with a clear reason for your position.

distinctions.note: Impartial is more formal and suits judges, referees and arbitrators, while neutral is the everyday word for not taking sides.
Unbiased is common in data, research and reporting, where it means free of systematic distortion.
Indifferent means not caring, which is different from neutral, which means not favoring either side while still caring about the outcome.

examples.everyday: Let's meet at a neutral spot, like the coffee shop, so nobody feels like they're on home turf.
examples.professional: I'd like to act as a neutral party when the two teams disagree about the release schedule.
examples.analytical: A truly neutral reading of the evidence must first admit the assumptions the reader brings to the text.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee who calls fouls on both teams by the same rule.
nuance.etymology: From Latin neutralis, from neuter (neither).
common_mistakes: Using neutral in speech to mean boring or plain; in conversation it means not taking a side.
Saying I am neutral about a food when you mean you have no preference; the usual phrase is I don't have a preference.

senses.definition: Never again; at no time in the future.

core.definition: Never again; at no time in the future. It is a literary and mostly poetic word.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, NEV, with a lighter stress on MOR. The final syllable is pronounced with an r, so say it like door, not mo.

nuance.connotation: Dramatic, somber and poetic; in casual speech it sounds theatrical or joking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans know nevermore mainly from Edgar Allan Poe's poem The Raven, where the bird repeats the word. In everyday speech it sounds theatrical, so say never again instead. It works in poetry, a eulogy or a deliberately dramatic joke.

distinctions.note: Never again is the everyday phrase, while nevermore is literary and dramatic.
Evermore means always in the future, the opposite of nevermore, and is also literary.

examples.everyday: After that camping trip in the rain, I swear, nevermore!
examples.professional: The old vendor is gone, and we will nevermore sign a contract without an audit clause.
examples.analytical: Poe's raven answers every question with the single word nevermore, sealing a grief the speaker cannot escape.

nuance.analogy: Like a door that closes with a click and never opens again.
nuance.etymology: A compound of never and more, both from Old English.
common_mistakes: Using nevermore in everyday speech, where it sounds theatrical.
Stressing the last syllable, as in nev-er-MORE; the main stress belongs on NEV.

nevermore.etymology: From Middle English *nevermore*, from the Old English phrase *nǣfre mā*.

senses.definition: Pleasant, satisfactory, complimentary.
senses.example: The hotel room was clean and the staff were nice to us.

senses.definition: Shows that the given adjective is desirable, or acts as a mild intensifier; pleasantly, quite.
senses.example: The soup is nice and hot.

senses.definition: Of a person: friendly, attractive.
senses.example: You weren’t nice to me this morning.

senses.definition: Respectable; virtuous.
senses.example: What is a nice person like you doing in a place like this?

senses.definition: Giving a favorable review or having a favorable impression.
senses.example: For Candy Crush Saga, the critics were far nicer than the audience (7.9/10 vs. 3.1/10).

senses.definition: Showing refinement or delicacy, proper, seemly.
senses.example: a nice way of putting it

senses.definition: Showing or requiring great precision or sensitive discernment; subtle.
senses.example: The calibration required a nice adjustment of the sensor's gain setting.

senses.definition: (rare) Particular in one's conduct; scrupulous, painstaking; choosy.
senses.example: He was very nice about keeping receipts for every business expense.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (dated) Having particular tastes; fussy, fastidious.
senses.example: My grandmother was nice about her teacups and would never let us touch them.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Nicely.
senses.example: Children, I told you to play nice. Don't make me come out there and set you straight.

senses.definition: Used to signify a job well done.
senses.example: Nice! I couldn't have done better.

senses.definition: Used to signify approval.
senses.example: Is that your new car? Nice!

senses.definition: Niceness.
senses.example: Under all that sharpness was a genuine nice that few people ever saw.

senses.definition: To run a process with a specified (usually lower) priority.
senses.example: You can nice the backup script so it doesn't slow down the production database.

core.definition: Pleasant, friendly, or kind; a common word for describing people, places, and things you like.

pronunciation.tip: Use a single long i sound and end with a clear s. Do not add a y sound or stretch it into two syllables.

nuance.connotation: Positive in most contexts, but sarcastic in phrases like 'Nice going' after a mistake.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nice constantly, in everyday talk, in small talk, and at work. It is friendly but can sound vague when used alone. Adding a more specific word, such as 'a nice meal' or 'a nice person', is more natural. In sarcasm, 'Oh, nice' signals disappointment.

distinctions.note: Pleasant is more formal and describes experiences or atmosphere; nice is more casual and general.
Kind describes someone's character and generosity, while nice can refer to appearance, food, or a general impression.

examples.everyday: That coffee shop downtown has a really nice patio, so let's sit outside.
examples.professional: Thanks for sending the report so quickly, that was really nice of you.
examples.analytical: A nice argument can still be wrong, so we must examine the evidence rather than admire the style.

nuance.analogy: Like a comfortable sweater, nice is pleasant and easy to like, though it does not say much about its special qualities.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English nice, meaning foolish or ignorant, via Latin nescius 'ignorant'; its positive sense developed in the 1700s.
common_mistakes: Overusing nice in writing, where a more precise word is better.
Using nice as a sarcastic remark without tone, which can confuse learners.

nice.etymology: From Middle English *nyce*, *nice*, *nys*, from Old French *nice*, *niche*, *nisce* (“simple, foolish, ignorant”), from Latin *nescius* (“ignorant, not knowing”); compare *nesciō* (“to know not, be ignorant of”), from *ne* (“not”) + *sciō* (“to know”).

conversation.text: We had a really nice dinner at their place.
Your new neighbors seem really nice and friendly.
"My car got towed." "Oh, nice. Just what you needed."

senses.definition: The ordinal form of the number ninety-six, describing a person or thing in position number 96 of a sequence.
senses.example: The answer appears on the ninety-sixth page of the book.

senses.definition: One of ninety-six equal parts of a whole.
senses.example: A ninety-sixth of 1920 is 20.

core.definition: The ordinal form of ninety-six; coming in position number 96 in a sequence.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SIKTH and keep the cluster compact. The s before th is often dropped in fast speech, so the ending sounds like 'sikth'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is used for ordinal positions in lists, rankings, and sequences.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ninety-sixth in plain counting, such as a numbered item, a rank, or a floor. The number is often written as 96th in print. Speakers usually say it in a neutral tone, and it is rarely used in casual speech except to point to an exact position.

distinctions.note: Ninety-sixth is position 96 and ninety-fifth is position 95, so the two are easily confused when counting.

examples.everyday: I'm the ninety-sixth person in line, so I'll be waiting a while for the new phone.
examples.professional: The ninety-sixth sprint was the first to pass all of the integration tests, so we can release it.
examples.analytical: The ninety-sixth sample in the dataset is an outlier, and we should examine it before drawing a conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Like a number on a race bib: a fixed label that tells you exactly where someone stands.
nuance.etymology: From ninety-six plus the ordinal suffix -th, using sixth from Old English sixta.
common_mistakes: Dropping the sixth ending and saying 'ninety-six' for the ordinal.
Confusing the -sixth ending with 'sixteenth' or 'sixtieth'; these are different words.

senses.definition: A member of a society or class who herd animals from pasture to pasture with no fixed home.
senses.example: The Bedouin nomad moved his goats and tents across the desert every few weeks.

senses.definition: Synonym of wanderer: an itinerant person.
senses.example: The lonely nomad drifted from town to town, never staying anywhere longer than a season.

senses.definition: A person who changes residence frequently.
senses.example: My cousin is a nomad who has moved fourteen times since college.

senses.definition: A dragonfly of Afroeurasia, Sympetrum fonscolombii.
senses.example: Entomologists photographed a nomad perched on the reeds beside the pond.

senses.definition: A player who changes teams frequently.
senses.example: The veteran shortstop was a nomad who had played for six different clubs.

senses.definition: Synonym of nomadic.
senses.example: The nomad tribes followed the seasonal rains across the grasslands each year.

core.definition: A person who moves from place to place with no permanent home, often following herds or seasonal work.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the second a short a, as in cat. Keep the final d light, not a separate uh sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, suggesting freedom and adventure, though it can imply instability in some contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nomad for traditional herding peoples and, figuratively, for people who move often, such as digital nomads who work remotely from different countries. It is informal enough for everyday talk. Describing yourself as a nomad is usually playful.

distinctions.note: Wanderer suggests aimless roaming; nomad implies a regular pattern of movement, often for survival or work.
Migrant usually refers to people moving to find work or to settle; nomad suggests ongoing movement without settling.
A refugee is forced out of a home by danger; a nomad moves by choice or tradition.

examples.everyday: My sister is a bit of a nomad; she has lived in five cities in the last six years.
examples.professional: Our remote team includes several digital nomads, so we schedule meetings across time zones.
examples.analytical: The author treats the nomad as a figure of the restless soul, one who has no settled dwelling in this world.

nuance.analogy: A nomad is like a tent rather than a house: it is built to be packed up and carried to the next place.
nuance.etymology: From Greek nomas, 'roaming for pasture', from nemein, 'to distribute, pasture'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with the stress on the second syllable, as in no-MAD.
Using nomad to mean any traveler on a short trip; it implies regular, ongoing movement.

nomad.etymology: From Middle French *nomade*, from Latin *Nomas* (“wandering shepherd”), from Ancient Greek *νομάς* (“roaming, wandering, esp.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see nothing,‎ doing: nothing that is currently occurring; nothing going on.
senses.example: Anything happening downtown tonight? Nothing doing, so let's just order pizza.

core.definition: Absolutely not; a flat, informal refusal to do or allow something.

pronunciation.tip: The first word is pronounced with a voiceless th, as in 'thing', not a d or s sound, and the -ing ends with the velar ng, not a hard g. Say it quickly, with the main stress on 'doing'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or blunt. It shuts a request down firmly and can sound rude if said to a boss, a customer or a stranger.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in casual speech among friends, family and coworkers when they refuse a request or dismiss an idea, often with a laugh. Answers such as 'No way' or 'Not a chance' are close alternatives, and a softer reply like 'I'd love to, but I can't' is better in polite settings. Its everyday meaning is refusal, not a neutral report of what is happening.

distinctions.note: 'No way' is equally informal and often expresses surprise or disbelief as well as refusal, so it is less purely a rejection.
'Not a chance' suggests that something is extremely unlikely, while 'nothing doing' is a direct refusal of a specific request.

examples.everyday: Can I borrow ten bucks until Friday? Nothing doing, I'm broke too.
examples.professional: We asked the vendor for a discount on renewal, but their answer was nothing doing; the price stays the same.
examples.analytical: When the reformers asked for a second vote, the leadership's reply was a flat nothing doing, and the debate was over.

nuance.analogy: It works like a closed door with a sign on it: the answer is clear, and no one needs to explain.
nuance.etymology: An American colloquial phrase combining 'nothing' and 'doing' (in the sense of activity); its exact origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Answering a neutral question such as 'What are you doing this weekend?' with 'Nothing doing', which sounds like a refusal rather than 'Nothing much'.
Pronouncing the th in 'nothing' as a d or s sound instead of the voiceless English th.

senses.definition: A lump; a block.
A piece of marijuana.
A chicken nugget.

core.definition: A small lump or chunk. Informally, a chicken nugget, or a bud of marijuana.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short, relaxed vowel of 'cup' and end with a hard g. It rhymes with 'rug' and 'mug'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to casual; the cannabis sense is informal and can be considered unprofessional or drug-related depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use nug informally as a short form of chicken nugget, usually in the plural ('chicken nugs'). In cannabis contexts it refers to a small bud, mainly among young people or in legal dispensaries. Outside these informal settings, people normally say 'nugget' or 'chunk', and it sounds out of place in professional writing.

distinctions.note: Nugget is the standard word for a small lump or chicken piece; nug is a clipped, informal form used mostly in speech.
Chunk is a general, neutral word for a thick piece of something; nug is informal and often refers to a specific food or cannabis bud.

examples.everyday: Can we get a ten-piece of chicken nugs with honey mustard for the kids?
examples.professional: The lab found a small nug of metal in the sample, so we need to recheck the filter before sending the report.
examples.analytical: Nug is a clipped slang form of nugget, showing how informal speech shortens words to fit everyday rhythm.

nuance.analogy: A nug is a small, dense lump, like a little clump of dough that has been pinched off.
nuance.etymology: Clipped form of nugget, itself of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Using nug in formal writing or professional emails where nugget or piece is expected.
Saying it with a long u sound, as 'noog', instead of the short vowel of 'cup'.

senses.definition: To count.
senses.example: Before the audit, the clerk had to numerate every box in the warehouse, one by one.

senses.definition: Having numeracy.
senses.example: Her grandmother was numerate enough to run the family bakery's books without a calculator.

core.definition: Able to understand and work with numbers confidently in everyday life and in work.

pronunciation.tip: The adjective ends in a short 'it', while the verb is 'NOO-mer-ayt'. Americans say the first syllable as 'oo', and the stress is on NOO.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a useful skill that educators and employers value.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use numerate most in education, policy and workplace discussions, such as 'We need a numerate workforce'. In everyday talk people more often say 'good with numbers' or 'comfortable with math'. The verb sense 'to count' is rare in American English and sounds old-fashioned.

distinctions.note: Numeric describes data made of numbers or digits, while numerate describes a person who is skilled with numbers.
Mathematical describes a subject or a formal method, while numerate describes everyday comfort and reasoning with numbers.

examples.everyday: My dad is numerate enough to check the restaurant bill in his head before the card reader comes out.
examples.professional: We need numerate analysts who can question a chart before they trust the conclusion it shows.
examples.analytical: A numerate public is better able to judge claims about risk, probability and medical benefit.

nuance.analogy: Being numerate is like being literate with numbers: you can read the figures and understand what they say.
nuance.etymology: From Latin numerare, meaning 'to count,' from numerus.
common_mistakes: Saying numerate for a tool or method; it describes a person's skill.
Using the verb form 'NOO-mer-ayt' for the adjective; the adjective ends in 'it'.

numerate.etymology: From Latin *numerātus*, perfect past participle of *numerō* (see *-ate*).

senses.definition: To make dark; to overshadow.
senses.example: The squid's ink obfuscated its presence.

senses.definition: To deliberately make more confusing in order to conceal the truth.
senses.example: obfuscate facts

senses.definition: To alter code while preserving its behavior but concealing its structure and intent.
senses.example: We need to obfuscate these classes before we ship the final release.

core.definition: To make something unclear or confusing on purpose, so that the truth or real meaning is hidden.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AHB. The middle syllables are reduced to 'fuh', and the word ends with the long a of 'skate', not 'skit'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies deliberate dishonesty or evasion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'obfuscate' in politics, law, business, and academic criticism when someone muddies an issue on purpose. In casual talk, people say 'muddy the waters' or 'dodge the question' instead. Using it in a friendly chat might sound a little showy.

distinctions.note: Confuse can be accidental; obfuscate always implies intent to hide the truth.
Equivocate means to speak ambiguously to avoid commitment; obfuscate is broader and includes deliberately complicating a topic.

examples.everyday: When I asked my roommate who broke the coffee maker, he just started talking about the new filters to obfuscate the question.
examples.professional: Please stop obfuscating the timeline in your status updates, because the team needs to know which deliverables are actually late.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that corporate disclosures often obfuscate material risks through dense jargon, even when every individual sentence is technically accurate.

nuance.analogy: To obfuscate is like fogging a window: the view is still there, but it is hidden behind a deliberate haze.
nuance.etymology: From Latin obfuscare, 'to darken', from ob- 'over' plus fuscare 'to darken', from fuscus 'dark'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle 'fus' like 'fuse'; it is 'fuh-SKAY' in the stressed syllable of obfuscation, and the first syllable is 'AHB'.
Using obfuscate for simple mistakes; it implies intent, so do not use it when someone is only unclear by accident.

obfuscate.etymology: The adjective is, in Middle English, the verb in 1536; either Middle French *obfusquer*, from Old French *offusquer*, or directly from Late Latin *offuscātus*, the perfect passive participle of *offuscō* (see *-ate* and *-ate*), from Latin *ob-* + *fuscō*…

senses.definition: The difference between a measured value of a quantity and its true value.

core.definition: The difference between a measured value of a quantity and its true value, caused by limits in measurement or in the observer.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on VAY in observational and on the first syllable of error. The final syllable of error is a weak r-colored schwa, so it is 'EHR-ur', not 'eh-ror'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a measurement limit and does not imply a serious mistake.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in science, engineering and statistics to describe the uncertainty that every measurement has. In everyday speech, people say 'margin of error' or 'off by a little' instead. A natural reply to a report is 'Fine, but what's the margin of error?'

distinctions.note: Measurement error is the broader term for any gap between measured and true values; observational error is often used in astronomy and observation-based science.
Sampling error comes from which units were chosen; observational error comes from measuring the chosen units.
Random error varies unpredictably from one measurement to the next, while observational error can also be systematic.

examples.everyday: The thermometer said 71, but I think that's just observational error on my part.
examples.professional: We averaged five readings to reduce observational error before fitting the calibration curve.
examples.analytical: Any report of a measured quantity must acknowledge observational error, since the true value is never directly known.

nuance.analogy: Like reading a bathroom scale that jumps between two numbers: the gap between what it shows and your true weight is the error.
nuance.etymology: From observational plus error, from Latin errare 'to wander, go astray'.
common_mistakes: Thinking it means only mistakes made by the observer; it includes limits of instruments.
Using the plural errors incorrectly; in statistics, say observational errors when you mean several.

senses.definition: The quality of being obstreperous.

core.definition: The quality of being loud, unruly, and defiant, refusing to be quiet or controlled.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on STREP. The ending -ness is weak and short, sounding like 'nis', and the middle syllables are reduced, so do not pronounce every vowel clearly.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It names a noisy, defiant quality that others find irritating or disruptive.
nuance.usage_note: This is a formal noun. Americans would normally say he was being loud or she wouldn't stop arguing in conversation. You will see it in essays, reviews, or formal descriptions of a difficult person or group. Using it in a casual chat may sound stiff or overly literary.

distinctions.note: Defiance is a general refusal to obey; obstreperousness focuses on noisy, disruptive resistance.
Rowdiness is an everyday word for rough, boisterous behavior; obstreperousness is more formal and stresses argumentative resistance.

collocations: the sheer obstreperousness of the protest

examples.everyday: The kids' obstreperousness during the long car ride finally made Dad pull over.
examples.professional: The team's obstreperousness in the planning meeting slowed every decision for two weeks.
examples.analytical: Many critics read the novel's obstreperousness not as rudeness but as a principled refusal to accept the household's rules.

nuance.analogy: It is like the noise of a crowd at a stadium that will not settle down no matter how many times the referee blows the whistle.
nuance.etymology: From obstreperous, from Latin obstreperus, 'noisy, clamorous,' from obstrepere, 'to make a noise against.'
common_mistakes: Using it as a verb or adjective; the noun is obstreperousness, while the adjective is obstreperous.
Mispronouncing the middle syllables with full vowels, making it sound like 'ob-stre-PER-oo-ness'.
Using it for mere shyness or quiet, which is the opposite meaning.

senses.definition: The act of obviating; deterrence or prevention.
senses.example: Installing a fence was the surest obviation of further break-ins on our quiet street.

core.definition: The act of removing or preventing a difficulty or need so that it no longer arises.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on AY, with secondary stress on the first syllable. Say the middle syllable quickly as 'vee,' and do not stress it. Many learners mistakenly place the main stress on 'vee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a process of prevention and carries a formal, technical tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use obviation in everyday conversation. It appears in legal, academic, and bureaucratic writing, where a writer wants to say that a need or problem has been removed. In plain English you would usually say prevention, elimination, or avoiding the need for something.

distinctions.note: Prevention is a common general word for stopping something from happening, while obviation specifically means making a difficulty unnecessary.
Avoidance suggests staying away from something, while obviation means removing the need for it altogether.

examples.professional: The automated checks lead to the obviation of manual review for routine records.
examples.analytical: The theory's strength lies in its obviation of the dualism that troubled earlier accounts.

nuance.analogy: Like building a bridge so that no one needs to swim across the river.
nuance.etymology: From Latin obviare, 'to meet in the way, prevent,' from obvius 'in the way.'
common_mistakes: Confusing obviation with obviousness, which means the quality of being plain.
Using it in everyday talk where prevention or avoiding the need is more natural.

obviation.etymology: From Middle English *obviacioun*, from Medieval Latin *obviātiō*.

senses.definition: (dated, historical) Someone having one-eighth black ancestry.
senses.label: dated, historical

senses.definition: (dated, historical) Someone having 1/64th black ancestry: the child of a quintoon and a white man.
senses.example: Nineteenth-century novels often cast an octoroon as a tragic figure caught between two worlds.
senses.label: dated, historical

core.definition: A historical term for a person with one-eighth Black ancestry; the term is offensive and considered archaic.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, and keep the r sound in the middle of the word. Do not say the final syllable as roon with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because the term was used in racial classification and is now considered offensive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans now avoid this term except when discussing history, literature or the legal and social history of race classification. In modern conversation, use descriptive phrases or the person's own identity. The term appears in 19th-century novels and historical records.

distinctions.note: A quadroon had one-quarter Black ancestry, while an octoroon had one-eighth; both are archaic racial classifications.
Mulatto usually meant one Black and one white parent, while octoroon was a finer racial classification.

examples.everyday: In the history class, we talked about how the term octoroon was used in old census and legal records.
examples.professional: The archive note explains that the word octoroon appears in the 19th-century records and should be presented with historical context.
examples.analytical: The category octoroon reflects a racial taxonomy that assigned social status by fractional ancestry, a classification that modern scholarship rejects.

nuance.analogy: Octoroon is like an old map that reflects outdated and harmful beliefs; you study it to understand history, not to use it as a description.
nuance.etymology: Coined in the 19th century on the pattern of quadroon, from Latin octo eight.
common_mistakes: Using octoroon as a neutral description of someone today.
Pronouncing it oct-uh-ROON or with the wrong stress.

senses.definition: An odd or strange thing or opinion.
A strange person; an oddball.
Strangeness.

core.definition: An odd or strange thing, person or characteristic that stands out as unusual and draws attention.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AHD, and make the middle syllable very short and reduced, like the i in sit. The final syllable is a clear ee sound, not a long ay.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes something strange without strong judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use oddity in writing and polite speech for something strange, such as a curiosity in a collection or an unusual quirk in a process. In casual talk, people more often say quirk, weird thing or oddball. Calling a person an oddity can sound stiff rather than friendly.

distinctions.note: A quirk is a small, harmless habit or trait; an oddity can be a larger or more striking unusual thing.
A curiosity is interesting and often valued; an oddity stresses strangeness and can be less positive.

examples.everyday: It's a strange oddity: the store is open at midnight but closed on Sundays.
examples.professional: The spike in conversion rates on Tuesdays is an oddity we should check before we present the results.
examples.analytical: Scholars treat the sudden shift in tone in some prophetic books as an oddity that invites questions about how they were composed.

nuance.analogy: Like a stone with an unusual pattern on a beach, an oddity catches the eye because it departs from the usual.
nuance.etymology: From odd plus the suffix -ity, from Latin -itas, a state or quality.
common_mistakes: Using oddity for a whole group; it refers to one thing or person.
Stressing the last syllable; say AHD-ih-tee with stress on the first syllable.

core.definition: A unit of dry measure in the Bible, about a tenth of an ephah, and the amount that one omer holds.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on OH, and the second syllable reduces to a short 'mer'. The final word full rhymes with pull, not with fuel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: No standard English word omer-full exists, so the headword is most likely a hyphenated form of omer, the measure of manna in Exodus 16. In American Bible study, people say 'an omer of manna' or 'a full omer', so 'omer-full' should be treated as a phrase, not a dictionary term. Use it only when describing the measure in a sermon or Bible class.

distinctions.note: In Leviticus 23, omer can also mean a sheaf of grain offered at the Passover season, not a unit of measure.
An ephah is a larger dry measure, and an omer is one tenth of it.

examples.everyday: The group spent a while on Exodus 16, where every family had to gather exactly an omer of manna each morning.
examples.professional: In my lesson on Exodus 16, I explain that the omer was a daily measure, about a tenth of an ephah, so each household received the same portion.
examples.analytical: The rule that each person gather exactly one omer, no more and no less, presents the manna as a lesson in trust rather than hoarding.

nuance.analogy: A full omer is like a measuring cup of flour in a recipe: a fixed, small share that is enough for the day.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew 'omer, meaning a sheaf or a measure.
common_mistakes: Treating omer as a measure of weight or time; it is a dry-volume measure.
Assuming omer-full is a standard English term instead of a phrase built from omer.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word 'omer means a sheaf or a measure. Exodus 16:16 says each person should gather an omer of manna for his household. Exodus 16:36 explains that an omer is one tenth of an ephah. Leviticus 23:10-11 describes a sheaf of firstfruits, also called an omer, offered before the Lord at the beginning of the harvest.

senses.definition: Being sold at a big discount to clear out old stock.

core.definition: Being sold at a much lower price to get rid of old or extra stock, often marked with a clearance sign in a store.

pronunciation.tip: The word on is a weak function word, so it is pronounced quickly as ahn, and the stress falls on CLEAR in clearance. The r in clear is strong, so say it clearly.

nuance.connotation: Positive for shoppers, because it means a good deal. It can sound slightly negative if it suggests the item is old or unwanted.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this in stores, on shopping apps, and in everyday conversation about bargains. You might say the jacket is on clearance or I got these on clearance. A natural reply is Nice, that's a great deal! Americans may also say on sale for a regular discount, but on clearance usually means a bigger markdown on leftover items.

distinctions.note: On sale is a general discount on regular merchandise, while on clearance usually means older or leftover stock sold at a much larger discount.
A clearance sale is an event where many items are discounted; on clearance describes a single item or a category that is discounted.

examples.everyday: I bought these boots on clearance at the mall, so I got them for half the price.
examples.professional: The store manager said the winter coats are on clearance this week, so we should check the inventory list before the next delivery.
examples.analytical: Economists note that goods on clearance signal a shift in demand, as retailers reduce prices to move surplus stock.

nuance.analogy: On clearance is like a fire sale for old stock: the store wants to clear the shelves before the next season arrives.
nuance.etymology: Clearance comes from the verb clear, from Old French cleir, from Latin clarus (bright, clear), and the sense of getting rid of stock developed in English commerce.
common_mistakes: Saying in clearance instead of on clearance; Americans use on for items on sale at a reduced price.
Stressing the wrong syllable in clearance (klih-RANCE is wrong; the stress is on CLEAR).

conversation.text: All the patio furniture is on clearance now that summer's over.
I found this coat on clearance for thirty dollars.
Are these on clearance, or are they regular price?

senses.definition: Undecided; wavering in one's opinion.
senses.example: I am still on the fence about which way to vote.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see on,‎ the,‎ fence.

core.definition: Undecided and unable to choose between two options or opinions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FENCE, which ends in a voiceless s sound. Do not add a vowel after the n in fence.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes indecision without judging it harshly, though it can sound slightly weak in a workplace.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'I'm still on the fence about it' when they have not made up their minds. It is common in meetings, shopping, and family decisions. You can say 'I'm on the fence' to a colleague who asks for your vote. A natural reply is 'Fair enough, let's revisit it next week.'

distinctions.note: Undecided is neutral and general; on the fence implies you are weighing two clear sides and leaning neither way.
On the side of means supporting one option; on the fence means supporting neither yet.

examples.everyday: I'm still on the fence about the blue couch, so let's look at it again tomorrow.
examples.professional: A few of the directors are still on the fence about moving the project to the new platform.
examples.analytical: A person who remains on the fence may be exercising epistemic caution, withholding judgment until the evidence is strong enough.

nuance.analogy: Like someone standing on a fence post between two yards, not yet stepping down to either side.
common_mistakes: Saying 'in the fence' instead of 'on the fence'.
Using 'on the fence' to mean physically sitting on a fence in a formal sentence where it sounds odd.

conversation.text: I'm on the fence about going to the reunion.
Half the team is still on the fence about the new process.
"Are you buying the car?" "I'm still on the fence."
A few people are on the fence, so let's share more data.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to the quality of something that oozes.
senses.example: The oozy mud sucked at our boots with every step across the marsh.

core.definition: Covered in, full of, or resembling a thick, slow-moving, semi-liquid substance such as mud, sludge or sticky goo.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the vowel a long oo, like the word 'ooze'. Do not add a second stress on the final -y, which is a light 'ee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. It usually describes something unpleasant, such as a wet, sticky, or gooey surface, but it can be mildly neutral for food like melted cheese.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'oozy' casually to describe mud, wet cheese, sticky sauces, or a damp, slimy surface. It is not a formal word, and you will hear it more in speech than in writing. For a verb, Americans say 'the wound oozes' or 'the sauce oozes out,' not 'oozy.'

distinctions.note: Sticky describes something that clings to surfaces; oozy describes something that seeps or flows slowly.
Slimy suggests a repulsive, mucus-like texture and is stronger than oozy, which can describe food or mud without disgust.
Gooey is informal and often pleasant, as in gooey brownies; oozy is more neutral or negative.

examples.everyday: That sandwich was so oozy with melted cheese that I needed three napkins.
examples.professional: The sample came out oozy and inconsistent, so we need to rerun the extraction before analyzing it.
examples.analytical: The poem makes the swamp oozy and decaying, so the reader feels the rot beneath the surface of the landscape.

nuance.analogy: Like warm melted cheese that spreads slowly and will not hold its shape.
nuance.etymology: From ooze plus the suffix -y; ooze comes from Old English wos, meaning juice or moisture.
common_mistakes: Using oozy as a verb: say 'the paint oozes,' not 'the paint oozy.'
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.

senses.definition: Located directly across from something else, or from each other.
senses.example: She saw him walking on the opposite side of the road.

senses.definition: Facing in the other direction.
senses.example: They were moving in opposite directions.

senses.definition: Of either of two complementary or mutually exclusive things.
senses.example: He is attracted to the opposite sex.

senses.definition: Extremely different; inconsistent; contrary; antagonistic.
senses.example: Their views on the budget were completely opposite, so the meeting ended in argument.

senses.definition: Of leaves and flowers, positioned directly across from each other on a stem.
Something or someone opposite to something or someone else.
senses.example: She is the opposite of her ex-boyfriend who abused her both physically and verbally nearly every day for five years. She now works as an advocate and supportive listener for others who have endured abusive relationships.

senses.definition: A person or thing that is importantly (substantively) different from someone or something else.
senses.example: She is the opposite of her ex-boyfriend who abused her both physically and verbally nearly every day for five years. She now works as an advocate and supportive listener for others who have endured abusive relationships.

senses.definition: Especially, one that is different to the extreme degree of being the reverse.
senses.example: She is the opposite of her ex-boyfriend who abused her both physically and verbally nearly every day for five years. She now works as an advocate and supportive listener for others who have endured abusive relationships.

senses.definition: An opponent.
senses.example: The dogfighter fought closely with his opposite.

senses.definition: A counterpart.
senses.example: The Swedish diplomat worked closely with his opposite from Denmark.

senses.definition: An antonym.
senses.example: "Up" is the opposite of "down".

senses.definition: An additive inverse.
senses.example: In algebra, the opposite of five is negative five, since they sum to zero.

senses.definition: In an opposite position.
senses.example: I was on my seat and she stood opposite.

senses.definition: On another channel at the same time.
senses.example: The station aired the debate live, while the other network ran a cooking show opposite.

senses.definition: Facing, or across from.
senses.example: There’s a bus stop opposite the faculty entrance, right on the other side of the road.

senses.definition: In a complementary role to.
senses.example: He played opposite Marilyn Monroe.

senses.definition: On another channel at the same time.
senses.example: The game show Just Men! aired opposite The Young and the Restless on CBS.

core.definition: Located directly across from something else, or facing the other way; completely different in direction, position or effect.
