nuance.connotation: Positive
nuance.usage_note: In American public life, pluralism usually means respect for many groups and beliefs living together, which is a positive civic value. In philosophy and theology it names a specific theory that many distinct kinds of value or being are real and cannot be reduced to one. Use the philosophical sense only in academic or technical conversation, and clarify which sense you mean.

distinctions.note: Monism holds that reality is ultimately one thing or one principle, while pluralism holds that there are many fundamental things or values.
Diversity describes the fact of many different people or things, whereas pluralism is a philosophical or political position about how those differences should be understood or respected.

examples.everyday: My neighbor says the city's pluralism is what makes this place feel so alive.
examples.professional: Our product team wants a pluralism of design choices, so we are testing several onboarding paths instead of one.
examples.analytical: Value pluralism holds that goods such as liberty and equality can conflict without any single master value resolving the conflict.

nuance.analogy: A pluralist is like a potluck where many distinct dishes each keep their own flavor, instead of being blended into one soup.
nuance.etymology: From Latin pluralis (plural), with the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Using pluralism to mean simply having many people, when the word implies a principled stance.
Pronouncing the stress on the second syllable as in 'plu-RAL-ism'.

senses.definition: A person who holds multiple offices, especially a clergyman who holds more than one ecclesiastical benefice.
senses.example: The eighteenth-century pluralist collected the incomes of three parishes while living in London.

senses.definition: An advocate of pluralism (in all senses)
senses.example: As a committed pluralist, she argued that the city should fund schools representing every faith and culture.

senses.definition: Of, or related to pluralism.
senses.example: The pluralist society of the city welcomed immigrants from dozens of different countries.

core.definition: A person who believes that society, reality or moral values have many legitimate forms, and who supports pluralism.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the r is pronounced clearly. The final -ist is a short 'ist', not 'eest'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral in academic and political discussion, though critics may use it to suggest someone is soft on truth. The ecclesiastical sense (a clergyman holding several church offices) is rare today.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'pluralist' mainly in philosophy, politics and social commentary, for someone who welcomes many groups, faiths or viewpoints. You will hear it in discussions of democracy and public life. In casual talk, people more often say 'someone who's open to different views'.

distinctions.note: A relativist holds that truth itself depends on the perspective, while a pluralist may accept several values or views and still believe some are better than others.
Multicultural describes a society with many cultures; pluralist names a principle about how people should live together with those differences.

examples.everyday: My sister is a pluralist, so she loves that our neighborhood has so many kinds of food and churches.
examples.professional: As a pluralist, she argued the advisory board should include voices from every region we serve.
examples.analytical: Isaiah Berlin is often described as a value pluralist, because he held that genuine human goods can conflict without one being rationally ranked above the rest.

nuance.analogy: A pluralist is like a potluck host who expects many dishes on one table and sees the variety as the point.
nuance.etymology: From Latin plūrālis, 'of more than one', from plūs, 'more'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle vowel as 'ah' instead of the short 'uh' in 'PLUR-uh-list'.
Using 'pluralist' to mean simply someone who is diverse or has many friends, when it names a belief or principle.

senses.definition: A stochastic process in which events occur continually and independently of one another.

core.definition: A random process in which events occur continuously and independently at a constant average rate over time or space.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'PRAH' in 'process' most strongly and keep the first word's stress light. The 'ss' in 'process' is a clear 's,' and the final syllable is short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in probability, queueing theory, reliability and data science courses or papers. It is not used in casual conversation. In a meeting, saying 'we modeled arrivals as a Poisson process' is a clear and normal statement.

distinctions.note: A Markov process depends on the current state, while a Poisson process has independent increments at a constant rate.
A stochastic process is the general category; a Poisson process is one specific type.

examples.everyday: My brother is studying queueing theory and says customer arrivals can be modeled as a Poisson process.
examples.professional: We modeled server failures as a Poisson process so the team could estimate the chance of more than two outages a week.
examples.analytical: A Poisson process is characterized by independent increments whose counts follow a Poisson distribution with a constant intensity parameter.

nuance.analogy: It is like raindrops falling on a roof: they arrive at random moments, but on average at a steady rate, and one drop does not affect when the next one falls.
nuance.etymology: Named after Siméon Denis Poisson; process from Latin processus, 'progress or course'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'Poisson process' with the first word pronounced 'POY-son'; it is closer to 'PWAH-sahn' in careful statistics speech, though many Americans say 'POY-son' as well.
Calling it a general stochastic process; it is a specific type with constant rate and independent events.

poisson-process.etymology: From the related concept of *Poisson distribution*.

senses.definition: A person who makes something smooth or shiny.
A tool that makes something smooth or shiny.
A machine that makes something smooth or shiny.
senses.example: Where do you keep the floor-polisher?

senses.definition: A person who refines something.
senses.example: a polisher of stories

core.definition: A person, tool, or machine that rubs a surface until it becomes smooth and shiny.

pronunciation.tip: The Wiktionary IPA with 'oh' is not the American pronunciation of this word; Americans use the 'ah' vowel of cot. The final -er is a fully r-colored syllable, not a separate 'uh' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a tool, machine, or worker and carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: In American English this word is used mostly for equipment, such as a floor polisher or a car polisher, and for workers in trades like jewelry or metalwork. People say 'floor buffer' or 'buffer' for some machines, which is a related but different tool. Outside of these trades, the word is uncommon.

distinctions.note: A buffer usually spins a soft pad to remove light scratches and produce shine, while a polisher can refer to a broader range of tools and products.
A polishing cloth is a hand tool for wiping and shining, while a polisher is usually a powered machine or a person doing the work.
Polish refers to the product or the finish itself, while polisher refers to the person or tool doing the work.

examples.everyday: We rented a floor polisher from the hardware store to fix the dull kitchen tile.
examples.professional: The shop uses a rotary polisher on the aluminum parts before they go to inspection.
examples.analytical: Early industrial polishers were often skilled craftsmen whose hands determined the quality of the finish.

nuance.analogy: Like a sandpaper that has been trained to leave a mirror instead of a rough patch.
nuance.etymology: From polish (verb) plus the agent suffix -er, meaning one who or that which polishes.
common_mistakes: Using the 'oh' vowel from the spelling instead of the American 'ah' vowel.
Using 'polisher' for a person who is socially polished, which is not the meaning here.

senses.definition: Physical contamination, now especially the contamination of the environment by harmful substances, or by disruptive levels of noise, light etc.
senses.example: Pollution levels are almost always higher in cities rather than the countryside, what with the cars, industry and so on.

senses.definition: Something that pollutes; a pollutant.
senses.example: Industrial runoff is the main pollution entering the river from the upstream factories.

senses.definition: Moral or spiritual corruption; impurity, degradation, defilement.
senses.example: Her memoir describes the pollution of ambition that corroded the entire faculty.

senses.definition: (rare) The desecration of something holy or sacred; defilement, profanation.
senses.example: The mob's vandalism of the sanctuary was considered a pollution of holy ground.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Harmful contamination of air, water, soil or other parts of the environment by substances, or by disruptive levels of noise or light.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on LOO, and the last syllable is a weak, reduced -shun. Do not pronounce the o as in 'pole' or the final syllable as a full 'ten'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. The word always implies harm or spoiling, though in technical use it can be described neutrally, such as in a measurement report.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pollution in everyday talk about air quality, smog, water safety and noise, and in news and policy. They pair it with a type, as in 'air pollution,' 'noise pollution,' or 'light pollution,' which is a common concern for astronomers. The moral sense, meaning spiritual or moral corruption, is found mainly in literary or religious writing.

distinctions.note: Contamination is a general term for an unwanted substance entering something, such as bacteria in food, while pollution specifically implies harm to an environment or to the public.
Pollution is the condition or process of contamination; a pollutant is the specific substance that causes it.

examples.everyday: The air pollution in the city has been awful this week, so we've been keeping the windows shut.
examples.professional: The regional report links the rise in ozone pollution to truck traffic around the new warehouse.
examples.analytical: Pollution is not only a chemical fact but also a moral category, since it names what has been made impure and therefore should not be.

nuance.analogy: Pollution is like a drop of ink in a glass of water: a small amount spreads through the whole glass and cannot easily be taken back out.
nuance.etymology: From Latin pollutio, from polluere 'to defile, soil.'
common_mistakes: Saying POL-yoo-shun with a stress on the first syllable; the stress is on LOO.
Using pollution as a countable noun for individual sources; say a pollutant or a source of pollution instead.

pollution.etymology: From Middle English *pollucioun*, *pollucion* (“desecration, impurity”), from Anglo-Norman *pollutiun*, Middle French *pollution*, *pollucion*, and their source, post-classical Latin *pollūtiō* (“defilement, desecration; nocturnal emission”) (4th century),…

senses.definition: In a polygonal manner.

core.definition: In a polygonal manner; with straight sides and angles, forming or arranged as a many-sided shape.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on LIG, as in polygonal, not on the first syllable as in the dictionary's form. End with a clear 'lee' sound, not 'lie'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It describes how something is shaped or divided.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use polygonally outside mathematics, computer graphics, and technical writing. In conversation they would say 'with straight sides' or 'in a many-sided pattern' instead. It is correct and precise, but it sounds stiff in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Polygonal is the adjective describing a shape, while polygonally is the adverb describing how something is formed, drawn, or divided.
Circularly describes arrangement around a circle or curve, whereas polygonally describes straight-edged, many-sided arrangement.

examples.everyday: The quilt is sewn together polygonally, with straight seams and no curves anywhere.
examples.professional: We approximate the terrain polygonally, so the mesh has about fifty thousand triangles.
examples.analytical: The region is partitioned polygonally, which allows the error bound to be computed edge by edge.

nuance.analogy: Like a floor tiled with straight-edged pieces, where every boundary is a line segment.
nuance.etymology: From polygonal plus -ly, from Greek polygōnon 'many-angled'.
common_mistakes: Using polygonally to mean 'in many ways', which is a different idea entirely
Placing the stress on the first syllable instead of LIG

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to a pontiff.
senses.example: The pontifical mass was celebrated in St. Peter's Basilica before thousands of pilgrims.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to a bishop; episcopal.
Of or pertaining to a pope; papal.
Pompous, dignified or dogmatic.
senses.example: His pontifical tone irritated the team, since he lectured everyone on details they already knew.

senses.definition: Splendid; magnificent.
senses.example: The cathedral's pontifical decorations, with gold leaf and jeweled altars, dazzled every visitor.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to the pontifices of Ancient Rome.
senses.example: Scholars study the pontifical records to understand how Roman priests governed religious law.

senses.definition: (poetic) Of or relating to the building or forming of bridges.
senses.example: The poet's pontifical verses celebrated the arching spans that joined the river's two banks.
senses.label: poetic

senses.definition: A book containing the offices, or formulas, used by a pontiff.
senses.example: The old pontifical lay open on the altar, its pages marked with ribbons for each rite.

core.definition: Relating to the pope, or to a bishop; papal or episcopal. Also used to describe someone who acts self-importantly.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, TIF. The first syllable is 'pahn' with the cot-caught vowel, and the final syllable is reduced to 'kul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing church office, but it can sound pompous when used for a person's manner. Context decides the tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in religious, historical, or academic writing, such as 'a pontifical mass' or 'pontifical authority.' In casual speech, people say 'papal' for the pope and 'bishop's' or 'episcopal' for bishops. Calling someone's behavior pontifical is a sharp insult, so it is best saved for writing.

distinctions.note: Papal refers only to the pope and his office, while pontifical can refer to a pope or to a bishop.
Episcopal refers specifically to bishops or to churches governed by bishops, and is the more precise term for that sense.
Pompous describes any self-important person, while pontifical adds the idea of speaking with an air of unquestioned authority.

examples.everyday: My aunt got married in a small church, but the bishop who officiated was in full pontifical robes.
examples.professional: The vendor's pontifical email told our team exactly how the migration would go, with no room for questions.
examples.analytical: The encyclical was received in a pontifical spirit, as though its teaching settled every theological dispute.

nuance.analogy: Like a royal seal on a document, pontifical marks something as coming from the highest church office.
nuance.etymology: From Latin pontifex, 'high priest' or 'bridge-builder', from pons ('bridge') and facere ('to make').
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as 'pon' with an 'aw' vowel that sounds different from American 'pahn'; both are fine in US speech, but avoid stressing the first syllable.
Using pontifical as a general word for 'important'; it refers to church office or a pompous attitude.

senses.definition: A target to shoot at, typically stuffed with feathers or plumage.
senses.example: The archers aimed their arrows at the wooden popinjay swinging from the tall pole.

senses.definition: The green woodpecker, Picus viridis.
senses.example: Birdwatchers in the English countryside often spot a popinjay probing the lawn for ants.

senses.definition: (dated) A vain, gaudy person; someone who is shallow or superficial.
senses.example: Her brother was a vain popinjay who spent hours admiring himself in the mirror.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A vain, showy person who is more concerned with appearance and fashion than with substance or character.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle syllable is reduced to 'in.' The final syllable rhymes with 'day.' The IPA in the list had an unusual vowel sequence; this is the normal American pronunciation.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes someone who is vain, shallow, and showy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in everyday speech; it appears mainly in literature, satire, and older writing. You may hear it in a humorous comment about a vain coworker, but most Americans would say 'show-off,' 'peacock,' or 'dandy' instead. Calling someone a popinjay is an insult, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: Peacock is the everyday, somewhat playful term for a showy person; popinjay is more literary and more contemptuous.
A dandy is a man who cares very much about elegant clothing, while popinjay focuses on vanity and shallowness.
A show-off wants attention for their skills; a popinjay is mainly vain about appearance and social image.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor is such a popinjay; he checks his reflection in every window he walks past.
examples.professional: The consultant is a popinjay who spends more time talking about his title than about the actual results.
examples.analytical: Satire often exposes the popinjay, whose vanity hides an emptiness that the audience can see clearly.

nuance.analogy: A popinjay is like a brightly painted decoy bird: colorful and eye-catching, but hollow inside.
nuance.etymology: From Old French papegai, meaning parrot, probably from Arabic babbaghā, referring to a colorful bird.
common_mistakes: Using it as a friendly compliment; it is always an insult.
Confusing it with 'pop jay' or 'pop-in-jay,' which are not standard spellings.

popinjay.etymology: From Middle English *popinjay*, *popyngeay*, *popingay*, *popejay*, from Anglo-Norman *papegai*, *papejoie* et al. probably from Old Occitan *papagay*, ultimately from Arabic *بَبْغَاء* (“parrot”), of imitative origin.

senses.definition: That has, or is supplied with, inhabitants or content.
senses.example: The remote town is sparsely populated, with fewer than two hundred residents.

core.definition: Having people or animals living in it; inhabited.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final '-ated' reduces to a short 'id' sound. The middle 'pju' is often quick and light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a place's residents without implying any particular quality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use populated with adverbs like densely, sparsely, or heavily, as in 'sparsely populated area.' In data work, populated can also describe fields or records that contain values. It is a common everyday word, while inhabited is more formal and often used for places where people live historically.

distinctions.note: Populous means having a large number of people, while populated only means that people live there.
Inhabited is more formal and often used for historical or long-term residence, while populated is more common in everyday speech.

examples.everyday: The island is sparsely populated, so there are more goats than people out there.
examples.professional: Make sure the required fields are populated before the export runs, or the report will show blanks.
examples.analytical: Early settlement histories describe the region as densely populated, though such accounts often rely on tax records of uncertain accuracy.

nuance.analogy: A populated area is like a room with chairs in it: the room is not empty, even if it is not crowded.
nuance.etymology: From the verb populate, from Late Latin populare, 'to people,' from populus, 'people.'
common_mistakes: Using populated to mean popular, as in 'a populated singer' instead of 'a popular singer.'
Saying 'the population is populated' when the correct phrasing is 'the town is populated by' or 'the area is populated.'

senses.definition: An entrance, entry point, or means of entry.
senses.example: The local library, a portal of knowledge.

senses.definition: A large primary adit as the main entrance to a mine.
senses.example: The miners walked through the portal at dawn and descended into the shaft.

senses.definition: A website or page that acts as an entrance to other websites or pages on the Internet.
senses.example: The new medical portal has dozens of topical categories containing links to hundreds of sites.

senses.definition: An ePortal. (a web-based platform that serves as a gateway to various resources, services, or information, usually tailored for specific organizational or user needs.)
senses.example: I have already inputted my info on the portal.

senses.definition: A short artery that carries blood into the liver.
senses.example: Blood from the intestines drains through the portal vein before reaching the liver.

senses.definition: A magical or technological aperture leading to another location, period in time, or dimension.
senses.example: The wizard stepped through the portal and emerged in a snowy mountain kingdom.

senses.definition: A grandiose and often lavish entrance.
The space, at one end, between opposite trusses when these are terminated by inclined braces.
senses.example: Between the two trusses at the end of the hall, a portal opened under the angled braces.

senses.definition: A prayer book or breviary; a portass.
senses.example: The monk opened his portal and read the morning psalms by candlelight.

senses.definition: A connecting window between volumes, in portal rendering.
senses.example: In the rendering software, each portal connects two rooms of the virtual building.

senses.definition: A lesser gate, where there are two of different dimensions.
senses.example: Behind the main gate stood a smaller portal for carts and servants.

senses.definition: Formerly, a small square corner in a room separated from the rest of an apartment by wainscoting, forming a short passage to another apartment.
senses.example: The old house had a narrow portal beside the wainscoting that led to the neighboring apartment.

senses.definition: The NCAA transfer portal, a database and compliance tool designed to facilitate student-athletes who wish to change schools.
senses.example: The sophomore entered the transfer portal in April after losing his starting position.

senses.definition: To use a portal (magical or technological doorway).
senses.example: The explorers learned to portal across the desert in a single step.

senses.definition: Of or relating to a porta, especially the porta of the liver.
senses.example: the portal vein

core.definition: An entrance or gateway, often a grand one, or an online page that gives access to many websites, tools or services.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The second syllable is a syllabic 'l' with no vowel, so say 'PAWR-tl' with the l sound carrying the syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in everyday use it is practical, and in fiction it can sound mysterious or grand.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'portal' most often for online services, such as a patient portal, customer portal or employee portal. For an ordinary doorway, Americans normally say 'entrance' or 'doorway'. In fantasy and science fiction, 'portal' means a magical gateway to another world.

distinctions.note: Gateway is more general and often figurative, while portal is often a website or formal entrance.
A doorway is an ordinary opening in a wall, while a portal can be large, formal or digital.

examples.everyday: You can see your test results on the patient portal instead of calling the office.
examples.professional: Employees log into the HR portal to update their benefits and submit timesheets.
examples.analytical: Myth often serves as a portal through which a community confronts its deepest fears.

nuance.analogy: Like a grand front door that leads from the street into a whole building of services.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin portale 'gate', from Latin porta 'gate, door'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as a full 'uh-l' or 'ahl' rather than a light syllabic l.
Using 'portal' for an ordinary entrance in casual talk, where 'entrance' or 'doorway' sounds more natural.

portal.etymology: From Middle English *portal*, *porttol*, from Old French *portal* and Medieval Latin *portāle*, from *porta*.

senses.definition: The condition of being positive (in all senses); positivism; optimism.
The result of being positive.
The characteristic of possessing a positive electric charge.

core.definition: A cheerful, optimistic outlook that focuses on the good in situations; also, the quality of being positive in a more technical sense, such as having a positive electric charge.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on -TIV-, with a weaker stress on the first syllable, and the final -ity is a short 'ih-tee'. Do not say the last syllable as 'tee-uh'.

nuance.connotation: Positive in connotation. Americans often use it to praise someone's upbeat attitude, though some people find it overused in self-help culture.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, 'positivity' usually means a cheerful, hopeful attitude, as in 'she brings so much positivity to the team.' It is common in workplaces, on social media, and in self-improvement talk. In technical contexts such as physics or chemistry, it means having a positive charge or a positive result.

distinctions.note: Optimism is the belief that things will turn out well, while positivity is a broader attitude that also focuses on what is good in the present.
Positivity is a general attitude or charge; positivism is a specific philosophical doctrine about knowledge.

examples.everyday: Her positivity gets me through Monday mornings.
examples.professional: The team's positivity helped us recover quickly after the failed launch.
examples.analytical: Many modern readers confuse positivity as a mood with positivism as a philosophy, though the two ideas are unrelated.

nuance.analogy: Positivity is like sunlight in a room: it does not remove every problem, but it makes everything easier to see and work with.
nuance.etymology: From positive plus the suffix -ity, from Latin positivus, 'placed' or 'affirmative'.
common_mistakes: Using 'positivity' as if it means a fact or a proven result rather than an attitude.
Confusing 'positivity' with 'positivism', the philosophical view.

senses.definition: In AI: In Bayesian inference, the updated probability of a hypothesis after taking the observed data into account.
The posterior portions of the human body; especially, the buttocks.
senses.example: After the fall on the ice, his posterior was sore for days.

senses.definition: The probability that a hypothesis is true (calculated by Bayes' theorem).
Following in order or in time.
senses.example: The posterior chapters of the novel were written after the author's divorce.

senses.definition: Nearer the rear or hind end; nearer the caudal end of the body in quadrupeds or the dorsal end in bipeds.
senses.example: The posterior fins of the trout are smaller than the front ones.

senses.definition: Relating to or denoting presentation of a fetus in which the rear or caudal end is nearest the cervix and emerges first at birth.
senses.example: The doctor explained that the baby was in a posterior breech presentation, requiring careful monitoring.

senses.definition: Next to, or facing the main stem or axis.
senses.example: The posterior bracts are attached on the side facing the main stem of the plant.

core.definition: The back part of something, or informally a person's bottom; in Bayesian statistics, the updated probability of a hypothesis after taking the observed data into account.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, STEER, and say the ending as a weak, r-colored 'er'. Avoid stressing the first syllable, which is a common error.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in statistics. In everyday speech, the anatomical sense is informal and can sound crude, so use 'rear' or 'behind' instead.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use posterior in statistics, machine learning, and Bayesian analysis, where it is a precise technical term. In everyday speech, posterior means the buttocks, which is informal and sometimes humorous. Use 'rear' or 'behind' in casual conversation to avoid awkwardness.

distinctions.note: A prior is what you believe before seeing data; the posterior is what you believe after seeing data.
The likelihood measures how probable the data are under a hypothesis; the posterior combines likelihood and prior.

examples.everyday: Stop sitting on your posterior all day and go for a walk with me.
examples.professional: Our team's posterior estimate of churn dropped after we added last month's data, so we changed the forecast.
examples.analytical: The Bayesian posterior is proportional to the likelihood times the prior, so it encodes both the observed data and prior belief.

nuance.analogy: The posterior is like a weather forecast updated after you look out the window: the new information changes your belief.
nuance.etymology: From Latin posterior, comparative of posterus, 'coming after', from post, 'after'.
common_mistakes: Using posterior with an informal anatomical meaning in polite conversation.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'POH-steer-ior', instead of the second.

conversation.text: The posterior combines the prior with the likelihood of the observed data.
The posterior is still wide, so we need more data before we can make a confident call.
In anatomy, posterior just means toward the back of the body.

senses.definition: A flower; a small bouquet; a nosegay.

core.definition: A small bouquet of flowers, often given as a gift or pinned to clothing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -y is a clear 'ee' sound, like 'daisy'. Keep the first vowel long, as in 'pose', not short as in 'posse'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and sentimental; it suggests something small, sweet and personal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use posy mostly in poetry, fiction, or old-fashioned description. In everyday speech people say 'small bouquet' or 'flower arrangement.' Calling a gift a posy sounds charming and a little quaint, so it fits a romantic or nostalgic moment better than a business one.

distinctions.note: A bouquet is any arranged bunch of flowers, while a posy is specifically small and simple, often held in the hand.
A corsage is worn pinned or tied on clothing, as for a dance; a posy is carried or given as a small arrangement.

examples.everyday: She brought me a little posy of daisies from her garden, tied with a blue ribbon.
examples.professional: The florist sent a small posy for the speaker's table, so we'll set it out before the keynote.
examples.analytical: Victorian writers often used the posy as a sentimental emblem, each flower carrying a coded meaning.

nuance.analogy: A posy is a bouquet's little sibling, small enough to hold in one hand.
nuance.etymology: Shortened from 'poesy' (poetry), originally a short motto or verse, later applied to a small bunch of flowers.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a short o, like 'possy'; the vowel is long, POH-zee.
Using posy for any large bouquet; the word means a small one.

senses.definition: If one practices a lot, they become good at it.

core.definition: The more you repeat an activity, the better you become at it, so keep practicing even when you are not yet good.

pronunciation.tip: Link the words smoothly, so 'practice makes' sounds like 'PRAK-tis-mayks'. Stress PER in the adjective perfect, not the second syllable, as in 'per-FECT'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and encouraging. It is often used to comfort someone who is still learning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say practice makes perfect to encourage someone who is struggling, usually a student, child, athlete or colleague. A natural reply is 'I know, I'm trying' or 'Yeah, I need more reps.' Some people joke that practice makes permanent, which is a playful twist, not a correction.

distinctions.vs: Rome wasn't built in a day
distinctions.note: Practice makes perfect focuses on repetition improving skill; Rome wasn't built in a day stresses that big achievements take a long time.

collocations: as they say, practice makes perfect
keep practicing, because practice makes perfect
practice makes perfect in any skill
say practice makes perfect to encourage someone
practice makes perfect, so keep at it

examples.everyday: I've been practicing my Spanish every night, and as my tutor says, practice makes perfect.
examples.professional: Don't worry about the first few presentations; practice makes perfect, so run through the deck twice before Friday.
examples.analytical: The proverb suggests that repetition produces skill, but it does not explain whether the practice is well directed or merely habitual.

nuance.analogy: Practice makes perfect is like a path through tall grass: each walk makes the trail clearer, until the route is easy to follow.
common_mistakes: Using the phrase as a literal promise; it means improvement, not that you will become flawless.
Using the British spelling practise in the noun, which is wrong in American English.

senses.definition: Synonym of komboskini.
senses.example: My grandfather prayed quietly with a knotted prayer rope during his morning walks.

core.definition: A knotted cord used by Eastern Orthodox Christians to count repetitions of a short prayer, such as the Jesus Prayer.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on 'rope', and 'prayer' gets a weaker secondary stress. Both words have a clear American r, so say 'prair' with a strong r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and respectful. It is a religious object with a specific devotional meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use prayer rope mainly in Orthodox churches, monasteries, and discussions of spirituality. In other settings, people might say 'Orthodox prayer rope' or explain it as a 'knotted cord for prayer.' Outside Orthodoxy, the term may be unfamiliar, so explain it briefly when needed.

distinctions.note: A rosary is a Catholic string of beads used to count prayers; a prayer rope is a knotted cord, used especially in Eastern Orthodoxy.
Komboskini is the Greek name for the prayer rope; prayer rope is the English term used in most American writing.

collocations: count prayers on a prayer rope

examples.everyday: The monk at the church gave me a little prayer rope, and he showed me how to count the knots.
examples.professional: In our interfaith workshop, we compared the prayer rope with the rosary as tools for repetitive devotion.
examples.analytical: The prayer rope embodies the Orthodox practice of unceasing prayer, turning a physical object into a disciplined rhythm of attention.

nuance.analogy: A prayer rope is like a counting tool for prayer: each knot marks a repetition, so the mind can rest on the words.
common_mistakes: Saying 'prayer rope' with the stress on 'prayer' in the same way as 'rope'.
Using the word prayer rope for any religious cord, rather than the specific Orthodox devotional item.

senses.definition: To go before, go in front of.
senses.example: Cultural genocide precedes physical genocide.

senses.definition: To cause to be preceded; to preface; to introduce.
senses.example: The editor asked the historian to precede the memoir with a short note on its origins.

senses.definition: To have higher rank than (someone or something else).
senses.example: In the military hierarchy, a colonel precedes a major.

senses.definition: Brief editorial preface (usually to an article or essay).
senses.example: The journal's precede explained why the study had been delayed for two years.

core.definition: To come or go before something else in time, order, rank or place.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, SEED. Do not pronounce the first syllable as 'pre' in 'press'; it is a reduced 'pri'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise, formal word for sequence or rank.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use precede mainly in writing and formal speech, such as in academic papers, ceremonies or legal documents. In everyday talk they usually say 'come before' or 'go before'. The passive 'preceded by' is very common in writing.

distinctions.note: Proceed means to continue or move forward, while precede means to come before; the two are easily confused.
Antecede is rare and technical; precede is the everyday word for coming before.

examples.everyday: The fireworks were preceded by a long speech that nobody could hear.
examples.professional: The sprint review will precede the planning meeting, so please bring your updates.
examples.analytical: The theological claim of grace must precede any account of human response, since the response is itself a gift.

nuance.analogy: Precede is like the opening act at a concert: it comes first, and the main act follows.
nuance.etymology: From Latin praecedere, 'to go before', from prae, 'before', and cedere, 'to go'.
common_mistakes: Confusing precede with proceed: 'Please precede to the exit' is wrong; the word is 'proceed to'.
Writing 'precede from' instead of 'precede' with a direct object or 'be preceded by'.

precede.etymology: From Middle French *précéder*, from Latin *praecēdō*, from *prae-* + *cēdō*.

senses.definition: A condition that requires satisfaction before taking a course of action.
senses.example: A marriage license is a precondition for a wedding.

senses.definition: A medical illness, ailment, or adverse condition that exists before an insurance policy takes effect.
senses.example: Her insurer denied coverage because the knee injury was a precondition that predated the policy.

senses.definition: To condition in advance.
senses.example: Researchers preconditioned the cells in advance to see how they responded to stress.

core.definition: Something that must be true or happen before another action or process can take place.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on -DISH-, with a secondary stress on 'pree'. The ending is a reduced 'un' sound, not 'shun' with a strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a requirement in a neutral, practical way.
nuance.usage_note: In American workplaces, especially software and project planning, 'precondition' is a standard term for something that must be true before a step begins. In insurance, it means a medical condition that existed before coverage started. Everyday speakers usually say 'requirement' or 'what you need first'.

distinctions.note: A 'requirement' is what something needs in general; a 'precondition' is specifically something that must already be in place before an action can begin.
'Prerequisite' is common in school and training contexts for a course or skill; 'precondition' is more common in technical and logical contexts.

examples.everyday: Getting your passport renewed is a precondition for the trip, so let's do that first.
examples.professional: Before we merge the feature branch, the precondition is that all unit tests pass on the staging server.
examples.analytical: Kant treats the possibility of experience as a precondition of knowledge, not something we learn from experience.

nuance.analogy: A recipe step that says 'preheat the oven': the oven must already be hot before the bread can go in.
nuance.etymology: From pre- 'before' and condition, from Latin condicio 'agreement, state'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'precondition' with 'prerequisite' in school contexts; Americans more often say 'prerequisite' for a required course.
Using 'precondition' as a verb in everyday speech; it is mainly a noun.

senses.definition: Of, or relating to the period of innocence before the Fall of man; innocent, unspoiled.

core.definition: Relating to the time before the Fall of humanity in Genesis, when people were innocent and without sin.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on SAIR, with a light secondary stress on 'pree'. The 'r' is pronounced in American speech, and the word ends in a soft 'un' sound, not 'ian' as in 'Ian'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in theology, philosophy, literature and ethics, rarely in ordinary conversation. In a church or Bible study you might hear it when people discuss Eden. Say 'before the Fall' if you want a plainer phrase.

distinctions.note: Prelapsarian refers to the state before the Fall; postlapsarian refers to the state after it, when sin and suffering entered the world.
Innocent is general and everyday; prelapsarian refers specifically to a theological or literary state before the Fall.

examples.everyday: My mom always says kids are born with a kind of prelapsarian innocence.
examples.professional: In the sermon series, the pastor described Eden as the prelapsarian ideal our community works toward.
examples.analytical: Milton's prelapsarian Paradise presents an unfallen order whose loss structures the entire epic narrative.

nuance.analogy: Like a photograph taken before a flood damages the film, showing the original, untouched scene.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'prae-' (before) and 'lapsus' (the fall) plus '-arian', coined in English theology.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'postlapsarian', the opposite term.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying 'pre-LAP-sair-ee-un' instead of 'pree-lap-SAIR-ee-un'.
nuance.biblical_note: The word itself is not in Scripture; it is a theological term for the condition described in Genesis 2 and 3. The Hebrew word for 'Adam' (adam) and the Hebrew word for 'sin' (chata') appear in the account of the Fall. Key passages: Genesis 2:25 describes the man and his wife as naked and not ashamed, the prelapsarian state of innocence. Genesis 3:1-7 narrates the disobedience and the sudden awareness of shame that marks the Fall. Romans 5:12 says sin entered the world through one man, which theologians use to explain why the human condition is changed after the Fall.

traditions.view: Orthodox theology stresses that the first humans were created good and in communion with God, but it rejects the idea of inherited guilt, seeing the Fall as bringing mortality and corruption rather than guilt passed down.
Catholic teaching holds that Adam and Eve were created in original justice and holiness, and that their sin deprived humanity of this grace, a wound transmitted to all people as original sin.

Protestants generally teach that the Fall corrupted human nature totally, though Reformed and Lutheran views differ on how far the original goodness of creation persists after it, and Anglican and Baptist views vary in emphasis.

senses.definition: To meditate, consider, or plan beforehand; to think about and revolve in the mind beforehand.
senses.example: Prosecutors argued that the defendant had premeditated the robbery for weeks before acting.

core.definition: To plan or think carefully about something in advance, especially a harmful act.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, -MED-. The first syllable is pree, not pre as in pressure. The final -ate is pronounced like the word eight.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative. It is most often used for planning crimes or harmful acts, and it emphasizes that the act was intentional.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use premeditate mostly in legal, police and news contexts, such as premeditated murder. In everyday speech, people usually say plan or think about. Using it for a friendly plan can sound stiff or dramatic.

distinctions.note: Plan is neutral and everyday. Premeditate is formal and stresses that something was thought out beforehand, often with harmful intent.
Intend focuses on a goal. Premeditate focuses on the thinking and planning done in advance.

examples.everyday: I don't think he premeditated the argument; he just got angry.
examples.professional: The team did not premeditate the outage, but they should have caught the warning signs.
examples.analytical: Whether an agent can premeditate a choice depends on how we define intention and foresight.

nuance.analogy: Like writing a route on a map before a road trip, so every turn is decided before you leave.
nuance.etymology: From Latin praemeditari, to think beforehand, from prae (before) and meditari (to think over).
common_mistakes: Confusing premeditate with predict or prevent; it means to plan or think ahead.
Pronouncing the first syllable as pre- in pressure; say pree-.

senses.definition: The state of being preoccupied or an idea that preoccupies the mind; enthrallment.
The act of occupying something before someone else.

core.definition: Something that fills your thoughts so much that you give it most of your attention.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on -PAY-, the fourth syllable. The middle syllables are quick and reduced, and the first vowel in ock is the short ah of cot in General American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, because it often implies that someone is distracted or fixated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use preoccupation to describe a worry or interest that dominates someone's attention, for example being preoccupied with work. In casual speech, people often say I've been so distracted or I've got a lot on my mind. The noun is more formal than the adjective preoccupied, which is very common in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: An obsession is an intense, sometimes unhealthy fixation. A preoccupation can be milder and more temporary.
A distraction pulls your attention away from something. A preoccupation is a thought that fills your mind and keeps returning.

examples.everyday: Sorry I forgot your call, my preoccupation with the kids' schedule took over.
examples.professional: Our main preoccupation this quarter is reducing the cost of cloud storage.
examples.analytical: A philosopher's preoccupation with certainty often hides a deeper concern about meaning.

nuance.analogy: A preoccupation is like a song stuck in your head: it keeps playing no matter what else you are doing.
nuance.etymology: From Latin praeoccupare, to take possession beforehand, from prae (before) and occupare (to seize).
common_mistakes: Using preoccupation without with, as in preoccupation of work; say preoccupation with work.
Confusing preoccupation with occupation, which means a job or activity.

senses.definition: A warning of a future event; an omen.
senses.example: The sudden silence in the forest was a presage of the coming storm.

senses.definition: An intuition of a future event; a presentiment.
senses.example: I had a strange presage that something was wrong before the phone even rang.

senses.definition: To predict or foretell something.
senses.example: Those dark clouds presage a severe thunderstorm rolling in over the valley tonight.

senses.definition: To make a prediction.
senses.example: Nobody dared to presage how the election would turn out, given the polling errors.

senses.definition: To have a presentiment of; to feel beforehand; to foreknow.
senses.example: My grandmother seemed to presage every illness in the family before anyone else noticed symptoms.

core.definition: A sign or warning that something important is about to happen, often something bad.

pronunciation.tip: As a noun, the stress falls on the first syllable, PREH. As a verb, the stress shifts to the second syllable: pri-SAYJ. Keep the g soft, like the j in judge.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It usually signals a warning or ominous sign, though it can also be used for a hopeful feeling.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use presage in formal writing, literature, and speeches. In everyday speech they would say sign, warning, or feeling. The verb form, to presage something, is common in journalism and essays. It often sounds heavy, so use it when a sense of foreboding is part of the point.

distinctions.note: An omen is a sign of good or bad luck, often folkloric, while a presage is more of a warning or intuition about what is coming.
Portent is more dramatic and often refers to something big and unusual, while presage is more general and subtler.

examples.everyday: The sudden silence at the table was a presage that someone was about to say something awkward.
examples.professional: The early drop in user engagement may presage a larger problem with the new onboarding flow.
examples.analytical: In Hamlet, the ghost's appearance serves as a presage of the political corruption that will destroy the court.

nuance.analogy: A presage is like dark clouds gathering before a storm: you feel the change coming before it arrives.
nuance.etymology: From Latin praesagium, from praesagire, to perceive beforehand, from prae- before plus sagire, to perceive keenly.
common_mistakes: Using the noun stress pattern PREH-sij for the verb, which is pri-SAYJ.
Using presage as a casual word for warning, which can sound overly dramatic in everyday speech.

senses.definition: An experience of something in advance.
An advance showing of a film, exhibition etc.
senses.example: Critics were invited to a preview of the new museum exhibition last Thursday evening.

senses.definition: A short collection of clips edited together to advertise a film, television show, etc. a trailer.
senses.example: Before the movie opened, the theater played a preview that gave away the best jokes.

senses.definition: The act of seeing something in advance.
senses.example: (Can we add an example for this sense?)

senses.definition: A facility for viewing and checking a document or photo, or changes to it, before saving or printing it.
senses.example: Use the print preview to check the margins before sending the report to the printer.

senses.definition: To show or watch something, or part of it, before it is complete.
senses.example: The studio will preview the pilot episode for focus groups before it airs.

senses.definition: To show something in advance, a facility for viewing and checking a document or photo, or changes to it, before saving or printing it.
senses.example: Before printing, I always preview the spreadsheet to catch formatting errors.

core.definition: An advance look at a movie, show, product or document before it is released or fully finished.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable for both the noun and the verb. The ending 'view' is pronounced 'vyoo', so do not stress the second syllable as in 'pre-VIEW'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral: a preview promises a sneak look and builds interest.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use preview for a movie trailer, a sneak peek at a show, or a software feature like print preview. In everyday speech, 'trailer' is the usual word for the ad clip of a movie, while 'preview' can also mean an early screening. Saying 'I got a preview' is a natural way to say you saw something early.

distinctions.note: A trailer is a short promotional clip for a film; a preview can be a trailer, but it can also be an early screening or any advance look.
A review is an evaluation given after something is done or released; a preview is an advance look before it is complete or public.

examples.everyday: Did you see the preview for that new comedy? It looks hilarious.
examples.professional: Can you send me a preview of the dashboard before the client meeting tomorrow?
examples.analytical: A preview of a text reveals its structure, but it cannot show how the argument develops.

nuance.analogy: A preview is like a tasting menu: a small sample that lets you decide what to order.
nuance.etymology: From pre- 'before' and view, from Old French veue, 'sight'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (pre-VIEW), which is a common error for the verb.
Using preview to mean a critical evaluation; that meaning belongs to review.

preview.etymology: From *pre-* + *view*; compare, past participle of *preveoir* (“to foresee”).

senses.definition: To eat (as prey).
senses.example: Owls prey on small mammals, such as mice.

senses.definition: To exploit or victimize.
senses.example: Loan sharks preyed on desperate families who had no other options for credit.

senses.definition: To weigh heavily upon (a person's mind).
senses.example: The unpaid bills preyed on her mind during every sleepless night.

core.definition: To take advantage of and harm people who are weak, vulnerable or easy to trick.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PREY, and 'on' is unstressed, so it is quick and often sounds like 'uhn' or 'un'. Do not confuse it with the homophone 'pray on'.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative: it implies deliberate, repeated targeting of people who cannot easily defend themselves.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use prey on for scammers, bullies, or predators who target the elderly, students, or people in crisis. It is common in news and everyday conversation about fraud and abuse. For animals, it means to hunt and eat, but in people talk it always carries a moral charge.

distinctions.note: Take advantage of can be mild or occasional; prey on implies a pattern of deliberately targeting someone vulnerable.
Target is neutral and can be legitimate, as in target customers; prey on is always negative.

examples.everyday: Be careful with those phone calls; scammers often prey on older people who live alone.
examples.professional: Phishing emails prey on employees who are rushing to approve invoices.
examples.analytical: The novel shows how a corrupt landlord preys on tenants who have no legal protection.

nuance.analogy: A hawk preys on mice; a loan shark preys on desperate borrowers.
nuance.etymology: From Old French preie, 'booty', from Latin praeda, 'plunder'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'pray on', which is a homophone but means to pray about something.
Using 'prey to' instead of 'prey on'; the preposition is always 'on' (or 'upon' in more formal writing).

senses.definition: Capable of producing something, especially in abundance; fertile.
senses.example: The rich volcanic soil made the valley highly productive for generations of farmers.

senses.definition: Yielding good or useful results; constructive.
senses.example: Our weekly meeting was productive, and we finally agreed on the project timeline.

senses.definition: Of, or relating to the creation of goods or services.
senses.example: The factory's productive output rose sharply after the new assembly line opened.

senses.definition: Consistently applicable to any of an open set of words.
senses.example: In English, the suffix -ness is productive, so speakers easily form new nouns with it.

senses.definition: A type of set of natural numbers, related to mathematical logic; a set S is productive if there exists a total recursive function f such that ∀x∈ℕ,Wx⊆S⇒f(x)∈A∖Wx, where Wx is a recursive function whose Gödel number is x.
senses.example: a productive set

senses.definition: Of a cough, producing mucus or sputum from the respiratory tract.
senses.example: Her productive cough brought up thick mucus every morning, so the doctor ordered a chest X-ray.

senses.definition: Of inflammation, producing new tissue.
senses.example: The biopsy showed productive inflammation, with new granulation tissue forming around the wound.

core.definition: Producing a lot of useful results or output; efficient at getting work done.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DUK, the second syllable; the first syllable is a reduced schwa. The final 'tive' is short and unstressed, so avoid giving it a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it praises useful output, though it can sound dry when used of people.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'productive' for people, meetings, days and companies, as in 'That was a productive meeting.' Saying 'a productive day' at the end of work is a common friendly remark. A natural reply is 'Yeah, we got a lot done.' In farming contexts it can also mean fertile.

distinctions.note: Productive focuses on how much is produced; efficient focuses on how little waste or effort is used to produce it.
Fruitful often describes results or ideas that turn out well over time; productive is more about output and work done.

examples.everyday: We had a productive afternoon, so let's grab coffee before the next meeting.
examples.professional: The sprint review was productive, and we closed most of the open tickets.
examples.analytical: A productive argument is one that generates new insights, not merely one that ends in agreement.

nuance.analogy: A productive team is like a well-watered garden: it reliably yields a harvest.
nuance.etymology: From Latin productivus, from producere, 'to bring forth'.
common_mistakes: Using 'high productive' instead of 'high productivity'; 'productive' is the adjective and 'productivity' is the noun.
Using 'productive' to describe a good mood or feelings; it describes output and results.

senses.definition: Great fecundity.
Producing of a large number of literary or artistic works.

core.definition: The quality of producing a large number of offspring, works, or results; great productivity.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, LIF, and keep the other syllables short. The final -cy is a soft see sound, not a hard say sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, suggesting abundance and creativity, though it can sound a bit stiff in conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use prolificacy mainly in formal, literary, or scholarly writing about the output of a writer, artist, or species. In everyday talk people say productivity or the adjective prolific. Using prolificacy in a meeting may sound a little formal, so reserve it for written reviews or essays.

distinctions.note: Productivity measures output relative to effort or time, while prolificacy emphasizes the sheer abundance of what is produced.
Fecundity refers to biological fertility or reproduction, while prolificacy can describe creative or literary output as well.

examples.everyday: Her prolificacy as a painter is amazing, since she finishes a new canvas almost every week.
examples.professional: The team's prolificacy in shipping features is impressive, but we should check whether the quality is holding up.
examples.analytical: The critic admired the prolificacy of the novelist, yet she argued that quantity had sometimes diluted the depth of her characters.

nuance.analogy: Prolificacy is like a fruit tree that bears so much fruit every season that the branches sag.
nuance.etymology: From prolific, from Latin prolificus, fruitful, from proles, offspring, and facere, to make, with the suffix -acy.
common_mistakes: Using prolificacy in casual conversation where productivity or prolific sounds more natural.
Mixing up the noun prolificacy with the adjective prolific when describing a person.

senses.definition: A prom (dance).
senses.example: Our school's promenade was held in the gym, with paper lanterns hanging from the ceiling.

senses.definition: A walk taken for pleasure, display, or exercise; a stroll.
A place where one takes a walk for leisurely pleasure, or for exercise, especially a terrace by the seaside.
senses.example: On warm evenings, couples stroll along the seaside promenade near the old pier.

senses.definition: A dance motion consisting of a walk, done while square dancing.
senses.example: In the square dance, the caller asked us to do a promenade around the circle.

senses.definition: To walk for amusement, show, or exercise.
senses.example: After dinner we promenade along the riverfront to enjoy the cool evening air.

senses.definition: To perform the stylized walk of a square dance.
senses.example: The dancers promenade counterclockwise while the caller announces the next figure.

core.definition: A leisurely walk taken for pleasure, or a public path, often along a waterfront, where people stroll.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on the last syllable, NAYD. The middle syllable is a reduced 'uh', and the first syllable sounds like 'prom' in 'promise'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to pleasant. It sounds slightly formal or old-fashioned, and it often suggests a scenic setting or a stroll meant to be seen.
nuance.usage_note: In American speech, people more often say 'walk', 'stroll', or 'boardwalk' for a seaside path, and promenade is most common in place names and real estate descriptions, such as 'the riverside promenade'. The verb 'to promenade' sounds stylized, so it is used mostly in writing or humorous speech. Americans also use the word for a formal dance figure, but that is uncommon.

distinctions.note: A stroll is a casual, relaxed walk, while a promenade suggests a more formal walk in a designated public area.
A boardwalk is the typical American word for a wooden seaside walkway, whereas promenade describes a paved or landscaped walkway in a city or resort.

examples.everyday: After dinner we took a slow promenade along the waterfront and watched the boats.
examples.professional: The city plans to rebuild the downtown promenade with better lighting and more benches for the office workers.
examples.analytical: The eighteenth-century promenade was less about exercise than about display, a public arena in which status was measured by dress and companionship.

nuance.analogy: A promenade is a walk that is also a small stage: people walk slowly so that others can see them.
nuance.etymology: From French promenade, from promener 'to take for a walk'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in PROM-uh-nade; the stress is on the last syllable.
Using promenade for prom, the school dance, which is a different word.

senses.definition: One who engages or undertakes; a promiser.

core.definition: A person who makes a promise, especially a legally binding promise to pay or perform something under a contract.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, PROM. The middle syllable is a reduced schwa, so say 'PRAH-mih-sur' rather than 'pro-MY-sor'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise legal or contractual term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in contracts, loan documents, and legal or financial discussion. In everyday speech they would say 'the person who promised' or 'the one making the promise' instead. In a contract, the promisor is the party who commits to do something.

distinctions.note: The promisee is the person who receives the promise, while the promisor is the one who makes it.
Promiser is a general word for anyone who makes a promise, while promisor is mostly used in legal and contractual writing.

examples.everyday: I'm the promisor on this lease, so if the rent is late, the landlord will come to me.
examples.professional: The promisor on this contract is our vendor, so they are responsible for meeting the delivery dates.
examples.analytical: In contract theory, the promisor's obligation becomes enforceable only when the promise is supported by consideration.

nuance.analogy: The promisor is like the one who signs the IOU, the person whose signature turns a casual word into a binding commitment.
nuance.etymology: From Latin promissor, from promittere, 'to send forth, promise.'
common_mistakes: Confusing promisor with promisee, which reverses the roles in a contract.
Stressing the wrong syllable as 'pro-MIS-or' instead of PROM-ih-sur.

senses.definition: One who supports something; an advocate.
One who makes a proposal or proposition.
senses.example: The main proponent of the new budget argued that it would cut costs without layoffs.

senses.definition: One who propounds a will for probate.
senses.example: The proponent of the will asked the court to admit the document to probate.

senses.definition: Making proposals; proposing.
senses.example: The proponent parties at the meeting outlined three new ideas for the school budget.

core.definition: A person who strongly supports or argues for an idea, policy, or plan.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on POH, and the last syllable is reduced to 'nunt', not 'nent'. The middle 'o' is a long oh sound, and the first vowel is a quick schwa-like sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It names someone who champions a cause, though it can carry a slightly formal or detached tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in politics, business, academia, and news reporting, often as a formal way to describe a supporter. In casual speech they would more likely say 'a fan of' or 'someone who backs'. It does not describe a legal proponent in most everyday contexts.

distinctions.note: Advocate is more common and can describe someone who speaks for another person. Proponent usually describes someone who champions an idea or policy.
Opponent is the opposite, someone who argues against an idea. Confusing them is a common error.

examples.everyday: My brother is a big proponent of biking to work, and he rides every day.
examples.professional: She is the main proponent of the new deployment process, so ask her about the rollout plan.
examples.analytical: Rawls is a proponent of a theory of justice that prioritizes the least advantaged members of society.

nuance.analogy: Like a coach who cheers loudly for a plan, a proponent is the person pushing an idea forward.
nuance.etymology: From Latin proponere 'to put forward', via proponens.
common_mistakes: Using proponent to mean opponent, which reverses the meaning.
Pronouncing the stress on the last syllable instead of on POH.

proponent.etymology: From Latin *prōpōnēns*, present participle of *prōpōnō* (“to put forward; propose”).

senses.definition: One who supplies provisions.
One who or that which provisions (sets up an account, resources, etc.).
senses.example: The hotel's provisioner ordered fresh linens and food every Tuesday before the weekend guests arrived.

core.definition: A person or company that supplies food, equipment, and other provisions, especially to a ship, expedition, or group.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on VIZH, the second syllable, and the final '-er' is a reduced American 'r' sound, so do not stress the ending. The 'si' sounds like 'zh' as in 'vision'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a descriptive job or role term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: This word is correct American English but is rare in everyday speech. Americans usually say 'supplier,' 'caterer,' 'outfitter,' or 'quartermaster' for the same function. You will mostly see it in historical, maritime, or expedition writing.

distinctions.note: Supplier is the everyday business word for any company that sells goods, while provisioner suggests supplying food and necessities for a voyage, camp, or long trip.
Purveyor is a formal word for a seller of goods, often food, and is more common in restaurant and hotel contexts than provisioner.

examples.everyday: My uncle was the provisioner for our camping trip, so he packed all the food and water.
examples.professional: The logistics team hired an outside provisioner to restock the research station before winter.
examples.analytical: In early colonial accounts, the provisioner is often a shadowy figure whose decisions determined which settlements survived.

nuance.analogy: A provisioner is like a pantry manager for a ship: someone who makes sure the crew never runs out of what it needs.
nuance.etymology: From provision, from Latin providere, 'to foresee, prepare', plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Stressing the final syllable instead of VIZH.
Using it as a general word for any seller, when Americans would say 'supplier' in business contexts.

senses.definition: The branch of medicine that focuses on mental and behavioral health by subjectively diagnosing, treating, or preventing mental disorders (mental illnesses) and behavioral conditions.

core.definition: The branch of medicine that diagnoses, treats, and prevents mental illnesses and emotional or behavioral disorders.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on -KY-, and the final syllable is a light 'ee'. Keep the p silent, and do not pronounce the middle syllables too strongly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In everyday American speech it is a serious, professional term, though it can carry some stigma for those who feel uncomfortable with mental health care.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use psychiatry in medical, academic, and policy discussions, as well as in news about mental health. In casual talk people more often say mental health care or therapy. The word refers to the medical field, so it implies that a doctor is involved.

distinctions.note: Psychology is the scientific study of the mind and behavior, while psychiatry is the medical practice of treating mental disorders.
Psychoanalysis is a specific therapy developed by Freud, while psychiatry is a broad medical field that may use many treatments.

examples.everyday: My cousin went into psychiatry after medical school because she wanted to help people with depression.
examples.professional: Our hospital is expanding its inpatient psychiatry unit to meet the growing demand for mental health beds.
examples.analytical: Psychiatry's claim to scientific status remains contested, since its diagnostic categories depend heavily on clinical judgment.

nuance.analogy: Psychiatry is like the cardiology of the mind: it uses medical knowledge to treat a problem that is hard to see.
nuance.etymology: From Greek psychē, meaning soul or mind, plus iatreia, meaning healing.
common_mistakes: Confusing psychiatry with psychology, which is a different field.
Pronouncing the initial p, which is silent.

senses.definition: To withdraw; especially of military forces; to retreat.
senses.example: The troops pulled out of the conflict.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see pull,‎ out.
senses.example: I need to pull the splinter out of my hand.

senses.definition: To transition from a dive to level or climbing flight.
senses.example: After releasing its bomb, the plane pulled out of its dive.

senses.definition: To use coitus interruptus as a method of birth control.
senses.example: Pulling out is not a reliable form of birth control, the nurse told us during the visit.

senses.definition: To remove something from a container.
senses.example: He pulled his gun out before she had a chance to scream.

senses.definition: To maneuver a vehicle from the side of a road onto the lane.
senses.example: When joining a road, you should check for traffic before pulling out.

senses.definition: To draw out or lengthen.
senses.example: The meeting pulled out for hours as everyone repeated the same complaints.

senses.definition: To draw out by dragging or tugging.
senses.example: The rescuers pulled out the injured driver from the wreckage using ropes and a winch.

senses.definition: To succeed despite long odds.
senses.example: Nobody thought they'd win, but the football team pulled out a victory.

core.definition: To leave a place, especially by driving away from a curb or parking spot, or to withdraw from a commitment or activity.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on out, so say pool OUT with a clear diphthong. In everyday speech, the l in pull is light and the vowel is short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes leaving or withdrawing, and can sound negative when someone backs out of a promise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pull out in everyday driving talk, as in 'Wait for the bus to pull out before you cross.' It is also common for withdrawing from a deal, a project, or a team. In business and news, it is used for troops or companies leaving an area or market.

distinctions.note: Leave is the general word for going away; pull out emphasizes moving away by vehicle or withdrawing from a commitment.
Back out is informal and suggests breaking a promise or abandoning a plan, while pull out can describe a neutral withdrawal.

collocations: pull out of the parking lot
pull out at the last minute

examples.everyday: Wait till that truck pulls out before you back up.
examples.professional: The vendor pulled out of the contract two weeks before launch, so we need a replacement quickly.
examples.analytical: The philosopher argues that a rational agent cannot pull out of a moral commitment without revising its own values.

nuance.analogy: Pull out is like a cork coming out of a bottle: something that was fixed in place is removed by a steady motion.
nuance.etymology: Pull comes from Old English pullian; out is from Old English ut.
common_mistakes: Using pull out as a noun in place of pullout, which is the noun for a turnout or withdrawal.
Mixing up pull out with pull over when talking about police stops.

conversation.text: Look both ways before you pull out of the driveway.
The train was pulling out just as we ran onto the platform.
The investor pulled out of the deal at the last minute.
She pulled out her phone to check the directions.

senses.definition: To sit down on a chair: to go from a non-seated position to sitting on a chair.
senses.example: Pull up a chair! The meeting's about to begin.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see pull up,‎ chair.
senses.example: Please pull up a chair and sit down.

core.definition: To move a chair closer to a table or group and sit down, often as a friendly invitation to join.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'chair', and 'a' is a reduced schwa. Link the phrase so it sounds like 'pool-up-uh-CHAIR', and keep the American r in 'chair'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and friendly; it is a warm invitation, usually offered to make a guest feel welcome.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this in homes, offices, or at a table to invite someone to join a conversation or meal: 'Pull up a chair and tell us about your trip.' It is casual and warm, so with a formal guest you might say 'Please, have a seat.' A natural reply is 'Thanks, I will.'

distinctions.note: 'Have a seat' is polite and general, used for guests to sit down; 'pull up a chair' is more hospitable and implies joining in.
'Take a seat' is a common, neutral invitation, but it does not necessarily imply that you are welcome to join a group conversation.

collocations: pull up a chair and sit
pull up a chair next to me
pull up a chair and join us
pull up a chair by the fire

examples.everyday: Hey, you made it! Pull up a chair, we just ordered the pizza.
examples.professional: We're starting the review now, so pull up a chair and bring your laptop to the table.
examples.analytical: In seminar, the professor would say 'pull up a chair' to invite students into the argument rather than lecturing from above.

nuance.analogy: Like making room by the campfire: you shift over and bring someone into the circle.
nuance.etymology: Pull is from Middle English pullen; chair is from Middle English chaiere, from Old French chaiere, from Latin cathedra.
common_mistakes: Dropping the American r in 'chair', which can make it sound like 'char' or 'chay'.
Using 'take up a chair' instead of 'pull up a chair' when inviting someone to sit down.

senses.definition: A simple hand-powered device used to impart a rapid rotating motion to a rod (the spindle or drill shaft), used to start a fire or to drill holes.

core.definition: A simple hand-powered tool that uses an up-and-down pumping motion to spin a drill shaft, used to start fires or bore holes.

pronunciation.tip: As a compound noun, Americans put the main stress on PUMP, the first word, and a weaker stress on drill. Do not stress both words equally.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a tool, usually in survival training or archaeology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pump drill mainly in survival training, primitive skills courses, and archaeology, where it is distinguished from the bow drill. In everyday talk, most people would not use it, and they might just say 'hand drill' or 'fire drill' for other tools. A natural mention in a class is 'We practiced with the pump drill this morning.'

distinctions.note: A bow drill uses a bowstring to spin the spindle, while a pump drill uses an up-and-down pumping handle.
A hand drill, or brace, is turned by hand, often with a crank; a pump drill uses a pumping motion instead.
A power drill is an electric or battery tool; a pump drill is entirely hand-operated and primitive.

examples.everyday: We spent the afternoon trying to start a fire with a pump drill, and it finally caught.
examples.professional: The survival course instructor used a pump drill to show how early tools worked.
examples.analytical: Archaeologists have reconstructed the pump drill to test whether it could have produced the perforations found on shell beads.

nuance.analogy: A pump drill works like a sewing machine's foot pedal: an up-and-down motion turns into a fast rotation.
common_mistakes: Stressing drill as the main word, when the compound usually puts the main stress on PUMP.
Confusing a pump drill with an electric power drill, which is a completely different tool.

senses.definition: Pumped up; excited.
senses.example: I'm feeling pumped for the game on Friday.

senses.definition: Pumped up; having muscles in an engorged state following exercise.
senses.example: After the workout, his arms looked pumped, and he felt ready for another set.

senses.definition: Wearing pumps (the type of shoe).
senses.example: The pumped dancers stepped lightly across the stage in their satin shoes.

senses.definition: Very tired, especially when too fatigued to grip handholds well.
senses.example: I was so pumped by the end of the climb that I could barely hold onto the jugs.

core.definition: Very excited and energized about something that is about to happen, such as an event, trip or game.

pronunciation.tip: Pumped is one syllable, with the stressed short u followed by the mpt cluster. Do not insert a vowel between the p and the t or pronounce the ed as a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive and enthusiastic, though very casual and sometimes seen as juvenile in formal settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pumped in casual speech among friends, coworkers and family, usually with for or about, as in 'I'm pumped for the concert.' In formal writing or serious discussion, excited or eager is more appropriate. A natural reply is 'Me too, it's going to be awesome.'

distinctions.note: Excited is broader and suits any context, while pumped is more energetic and casual.
Psyched is a close informal synonym; both are casual, and the choice is largely regional or personal.
Pumped refers to positive anticipation, while nervous suggests anxiety about what might happen.

examples.everyday: I'm so pumped for the concert on Friday!
examples.professional: The team is pumped about the launch, so let's keep the timeline tight.
examples.analytical: Sociologists of sport have noted that a crowd's pumped anticipation can shape the emotional tone of an entire event.

nuance.analogy: Like a tire filled with air, full and ready to roll.
common_mistakes: Using pumped to mean nervous or anxious, which is a different feeling
Using pumped in formal writing where excited or eager is more appropriate

conversation.text: I'm pumped for the game on Sunday!
The whole team was pumped after the coach's speech.
