senses.definition: To reinvigorate or revitalize.
(rare) To reactivate (a catalyst, reagent etc.).
senses.example: The chemist attempted to revivify the spent catalyst by heating it under controlled conditions.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (rare) To become effective again as a reagent etc.
senses.example: The old reagent seemed to revivify after the solution was warmed and filtered.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To give new life, energy or vigor to something that has become weak, dull or lifeless; to revitalize it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, -VYE-. The final -ify is pronounced 'fye' like 'fly', not 'fih'. Keep the first syllable weak.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests the renewal of energy after decline, but it sounds elevated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use revivify mostly in writing, sermons and editorial prose about organizations, cities or spirits. Ordinary speech says revive, bring back or give new life to. The chemistry sense (reactivating a catalyst) is rare and appears only in technical texts.

distinctions.note: Revive is common and everyday; revivify is more formal and stresses giving life or vigor again.
Reinvigorate stresses restoring strength or energy; revivify can also mean literal reanimation of something lifeless.

examples.everyday: The new manager's energy really revivified the whole office after a rough year.
examples.professional: We hope the new product launch will revivify our sales in the Midwest.
examples.analytical: Romantic writers sought to revivify a sense of wonder that they believed industrial rationalism had suppressed.

nuance.analogy: Like jump-starting a dead battery, revivify restores the spark that was already there but drained.
nuance.etymology: From Latin re- plus vivificare, from vivus ('alive') plus facere ('to make').
common_mistakes: Using revivify in casual conversation where revive is far more natural.
Stressing the first syllable; it is rih-VYE-vih-fye, not REV-ih-vye-fy.
nuance.biblical_note: In John 6:63 Jesus says the Spirit gives life, using the Greek zōopoieō ('to make alive'). In Romans 8:11 Paul says that God, who raised Christ Jesus, will give life to mortal bodies through his Spirit, using the same Greek root.

revivify.etymology: Partly from French *revivifier* and partly from Latin *revīvificō*, corresponding to *re* + *vivify*.

senses.definition: Rhomboid, having a rhomboid shape.

core.definition: Shaped like a rhomboid: a parallelogram with adjacent sides of unequal length and no right angles.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the second syllable, on the diphthong 'boy', not on the first syllable. Non-native speakers often stress 'rom' or pronounce the -oid ending as 'oyd' with too much length.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in geometry, design drawing and anatomy. In everyday talk they would say 'diamond-shaped' or 'slanted rectangle' instead. The rhomboid muscles of the upper back, which appear in fitness and physical therapy talk, are a common everyday use of the related noun 'rhomboid'.

distinctions.note: A rhombus has four equal sides, while a rhomboid has opposite sides equal but adjacent sides unequal.
A parallelogram is the general category with two pairs of parallel sides; a rhomboid is one specific kind of parallelogram.

examples.everyday: The quilt has a rhomboidal pattern in blue and white that my grandmother made.
examples.professional: The CAD sketch shows a rhomboidal bracket, so the mounting holes won't line up with the frame.
examples.analytical: A rhomboidal figure is a parallelogram whose adjacent sides are unequal and whose angles are not right angles.

nuance.analogy: Like a rectangle pushed sideways until its corners lean over.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin rhomboides, from Greek rhomboeidēs, meaning rhombus-like.
common_mistakes: Stressing the middle syllable as in rom-BOID-al; the stress belongs on the -boy- syllable.
Confusing a rhomboid with a rhombus, which has four equal sides.

senses.definition: Having ribs.
Intercalated with slate; said of a seam of coal.
senses.example: The coal seam was ribbed with slate, so the miners had to sort the rock carefully.

core.definition: Having raised parallel ridges across its surface, as in ribbed sweaters, socks or cuffs.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable, with the b and d pronounced together and no vowel between them. Do not insert a vowel and say RIB-id.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a descriptive term for texture.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'ribbed' often in clothing and products, as in 'a ribbed tank top' or 'ribbed socks'. It also describes surfaces such as tires, glass or a ribbed dome. Do not confuse it with 'ribs', the noun for the bones of the chest, or 'ribbing', which means good-natured teasing.

distinctions.note: Corrugated describes a regular wave-like pattern, mainly in metal or cardboard; ribbed is broader and common for knitwear.
Grooved means cut with channels; ribbed means raised ridges on the surface.

examples.everyday: I bought a ribbed tank top for the summer, and it fits better than the plain ones.
examples.professional: The new prototype has a ribbed grip texture so the handle won't slip when hands are wet.
examples.analytical: The ribbed surface increases the friction between the grip and the hand, which explains its better performance in wet conditions.

nuance.analogy: Like a washboard or a corduroy road: raised lines that give a regular, textured surface.
nuance.etymology: From rib plus -ed; the noun rib comes from Old English ribb.
common_mistakes: Adding a vowel, saying RIB-id instead of RIBD.
Confusing ribbed with ribbing; ribbing as a noun means good-natured teasing.

senses.definition: Any extended protuberance; a projecting line or strip.
senses.example: The plow threw up ridges of earth between the furrows.

senses.definition: The line along which two sloping surfaces meet which diverge towards the ground.
senses.example: mountain ridge

senses.definition: The highest point on a roof, represented by a horizontal line where two roof areas intersect, running the length of the area.
senses.example: The roofers nailed the last shingles along the ridge before the storm arrived.

senses.definition: The highest portion of the glacis proceeding from the salient angle of the covered way.
senses.example: Engineers reinforced the ridge of the glacis so enemy artillery couldn't easily reach the covered way.

senses.definition: A chain of mountains.
senses.example: We hiked along the ridge for three days, with peaks rising on both sides.

senses.definition: A chain of hills.
senses.example: Our cabin sits on a wooded ridge overlooking the valley and the river.

senses.definition: A long narrow elevation on an ocean bottom.
senses.example: The research vessel mapped a long ridge on the Atlantic seafloor using sonar.

senses.definition: An elongated region of high atmospheric pressure.
senses.example: A strong high-pressure ridge over the Plains kept the region dry all week.

senses.definition: A long tentpole that holds up the ceiling of a tent and is in turn held up by uprights.
senses.example: Dad snapped the ridge into place, and the tent stood up straight at last.

senses.definition: The back of any animal; especially the upper or projecting part of the back of a quadruped.
senses.example: The horse's ridge was damp with sweat after the long gallop up the hill.

senses.definition: To form into a ridge.
senses.example: The wind ridged the sand into long, rippled lines along the beach.

senses.definition: To extend in ridges.
senses.example: The hills ridge across the county, forming a natural barrier between the two towns.

core.definition: A long, narrow raised line of high land, or the line where two sloping surfaces meet, like a roof peak.

pronunciation.tip: It is a single syllable with a short i and a j sound at the end. Do not insert a vowel between the d and the j, and keep the r strong.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes terrain or structure without emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ridge for mountain crests and hiking routes: 'We hiked along the ridge.' In home construction, the roof ridge is the top horizontal line of a roof. Crest is used for the top of a wave or a hill, not usually for a long mountain line.

distinctions.note: A crest is the top of a hill, wave, or bird's head; a ridge is a long, narrow line of high land.
A hill is a single rounded elevation; a ridge is an extended linear feature with a crest line.

examples.everyday: Let's hike the ridge trail before the sun goes down.
examples.professional: The survey crew marked the ridge where the new fiber route will run.
examples.analytical: Her argument follows a sharp ridge between two competing theories, never falling into either.

nuance.analogy: A ridge is like the spine of a book, the line where two pages meet.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hrycg, meaning back or spine.
common_mistakes: Blurring ridge and bridge in speech; the d-j sound at the end is the key difference.
Using ridge for a small bump; it means a long, raised line.

ridge.etymology: From Middle English *rigge*, *rygge*, (also *rig*, *ryg*, *rug*), from Old English *hryċġ* (“back, spine, ridge, elevated surface”), from **hrugi*, from Proto-Germanic **hrugjaz* (“back”), from Proto-Indo-European **krewk-*, **ker-* (“to turn, bend”).

conversation.text: The trail follows the ridge for about a mile.
It gets really windy up on the ridge.
We watched the sun come up over the ridge.

senses.definition: Related to a rite or repeated set of actions.
senses.example: They performed the ritual lighting of the candles.

senses.definition: A rite; a repeated set of actions, especially in religious contexts (that is, a service).
senses.example: The priests carried out the religious ritual carefully.

core.definition: A set of actions performed in a fixed order, often as a religious ceremony or as a regular personal habit.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and make the middle syllable a quick, light schwa-like sound so the word has only two beats after the stress. Do not say it as three full syllables. Note that the ch sound is the American tch.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can be positive (comforting tradition) or negative (empty routine), depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ritual for religious ceremonies and also for everyday habits, such as a morning ritual of coffee and news. Calling a habit a ritual is friendly and natural. For formal religious worship, Americans may say ceremony or liturgy.

distinctions.note: Rite is more formal and usually religious, while ritual can describe any repeated action, including personal habits.
A habit is simply something you do regularly, while a ritual usually has a meaningful or symbolic structure.

examples.everyday: My morning ritual is making coffee and reading the news before I check my phone.
examples.professional: Our team has a Monday ritual where everyone shares one blocker before the stand-up begins.
examples.analytical: Victor Turner treated ritual as a process that moves participants through separation, transition, and reintegration.

nuance.analogy: A ritual is like a song whose lyrics and melody never change, so everyone who knows it can join in at once.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ritualis, relating to ritus, custom or religious usage.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable or saying three full syllables with equal stress.
Using ritual as a verb; it is a noun or adjective.

senses.definition: Having a relationship of rivalry.
senses.example: The two siblings were fiercely rivalrous, competing over every grade, sport, and friend.

senses.definition: Which can be consumed by no more than one person at the same time.
senses.example: Unlike a public park, a pizza is rivalrous, since one slice cannot be eaten twice.

core.definition: Characterized by rivalry, meaning competing or contesting with others for the same thing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, RYE. The -rous ending is a reduced r-sound followed by a quiet uhs, not a full rus or rowss.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It describes competitive or contested relationships, and in economics it is a neutral technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use rivalrous in everyday speech, where they say competitive or in competition. You will mostly see it in economics, where it describes goods that one person can use at a time, such as a sandwich. In casual talk about siblings or teammates, saying they are competitive is more natural.

distinctions.note: Competitive is everyday and broad, while rivalrous implies a more personal or head-to-head relationship between particular rivals.
In economics, rivalrous concerns whether one person's use prevents another's, while excludable concerns whether others can be kept from using a good at all.

examples.everyday: My two brothers are very rivalrous, and they still fight over who gets the best seat in the car.
examples.professional: Our two product teams have a rivalrous relationship, so they hoard data instead of sharing it openly.
examples.analytical: In economics, a sandwich is rivalrous because one person eating it prevents another from eating it, while national defense is non-rivalrous.

nuance.analogy: Rivalrous goods are like the last parking space downtown: once one car takes it, no other car can use it.
nuance.etymology: From rival with the adjectival suffix -ous, related to rivalry.
common_mistakes: Using rivalrous as a noun in place of rival, as in he is my rivalrous.
Confusing rivalrous in economics with excludable, which is a different property of goods.

senses.definition: A tool used by a riveter for joining pieces of metal together with a rivet.

An adjustable-impulse pneumatic hammer, fitted with a rivet set which matches the shape of the factory head of a solid rivet, used by a riveter (or gunner) to impact the factory head of that rivet (which has been heated if necessary to soften it), while a heavy bucking bar or similar is held against the bucktail of the rivet, upsetting it to form the field head.
senses.example: The factory crew used a rivet gun to set the steel rivets along the aircraft's fuselage seams.

senses.definition: A ratchetting lever mechanism which is attached to the frangible mandrel passing through a typical blind rivet, which when pulled upsets the bucktail to form the field head of the rivet without needing access to the field-head side of the construction.
senses.example: Without access to the back of the panel, the technician pulled the rivet gun to form the blind head.

core.definition: A hand-held pneumatic tool that drives rivets to join metal parts, used in construction, shipbuilding and aircraft assembly.

pronunciation.tip: In a compound noun the first word usually takes the main stress, so say RIV-it with the stress on the first syllable and gun lighter. Keep the vowel in RIV short and say the final t as a soft flap.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term mainly in manufacturing, construction, aviation and trades. Workers in these fields may also say air hammer or riveting hammer, and an informal speaker might just say rivet. In casual talk, most people would not know the term, so explain it as a power tool for hammering rivets.

distinctions.note: A rivet gun is the tool, while a riveter is the worker who uses it.
A nail gun drives nails into wood or other materials, but a rivet gun forms a permanent metal joint by compressing a rivet head.

examples.everyday: My uncle used a rivet gun to repair the aluminum frame of his trailer.
examples.professional: We need two more rivet guns on the assembly line before the second shift starts.
examples.analytical: The rivet gun transmits repeated impact through the operator's arm, so engineers design its handles and dampers to reduce vibration injury.

nuance.analogy: A rivet gun is like a staple gun for metal, except that it hammers a permanent fastener that is meant never to come loose.
nuance.etymology: Rivet comes from Old French rivet, meaning small nail; gun comes from Middle English gonne.
common_mistakes: Stressing gun instead of rivet, which makes the compound sound like a weapon phrase.
Using rivet gun for any metal tool, when the term refers specifically to a pneumatic hammer for rivets.

senses.definition: To steal from, especially using force or violence.
senses.example: He robbed three banks before he was caught.

senses.definition: To deprive of, or withhold from, unjustly or injuriously; to defraud.
senses.example: The best way to rob a bank is to own one.

senses.definition: To deprive (of).
senses.example: Working all day robs me of any energy to go out in the evening.

senses.definition: To burgle.
senses.example: Thieves rob empty houses in our neighborhood while families are away on vacation.

senses.definition: To commit robbery.
senses.example: Two masked men robbed the liquor store on Fifth Street just before closing.

senses.definition: To take possession of the ball, puck etc. from.
senses.example: The defender robbed the striker of the ball just outside the penalty box.

senses.definition: A syrup made of evaporating fruit juice over a fire, usually mixed with sugar or honey, and especially used for medicinal purposes.
senses.example: Grandmother boiled the elderberries down into a dark rob for her winter cough.

core.definition: To steal from a person or place, especially by using force, threats, or violence.

pronunciation.tip: This is a one-syllable word with a broad, open 'ah' vowel, the same as in 'cot' in General American speech. The r is rhotic, and the final b is a clear, unreleased sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes serious crime or unfair taking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'rob' for crimes where something is taken directly from a person or place, such as a store or bank, often with a weapon. 'Steal' is the general word and can be used for almost any theft. The noun 'rob' for a fruit syrup is an old, rare sense that is not used in everyday American English.

distinctions.note: Steal is the general word for taking something without permission; rob focuses on taking from a person or place, often by force or threat.
Burglarize refers to breaking into a building to steal when no one is present; rob usually involves the victim being there.
Mug is an informal, specific word for robbing someone in the street, often with violence.

examples.everyday: Someone robbed the corner store last night, so the owner is putting up new cameras.
examples.professional: The internal audit found that a former employee had robbed the company of nearly two hundred thousand dollars over three years.
examples.analytical: Many ethicists argue that deception can rob a person of informed consent, even when no property is physically taken.

nuance.analogy: To rob someone is like cutting the power line to a house: the value is taken directly from the people who were using it.
nuance.etymology: From Old French rober, to plunder, from a Germanic source related to the word robe, meaning booty or spoils.
common_mistakes: Using 'rob' for a theft with no victim present, where 'burglarize' or 'steal' is more accurate.
Saying 'rob me of' a thing as if it were a simple theft; in many cases 'deprive me of' is more natural in formal writing.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Hebrew Bible, the verb rob translates the Hebrew gazal, which means to rob, seize, or plunder. Malachi 3:8 in the RSV asks whether people rob God and charges the people with withholding their tithes and offerings. Leviticus 19:13 forbids oppressing one's neighbor or robbing him, and it treats unjust taking as a violation of the covenant community.

rob.etymology: From Middle English *robben*, from Anglo-Norman *rober*, from Late Latin *raubō*, from **raubōn* and Old High German *roubōn*, *raubōn* (“to rob, steal, plunder”), from Proto-Germanic **raubōną*.

senses.definition: Received.
To acknowledge by saying "roger".
senses.example: Pilots often roger the tower's instructions over the radio before they begin taxiing.

senses.definition: Of a man, to have sexual intercourse with (someone), especially in a rough manner.
senses.example: The bartender swore the drunk had rogered a sailor's wife, and nobody in the bar believed him.

senses.definition: To have sexual intercourse.
senses.example: Two lovers in the old novel roger in the hayloft while the rain pounds the barn roof.

senses.definition: An act of sexual intercourse.
senses.example: Their brief, clumsy roger in the back seat ended with both of them laughing nervously.

core.definition: Used to confirm that a message was received and understood, especially on a radio or in a clear instruction. It does not necessarily mean agreement.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the 'g' is pronounced like the 'j' in 'judge'. The final -er is a lightly r-colored unstressed vowel, not a full 'ah' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in radio, aviation and workplace use. The verb senses are vulgar slang for sex, so the word can shock in mixed company depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Roger that' or 'Roger' on radios, in aviation, in the military, and sometimes in workplace calls to confirm an instruction. In everyday conversation 'got it' or 'sounds good' sounds more natural. Avoid the verb senses, which are crude slang for sex and are not appropriate at work or in front of others.

distinctions.note: 'Got it' is everyday and friendly; 'roger' is radio-style brevity and can sound clipped in a casual conversation.
'Copy' or 'copy that' is the other radio confirmation of receipt, with the same meaning as 'roger' and no sexual slang.
'Affirmative' means yes, giving a positive answer; 'roger' only confirms that you received the message.

examples.everyday: Pick up some milk on your way home. Roger that.
examples.professional: Deploy the model to staging by noon and send me a note when it's live. Roger that, I'll confirm once it's up.
examples.analytical: In early radio procedure, a 'roger' signaled only that the message had been received, not that the operator agreed with it.

nuance.analogy: Like a 'got it' on a walkie-talkie: it confirms the signal arrived, not that you like the plan.
nuance.etymology: From the radio code word for the letter R, short for 'received'.
common_mistakes: Using 'roger' to mean 'I agree' or 'sounds good'; it only confirms receipt.
Pronouncing it with stress on the second syllable or with a full 'ah' in the final syllable; say RAH-jer.

roger.etymology: From *Roger*, used circa 1940 in UK and US military communication to represent "R" when spelling out a word.

senses.definition: Unprincipled or unscrupulous.
Mischievous and playful.

core.definition: Playful and mischievous in a charming way, sometimes with a slightly dishonest or unprincipled edge.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the ending a short 'ish' sound, like 'fish'. Don't stretch the second syllable into 'geesh'.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive or lighthearted, implying charm with a hint of naughtiness; more negative when it suggests unprincipled behavior.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'roguish' mostly for a grin, look or charm, as in 'a roguish smile'. It is more common in writing, reviews and descriptions than in casual speech. For serious dishonesty, use 'shady', 'dishonest' or 'corrupt' instead.

distinctions.note: Mischievous is common for children and playful people; roguish suggests a charming adult with a slightly daring streak.
Charming is general approval; roguish adds a hint of naughtiness.
Shady is informal and suggests suspicious dealings; roguish is lighter and more playful.

collocations: a roguish twinkle in his eye

examples.everyday: He gave me a roguish grin and said he had already eaten the last cookie.
examples.professional: Our product lead has a roguish streak, but she still hits every deadline.
examples.analytical: Fielding's roguish narrator charms the reader while quietly undermining every claim to moral authority.

nuance.analogy: Like a cat that looks innocent while nudging a glass toward the edge of the table.
nuance.etymology: From rogue with the suffix -ish.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in roh-GISH; say ROH-gish.
Using 'roguish' for serious crime; for real wrongdoing, say 'dishonest' or 'corrupt'.

senses.definition: The group of languages and cultures which are derived from Vulgar Latin.
senses.example: Linguists trace much of the Romance family back to spoken Latin.

senses.definition: Of or dealing with languages or cultures derived from Roman influence and Latin: French, Italian, Portuguese, Spanish, Galician, Romanian, Catalan, Occitan, etc.
senses.example: She is studying Romance languages, including Spanish, Italian, and Portuguese, at graduate school.

core.definition: A romantic relationship or love affair; also the feeling of excitement, mystery, and idealism that comes with love.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, MANS, and the final t is silent in American speech, so say roh-MANS, not ROH-mants. The first syllable is a full 'oh' sound, not 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it suggests love, excitement, and idealism. It can sound naive or sarcastic when someone says it with a teasing tone, such as 'Oh, how romantic'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use romance most often for a love affair or a loving relationship, as in 'Their romance started at a wedding.' For a sweet gesture or a feeling, it can also be used loosely. Calling a book or movie a romance usually means it is a love story, often a romance novel. The sense about the Romance languages is a specialist term that most Americans would not use in daily life.

distinctions.note: A love affair is usually a specific relationship, often secret or short-lived, while romance can describe any loving relationship or the feeling of love itself.
Romance is the noun and romantic is the adjective, so say 'a romantic dinner', not 'a romance dinner'.

examples.everyday: Their romance started at a friend's wedding, and they got engaged a year later.
examples.professional: The marketing team wants the ad to capture the romance of cooking at home, but it still has to highlight the low price.
examples.analytical: Many philosophers have argued that romance depends on imagination, and that what it promises often collapses once ordinary life begins.

nuance.analogy: Romance is like a movie trailer: it shows the exciting highlights, while real love is the full film with the slow parts too.
nuance.etymology: From Old French romanz, from Latin Romanicus, originally meaning a text written in the vernacular Romance language rather than Latin, later a story of adventure and love.
common_mistakes: Using romance as an adjective; say 'romantic' ('a romantic evening'), not 'romance evening'.
Pronouncing the final t, as in 'ROH-mants'; in American speech the t is silent.

romance.etymology: From Old French *romanz* (“vernacular language”), from Late Latin *rōmānicē*, from Latin *rōmānicus* < *rōmānus* + *-icus*.

senses.definition: A general guideline, rather than a strict rule; an approximate measure or means of reckoning based on experience or common knowledge.
senses.example: The usual rule of thumb says that to calculate when an investment will double, divide 70 by the interest rate.

senses.definition: Approximated, guesstimated.
senses.example: I made a quick, rule-of-thumb estimate of the manhours required for the job.

core.definition: A general guideline based on practical experience rather than a strict, exact rule.

pronunciation.tip: Stress "THUM," with a light secondary stress on "rule." In speech, "rule of" links into "rool-uhv," and the th is voiceless.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It suggests a useful, practical shortcut.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "rule of thumb" in workplace talk, cooking, and everyday advice, such as "As a rule of thumb, I tip about twenty percent." It signals that the guideline is approximate. A natural reply is "Sure, that's a good rule of thumb."

distinctions.note: A "principle" is a fundamental belief or law; a "rule of thumb" is a practical estimate.
A "guideline" can be formal or official; a "rule of thumb" is informal and based on experience.

examples.everyday: As a rule of thumb, I plan on about thirty minutes for every mile of driving.
examples.professional: As a rule of thumb, we budget ten percent extra for testing when the timeline is tight.
examples.analytical: The rule of thumb works well in practice, but it lacks the rigor of a formal derivation.

nuance.analogy: A rule of thumb is like a rough map drawn from memory: useful for getting close, but not precise.
nuance.etymology: Rule of thumb probably refers to measuring by the length of the thumb, a practical method used by craftsmen.
common_mistakes: Saying "a rule of thumb" when you mean a strict law; it is only approximate.
Using "rule of thumb" in very formal writing where "general guideline" fits better.

conversation.text: As a rule of thumb, I save ten percent of every paycheck.
A good rule of thumb is to keep slides under ten words each.
The rule of thumb is to cook chicken until it's no longer pink.

senses.definition: To hit someone with a car or other vehicle and injure or kill them.
senses.example: He was run down while crossing the main road.

senses.definition: To criticize someone or an organization, often unfairly.
senses.example: Whatever the company says, the media is going to run them down.

senses.definition: To find something or someone after searching for a long time.
senses.example: I finally managed to run down that report. I had filed it incorrectly.

senses.definition: To lose power slowly. Used for a machine, battery, or other powered device.
senses.example: You need to wind up the clock every day so that it doesn't run down.

senses.definition: To read quickly a list or other short text.
senses.example: Running down the list of suggestions, I can see three we can discard immediately.

senses.definition: To describe in the form of a rundown, a rough outline or summary.
senses.example: Please run down the project timeline so the team can see where we stand.

senses.definition: To decline in quality or condition.
senses.example: to run down in health

senses.definition: To chase till the object pursued is captured or exhausted.
senses.example: to run down a stag

senses.definition: To crush; to overthrow; to overbear.
senses.example: The bigger company tried to run down the startup by undercutting every price.

senses.definition: To approach (someone, thing or place) aggressively, as to attack.
senses.example: He ran down on Rashad and them.

senses.definition: To move (some copy) down to the next line.
senses.example: If they occasionally supply any additional copy after this element, run it down with a manual line break.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see run,‎ down.
To run against and sink, as a vessel.

core.definition: To hit a person with a vehicle and injure or kill them.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on DOWN, while RUN is secondary. The vowel in down is the diphthong 'ow', and the final n is clear, not nasal or dropped.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a serious accident, often in news or police reports.
nuance.usage_note: In news and conversation, run down describes a driver hitting a pedestrian, cyclist, or animal, usually with serious harm. The passive form 'got run down' is common in everyday talk. For a driver who flees the scene, Americans say hit and run.

distinctions.note: Hit is the general word for contact, while run down adds that a moving vehicle went over or into the person, often causing serious injury.
Knock down is less specific about the cause and does not imply a vehicle moving over someone.

collocations: get run down by a bus
the driver ran down a cyclist
was run down in a crosswalk

examples.everyday: My cousin got run down by a delivery van while biking, but she's recovering at home now.
examples.professional: The insurance report says the delivery driver ran down a pedestrian at the intersection, which triggers a formal review.
examples.analytical: The thought experiment asks whether an autonomous car would be morally responsible if it had to choose which pedestrian to run down.

nuance.analogy: Like a train that does not stop for a car stalled on the tracks, a vehicle that runs someone down keeps moving forward.
nuance.etymology: Run from Old English rinnan; down from Old English dune, meaning from a height.
common_mistakes: Using run down for a minor collision where no one is hurt
Confusing the verb with the adjective run-down, which means shabby or exhausted

senses.definition: In a rural way.
In a rural place; in the countryside.

core.definition: In a rural way, or in or toward the countryside rather than cities.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is a weak schwa, and the final -ly sounds like 'lee.' The word has one l sound, not two.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes location or manner without praise or criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use rurally mostly in policy, health and education contexts, such as 'rurally located schools' or 'serve rural and rurally isolated communities.' In everyday talk people more often say 'out in the country' or 'in the countryside.' The adverb is useful in formal writing and news reports.

distinctions.note: Rustically means in a simple, rough or old-fashioned style; rurally refers to location or setting.
In the country is a natural spoken phrase; rurally is more formal and usually modifies an adjective or verb in written English.

examples.everyday: We live rurally, so the nearest grocery store is about twenty minutes away.
examples.professional: The clinic serves patients who live rurally and often cannot reach specialists without a long drive.
examples.analytical: Broadband access is distributed unevenly, particularly for communities that are rurally isolated.

nuance.analogy: Living rurally is like living at the end of a long road: everything is farther away, but the quiet is closer.
nuance.etymology: Formed from rural and the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the last syllable as 'lay' instead of 'lee.'
Using rurally to describe a person's personality or style, where rustic is the better word.

senses.definition: The error caused by observing a sample instead of the whole population.

core.definition: The difference between a sample statistic and the true population value, caused only because the sample is a subset of the whole population.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on AIR, with a light secondary stress on SAM-pling; the final -er is a reduced r-colored vowel. Non-native speakers often say a full EH-ror, so keep the vowel quick and let the r color it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise statistical term with no emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in statistics, survey research, polling, data science and public reporting. Pollsters often write 'margin of error' for the same idea in public reports, which is a related but more specific term. In a technical discussion, 'sampling error' refers to random variation that shrinks as the sample grows, not to mistakes in data collection.

distinctions.note: Sampling error is random variation from using a subset, while bias is a systematic error that does not shrink with a larger sample.
Margin of error is a public summary, usually a range at a confidence level, derived from sampling error.
Measurement error comes from imprecise instruments or responses, not from observing only part of the population.

collocations: increase the sample size to reduce sampling error

examples.everyday: My uncle said the poll only surveyed a thousand people, so there's some sampling error in those numbers.
examples.professional: Before we report the A/B test lift, we need to quantify the sampling error so stakeholders see the confidence interval.
examples.analytical: Sampling error is a property of the estimator across repeated samples, so it cannot be eliminated by interpreting any single sample more carefully.

nuance.analogy: Tasting one spoonful of soup to judge the whole pot: the spoonful may be a little saltier or blander than average, and that gap is sampling error.
common_mistakes: Saying 'sampling error' when they mean a mistake or blunder; in statistics it is expected random variation.
Mispronouncing the final syllables as a full 'ror' rather than the reduced American r-colored vowel.

senses.definition: A standard formula to end a conversation, i.e. bye, see you soon.
senses.example: Got to run to the meeting, so say nothing and I'll catch you later.

core.definition: To keep quiet and not share information, an opinion or a comment about something.

pronunciation.tip: 'Nothing' has a voiceless th, so put your tongue lightly between your teeth and blow air. The stress falls on the first syllable of 'nothing', and the ending is '-ing', not '-in' or '-ting'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can be discreet and positive when keeping a secret, or evasive and negative when hiding something.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'say nothing' to tell someone to keep a secret or avoid a topic, such as 'If the boss asks, say nothing about the merger.' It is different from 'say nothing of,' which means 'not to mention.' A natural reply is 'My lips are sealed' or 'Got it, I won't say a word.'

distinctions.note: 'Keep quiet' is broader and can mean not making noise; 'say nothing' specifically means not speaking about a subject.
'Say nothing of' means 'not to mention' and introduces a further point, while 'say nothing' means to stay silent.

examples.everyday: Please say nothing to Mom about the surprise party.
examples.professional: If the auditors ask about the schedule, say nothing until legal has reviewed the draft.
examples.analytical: A philosopher who holds that ethics cannot be stated may conclude that the honest position is to say nothing about it.

nuance.analogy: Like a closed door: people know a room exists, but nothing comes out.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'nothing' as 'nothin' with a t or with a d sound instead of the voiceless th.
Using 'say nothing' to mean 'do nothing' when you only mean 'don't speak'.

senses.definition: The steep artificial slope below a fort's parapet.
senses.example: The fort's scarp was so steep that attacking soldiers could not climb it under fire.

senses.definition: A cliff at the edge of a plateau or ridge caused by erosion or faulting; the steeper side of an escarpment.
To cut, scrape, erode, or otherwise make into a scarp or escarpment.
senses.example: to scarp the face of a ditch or a rock

core.definition: A steep slope or cliff, especially one at the edge of a plateau or ridge, formed by erosion or faulting.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable. Keep the r clear after the vowel and end with a crisp, unvoiced p, with no extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term in geology, landscape description, and military fortification.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use scarp mainly in geology, landscape writing, or military history. In everyday talk, people would say 'steep slope', 'cliff', or 'bluff'. In geology, scarp often appears alongside escarpment, which usually refers to a larger feature.

distinctions.note: An escarpment is a long cliff or steep edge of a larger ridge, while a scarp is often the steep face itself or a single step-like slope.
Cliff is the everyday word for a steep rock face, while scarp is a technical term that can also describe a human-made slope.

examples.everyday: We hiked up to the top of the scarp and could see the whole valley below.
examples.professional: The survey team mapped a fault scarp along the proposed site, which limits where we can build.
examples.analytical: The scarp marks the boundary where erosion has pushed back the plateau edge, leaving a steep face above the lowland.

nuance.analogy: A scarp is like the broken edge of a stair made by nature, where the ground suddenly drops away.
nuance.etymology: From Italian scarpa, 'slope', and related to escarpment.
common_mistakes: Using scarp for any hill; the word refers to a steep face or step-like drop.
Confusing scarp with scarf because they sound similar at the start; scarp ends with a p sound, scarf with an f.

senses.definition: A stoneworker who removes large projections by boring slanting or transverse holes and using wedges etc. to split the stone.
senses.example: The scouter bored slanting holes into the granite block before inserting the wedges.

core.definition: An adult volunteer leader in a Scouting organization, especially the Boy Scouts of America.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the final syllable a soft, reduced American r-colored vowel. It is easily confused with scooter, which is SKOO-ter with a different vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive; the word respects adult volunteers who give their time to young people.
nuance.usage_note: Within Scouting, adult leaders are called scouters, and the term appears in troop meetings, camps, and Boy Scouts of America publications. Outside that world, most Americans have never heard it, so you may need to explain it to strangers. The older stoneworking sense, a worker who splits stone with wedges, is technical and historical, and you will rarely hear it in American speech.

distinctions.note: A scout is a youth member, while a scouter is an adult volunteer who leads, trains, or advises the youth.
A scooter is a small vehicle or a child's toy; the words look and sound similar but mean nothing alike, and the vowel differs.

examples.everyday: My husband is a scouter, so he is at the troop meeting every Tuesday night.
examples.professional: The council requires every new scouter to finish safety training before leading a weekend campout.
examples.analytical: The scouter's role has shifted from strict disciplinarian to mentor, a change that reflects broader views of youth development.

nuance.analogy: A scouter is like a coach who does not play but helps the young athletes learn the game.
nuance.etymology: Formed from scout with the agent suffix -er; the Scouting sense is a specialized American use.
common_mistakes: Using scouter to mean a young scout, when it refers to an adult leader
Pronouncing the vowel as in scooter, which gives a different word

senses.definition: The wrinkling of the brows or face in frowning; the expression of displeasure, sullenness, or discontent in the countenance; an angry frown.
senses.example: She made a scowl.

senses.definition: Gloom; dark or threatening aspect.
senses.example: A scowl of dark foreboding hung over the town as the storm approached.

senses.definition: To wrinkle the brows, as in frowning or displeasure; to put on a frowning look; to look sour, sullen, severe, or angry.
To look gloomy, dark, or threatening; to lower.
senses.example: The clouds scowled over the hills all afternoon, promising rain.

senses.definition: To look at or repel with a scowl or a frown.
senses.example: to scowl a rival into submission

senses.definition: To express by a scowl.
senses.example: to scowl defiance

core.definition: To wrinkle your brows and lower your face to show anger, displeasure, or disapproval; also an angry frown.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with the ow sound of owl and a clear l at the end. Do not say SKOL or SKOAL, which sounds like a drinking toast.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it shows anger or disapproval, though a playful scowl between friends or with children can be lighthearted.
nuance.usage_note: Americans scowl at people, traffic, or a bad call, and they use the word for displeasure rather than for a quick frown of concentration. In storytelling, saying someone scowled suggests strong feeling and can sound dramatic in formal writing. In casual talk, phrases like she gave me a scowl or he is scowling at the TV are common and natural.

distinctions.note: A frown is a general sign of worry or disapproval and can be mild, while a scowl is a stronger, angrier wrinkling of the brows.
A glare is a fixed, intense stare at someone, while a scowl is a facial expression that may occur without any staring.
Glower is more literary and suggests a long, sullen, threatening look, while scowl is the everyday word.

examples.everyday: When the waiter brought the wrong order, my friend just gave him a scowl.
examples.professional: When the QA lead saw the failing tests, she scowled and asked for a root-cause review before the release.
examples.analytical: His scowl at the argument signaled an emotional objection that his logical objections did not fully express.

nuance.analogy: A scowl is like storm clouds gathering on a face, warning of a squall before any words fall.
nuance.etymology: Middle English scoulen, probably of Scandinavian origin.
common_mistakes: Using scowl to with a person; say scowl at someone
Spelling it scoul or scowel, or pronouncing the vowel like the one in skoal; the vowel is the ow of owl

scowl.etymology: From Middle English *scowlen*, *scoulen*, *skoulen*, probably of origin.

senses.definition: Synonym of centipede (“many-oared Chinese smuggling boat”).

core.definition: A long, many-oared Chinese boat used for smuggling, also called a centipede.

pronunciation.tip: Secondary stress falls on scram and primary stress on drag, with the final syllable of dragon weak, so it sounds like DRAG-un. Keep the short a in both words and do not stress the word as DRAY-gon.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a historical or descriptive term with a slightly exotic flavor.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare term that Americans would meet only in historical, maritime, or dictionary contexts, and most would not recognize it. Do not confuse it with the dragon boat used in Chinese festival races, which is a different craft with a different name. If you need to describe such a boat in plain American English, say smuggling boat or centipede boat and explain its many oars.

distinctions.note: A dragon boat is a decorated racing boat used in festival races, while a scrambling dragon is a many-oared smuggling boat.
Dragon alone usually means the mythical winged creature; in this compound it names a specific kind of boat.

examples.everyday: I read about a scrambling dragon in a history book and had no idea what that boat looked like.
examples.professional: The maritime museum's catalog lists a scrambling dragon among the coastal boats used in smuggling cases.
examples.analytical: The name scrambling dragon joins a mythical creature with a vessel built for speed and concealment, revealing how smugglers and officials described their boats.

nuance.analogy: A scrambling dragon is like a centipede on water, its many oars moving together the way many legs move together.
nuance.etymology: English compound of scrambling and dragon; the Chinese source of the boat name is not documented here.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with a dragon boat, the decorated racing boat used in Chinese festival races
Stressing dragon as DRAY-gon instead of DRAG-un with a short a

senses.definition: To draw (an object, especially a sharp or angular one), along (something) while exerting pressure.
senses.example: She scraped the wooden plate with her fingernails.

senses.definition: To remove (something) by drawing an object along in this manner.
senses.example: Scrape the chewing gum off with a knife.

senses.definition: To injure or damage by rubbing across a surface.
senses.example: She tripped on a rock and scraped her knee.

senses.definition: To barely manage to achieve or attain.
senses.example: I scraped a pass in the exam.

senses.definition: To collect or gather, especially without regard to the quality of what is chosen.
senses.example: Just use whatever you can scrape together.

senses.definition: To extract data by automated means from a format not intended to be machine-readable, such as a screenshot or a formatted web page.
senses.example: They didn't provide an API, so I simply scraped their website.

senses.definition: To occupy oneself with getting laboriously.
senses.example: He scraped and saved until he became rich.

senses.definition: To play awkwardly and inharmoniously on a violin or similar instrument.
senses.example: Some people covered their ears when he started to scrape his violin.

senses.definition: To draw back the right foot along the ground or floor when making a bow.
senses.example: At the end of the recital, the dancer scraped her right foot back and bowed deeply.

senses.definition: To express disapprobation of (a play, etc.) or to silence (a speaker) by drawing the feet back and forth upon the floor; usually with down.
senses.example: The audience began to scrape the cheap musical down, stomping and hissing at every scene.

senses.definition: A broad, shallow injury left by scraping (rather than a cut or a scratch).
senses.example: He fell on the sidewalk and got a scrape on his knee.

senses.definition: The sound or action of something being scraped.
senses.example: The sharp scrape of a chair across the kitchen floor woke the baby upstairs.

senses.definition: Something removed by being scraped; a thin layer of something such as butter on bread.
senses.example: She spread a thin scrape of butter on her toast before leaving for work.

senses.definition: A fight, especially a fistfight without weapons.
senses.example: He got in a scrape with the school bully.

senses.definition: An awkward set of circumstances.
senses.example: I'm in a bit of a scrape — I've no money to buy my wife a birthday present.

senses.definition: A shallow depression used by ground birds as a nest; a nest scrape.
senses.example: The plover laid its eggs in a shallow scrape on the bare gravel beach.

senses.definition: An intermittent shallow pond in a wetland or floodplain, often artificially created to attract birds.
senses.example: Wildlife managers flooded the old field to create a scrape that shorebirds could use each spring.

senses.definition: A shallow pit dug as a hideout.
senses.example: The boys dug a scrape in the hillside and hid there until dark.

senses.definition: A diminutive of the bend (especially of the bend sinister) which is half its width.
senses.example: The heraldic shield bore a narrow scrape running diagonally across its surface, bordered in gold.

core.definition: To rub or drag something sharp or rough across a surface, removing a layer or causing a small injury.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single syllable and keep the diphthong 'ay' long. Don't drop the r after the k, and make sure the final p is not dropped.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses, but negative when describing an injury or a narrow escape.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'scrape' in everyday contexts such as removing ice from a windshield or scraping a plate after dinner. In the phrase 'scrape by' or 'scrape together,' it means to barely manage or gather resources with difficulty. For more forceful action, people may say 'scratch' or 'grate,' depending on the situation.

distinctions.note: 'Scratch' usually leaves a thin mark or a small cut, while 'scrape' removes material or causes a broader rubbed injury.
'Grate' suggests shredding food on a grater or making a harsh, grinding sound, while 'scrape' is more about dragging across a surface.

examples.everyday: I need to scrape the ice off the windshield before we leave.
examples.professional: Scrape the old paint from the wall before you apply the primer.
examples.analytical: The author argues that modern institutions scrape together legitimacy from procedures rather than from genuine consent.

nuance.analogy: Scraping is like running a spatula across a pan: it lifts away what sticks to the surface.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'scrapian' (to scrape).
common_mistakes: Saying 'scrape out' when the intended meaning is 'scrape off,' or vice versa, depending on whether something is removed from the surface or from inside.
Confusing 'scrape' with 'scratch' when describing a minor cut.

scrape.etymology: From Middle English *scrapen*, from Old Norse *skrapa* (“to scrape, scratch”) and Old English *scrapian* (“to scrape, scratch”), both from Proto-Germanic **skrapōną*, **skrepaną* (“to scrape, scratch”), from Proto-Indo-European **skrebʰ-* (“to engrave”).

conversation.text: It's just a scrape; you'll be fine.
He scraped his knee falling off his bike.
Clean the scrape and put some ointment on it.

senses.definition: A physical barrier that shelters or hides.
senses.example: a fire screen

senses.definition: A physical divider intended to block an area from view, or provide shelter from something dangerous.
senses.example: a fire screen

senses.definition: A stand of trees or other plants that can block wind.
senses.example: We planted a dense screen of cypress trees along the property line to block the winter wind.

senses.definition: A disguise; concealment.
senses.example: He hid his true intentions behind a screen of polite small talk.

senses.definition: A material woven from fine wires intended to block animals or large particles from passing while allowing gasses, liquids and finer particles to pass.
senses.example: Jones caught the foul up against the screen.

senses.definition: A mesh layer in a window or doorway that lets in fresh air but keeps out pests.
senses.example: The kitchen window screen had a tear, so mosquitoes kept getting inside.

senses.definition: A frame supporting a mesh of bars or wires used to classify fragments of stone by size, allowing the passage of fragments whose a diameter is smaller than the distance between the bars or wires.
senses.example: Archaeologists passed the sediment through a fine screen to recover small bone fragments.

senses.definition: Searching through a sample for a target; an act of screening, or the method for it.
senses.example: a drug screen, a genetic screen

senses.definition: A technique used to identify genes so as to study gene functions.
senses.example: The lab ran a genetic screen to find which genes affect cell growth.

senses.definition: A system intended to separate something into groups based on various criteria.
senses.example: The hiring process uses an automated screen to filter applicants by their qualifications.

senses.definition: A surface on which various forms or formats of information are displayed.
senses.example: After you turn on the computer, the login screen appears.

senses.definition: The viewing surface or area of a movie or of a moving picture or slide presentation.
senses.example: The image on the big screen was so sharp that we forgot we were in a theater.

senses.definition: A room in a cinema.
senses.example: We grabbed seats in screen four just as the previews started.

senses.definition: The informational viewing area of electronic devices, where output is displayed.
senses.example: My phone screen cracked when I dropped it on the sidewalk.

senses.definition: One of the individual regions of a video game, etc. divided into separate screens.
senses.example: The boss waits at the end of each screen, so you must clear every room first.

senses.definition: The visualized data or imagery displayed on a computer screen.
senses.example: After you turn on the computer, the login screen appears.

senses.definition: Definitions related to standing in the path of an opposing player.
Ellipsis of screen pass.
An offensive tactic in which a player stands so as to block a defender from reaching a teammate.
senses.example: She set a hard screen on the defender so her teammate could get open for a layup.

senses.definition: A dwarf wall or partition carried up to a certain height for separation and protection, as in a church, to separate the aisle from the choir, etc.
senses.example: The carved oak screen separated the nave from the choir in the medieval cathedral.

senses.definition: A military or nautical formation that blocks or separates; a collection of less-valuable vessels that travel with a more valuable one for the latter's protection.
senses.example: The destroyers formed a screen around the aircraft carrier during the night crossing.

senses.definition: The protective netting which protects the audience from flying objects.
senses.example: Jones caught the foul up against the screen.

senses.definition: A stencil upon a framed mesh through which paint is forced onto printed-on material; the frame with the mesh itself.
senses.example: The printer stretched a fresh screen onto the frame before running the T-shirt order.

senses.definition: An erection of white canvas or wood placed on the boundary opposite a batsman to make the ball more easily visible.
senses.example: The umpire stood near the white screen while the bowler ran in for the next delivery.

senses.definition: To filter by passing through a screen.
senses.example: Mary screened the beans to remove the clumps of gravel.

senses.definition: To filter.
senses.example: Passenger baggage was screened by X-ray to look for weapons.

senses.definition: To shelter or conceal.
To remove information, or censor intellectual material from viewing. To hide the facts.
senses.example: The news report was screened because it accused the politician of wrongdoing.

senses.definition: To present publicly (on the screen).
senses.example: The news report will be screened at 11:00 tonight.

senses.definition: To fit with a screen.
senses.example: We need to screen this porch. These bugs are driving me crazy.

senses.definition: To stand so as to block a defender from reaching a teammate.
To determine the source or subject matter of a call before deciding whether to answer the phone.
To examine patients or treat a sample in order to detect a chemical or a disease or to assess susceptibility to a disease.
To search chemical libraries by means of a computational technique in order to identify chemical compounds which would potentially bind to a given biological target such as a protein.

core.definition: The flat display surface on a phone, computer, or TV that shows images, text, or video.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long e. The r comes before the vowel and must be clear, so do not drop it or shorten the vowel to 'skrin'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical everyday word with no evaluative tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use screen for almost any display: phone screen, TV screen, or computer screen. For a physical divider, Americans say privacy screen or room divider, and screen alone is less common for a barrier. As a verb, screen means to check, filter, or vet something, as in 'We screen calls.' A natural phrase is 'Can you see my screen?'

distinctions.note: Display is the technical term for the output hardware, while screen is the everyday word for the surface you look at.
A monitor is a separate external display for a computer, while screen can refer to any display, including a phone or TV.

examples.everyday: I can't read the text on this screen because the sun is glaring off it.
examples.professional: Can you share your screen so we can walk through the dashboard together?
examples.analytical: The screen mediates our attention, so every interface is also a choice about what we are allowed to see.

nuance.analogy: Like a window that shows a picture instead of the outside view.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English screne, meaning a partition or shelter; the display sense developed with film and television.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it skrin with a short i; the vowel is a long e.
Using screen for a monitor in strict technical writing, where display or monitor may be more precise.

screen.etymology: From Middle English *scren*, *screne* (“windscreen, firescreen”), from Anglo-Norman *escren* (“firescreen, the tester of a bed”), Old French *escren*, *escrein*, *escran*, from Middle Dutch *scherm*, from *skirm*, from **skirmi*, from Proto-Germanic…

senses.definition: A professional writer; one whose occupation is to draw contracts or prepare writings.
senses.example: In medieval towns, the scrivener copied legal contracts and wills for merchants who could not write.

core.definition: A person who was paid to write or copy legal documents, contracts and business papers, especially before modern printing and law offices.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle vowel is a reduced schwa. Pronounce the final -er as a quick American r-colored vowel, not as a full ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly old-fashioned. It describes a historical profession, so it is not used as an insult in modern speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use scrivener in modern speech. You will see it in historical writing, literature or discussions of colonial and early modern legal practice. For a modern person who prepares contracts, say lawyer, paralegal or notary.

distinctions.note: A scribe copies texts in general, often religious or literary, while a scrivener specifically prepared legal and commercial documents.
A notary certifies signatures and documents today; a scrivener drafted or copied the documents themselves.

examples.professional: Modern contract drafting is handled by attorneys, not by a scrivener, but the work is similar in purpose.
examples.analytical: Early modern commerce depended on the scrivener, whose craft made agreements legible and enforceable.

nuance.analogy: A scrivener was like a human form-filler for the law, turning a spoken agreement into a written document.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English scrivener, from Anglo-Norman escrivein, from Latin scriba, 'scribe'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as skri-VEN-er; the stress is on the first syllable.
Using scrivener as a synonym for any writer; the word refers specifically to legal or business writing.

scrivener.etymology: From Middle English *scryvener*, alteration of *scryveyn*, from Anglo-Norman *scrivein* (“professional penman, copyist”), from Old French *escrivain*, from Vulgar Latin **scriba*, from Latin *scriba*, from *scrībō* (“to write”).

senses.definition: Ellipsis of Navy SEAL (“member of the Sea, Air, Land unit”).

core.definition: A member of the US Navy's elite special operations unit, trained for missions at sea, in the air and on land.

pronunciation.tip: Say it as one word, like the animal seal, not as the letters S-E-A-L. The vowel is long ee and the final l is a dark l in General American.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests elite skill and toughness, with an air of secrecy about training and missions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say Navy SEAL, or just SEAL, for members of the US Navy special warfare units. Use the full name when you are unsure, and do not apply it to foreign forces, which have their own names. Context matters in conversation because the same word also names the animal, but people rarely confuse the two.

distinctions.note: Green Beret is the informal name for US Army Special Forces, not the Navy; SEALs belong to the Navy.
Delta Force is an Army special operations unit with a separate mission and selection process from the Navy SEALs.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's son just finished SEAL training, and he still doesn't talk much about it.
examples.professional: Our security consultant is a former Navy SEAL who now trains corporate teams on crisis response.
examples.analytical: The SEAL selection process is often cited as a model of extreme physical and mental endurance in American military culture.

nuance.analogy: A SEAL is like a multitool of the military, built to handle water, air and ground operations in one package.
nuance.etymology: Acronym for SEa, Air and Land, the three environments in which the Navy unit operates; the unit was formed in 1962.
common_mistakes: Spelling out S-E-A-L letter by letter; Americans pronounce it as one word.
Using SEAL for any elite soldier; the term refers to US Navy special operations, and other countries have their own units.

senses.definition: Closed by a seal (something to prevent leakage).
senses.example: The jar was sealed tightly, so the soup stayed fresh for days in the fridge.

senses.definition: Preventing entrance.
senses.example: The fire marshal sealed the basement entrance after finding the flooding was dangerous.

senses.definition: Of a road: having an asphalt or macadamised surface.
senses.example: The county finally sealed the gravel road last summer, so it's smooth now.

senses.definition: Not subclassable; from which one cannot inherit.
senses.example: In the API, the class is sealed, so no other code can inherit from it.

core.definition: Closed so that nothing can get in or out, or officially secured against being opened.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long ee vowel and a voiced final d. Do not add an extra syllable like seel-ed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can suggest security, freshness or confidentiality, and sometimes finality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sealed for envelopes, containers, bids and court records, as in a sealed envelope or sealed bid. Sealed lips means refusing to talk about something. The word works in both casual and formal speech.

distinctions.note: Closed is general; sealed means closed with a barrier that prevents leaks or access.
Airtight stresses that air cannot pass through; sealed is broader and can refer to officially protected documents.
Locked requires a key or code; sealed may refer to a glued, tamper-evident or officially protected closure.

examples.everyday: The milk is still sealed, so it should be fine to drink.
examples.professional: Please send your bid in a sealed envelope marked with the project number.
examples.analytical: The court kept the witness's identity sealed, so the records remain closed to the public and to the press.

nuance.analogy: A sealed jar is like a closed mouth: nothing gets in or out until someone breaks the seal.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of seal, from Old French seel, from Latin sigillum meaning small sign.
common_mistakes: Confusing sealed (closed) with sealed off (blocked by a barrier), which is a separate phrasal verb.
Adding an extra syllable and saying seel-ed; sealed has one syllable.

senses.definition: A structure composed of a plank, balanced in the middle, used as a game in which one person goes up as the other goes down.
The game or pastime of seesawing.
A series of up-and-down movements.
A series of alternating movements or feelings.
An abnormal breathing pattern caused by airway obstruction, characterized by paradoxical chest and abdominal movement.
A tactic in which a piece repeatedly gains material, while simultaneously creating an inescapable series of alternating direct and discovered checks.
To use a seesaw.
To fluctuate.
To cause to move backward and forward in a seesaw fashion.
Fluctuating.

core.definition: A board balanced at its middle so that when one end goes up the other goes down; also the playground game of riding one.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SEE. The second syllable rhymes with 'saw', the cutting tool, with no 'r' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for the playground object; figuratively it suggests unstable, back-and-forth change that can be frustrating.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use seesaw for the playground board and, figuratively, for something that keeps reversing, like prices or polls. Many Americans also say teeter-totter for the same playground object, so both words are natural.

distinctions.note: Teeter-totter is a common American synonym for the playground board, while seesaw can also describe the back-and-forth movement itself.
Fluctuate is neutral and technical; seesaw suggests repeated, often dramatic reversals.

examples.everyday: The kids spent the whole afternoon on the seesaw at the park.
examples.professional: Our conversion rates have been seesawing all quarter, so I don't trust the weekly trend yet.
examples.analytical: The argument seesaws between economic determinism and moral agency without ever resolving the tension.

nuance.analogy: Like a real playground seesaw: when one side rises, the other must fall.
nuance.etymology: A reduplication of saw, from the back-and-forth motion of sawing.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in see-SAW; the first syllable is primary.
Using seesaw for a balanced scale; a seesaw moves up and down, while a balance stays level.

seesaw.etymology: Probably a frequentative of rhythmic back-and-forth, up-and-down or zigzagging motion, such as *teeter-totter*, *zigzag*, *flip-flop*, *ping pong*, etc. under the umbrella term of reduplication; also likely influenced by the verbs *see* and *saw* of…

senses.definition: A title of respect, formerly corresponding (especially in France) approximately to Sir.
(historical) A feudal lord; a nobleman who held his lands by feudal grant; any lord (holder) of a manor.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A feudal lord or nobleman who held land by grant, or a historical title of respect for a gentleman, especially in France.

pronunciation.tip: The g is silent, so say it like 'sane-yer' with stress on the first syllable. Do not say it like 'senior', which is SEEN-yer and a different word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to deferential; the word has a respectful, old-fashioned tone and sounds historical rather than modern.
nuance.usage_note: You will meet seignior mostly in history books, medieval studies or fiction set in feudal Europe. Americans rarely use it in conversation, and it is easily confused with the more familiar senior. For a modern equivalent, say lord, landowner or nobleman, or use the French seigneur in a French context.

distinctions.note: Lord is the common English word for a feudal or landholding superior; seignior is more specialized and historical.
Senior means older or higher in rank and is pronounced SEEN-yer; the two words share a Latin root but are unrelated in modern meaning.

examples.professional: Our museum exhibit label describes the seignior as the local lord who collected rents and ran the manor court.
examples.analytical: The seignior's authority depended less on personal merit than on a web of inherited rights, obligations and loyalties.

nuance.analogy: A seignior was like a landlord who also served as judge and tax collector for everyone living on his property.
nuance.etymology: From Old French seigneur, from Latin senior, meaning older or elder.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like senior (SEEN-yer), which is a different word.
Using seignior as a casual word for a modern boss or leader, which sounds odd and old-fashioned.

seignior.etymology: From Middle English *senyour*, from Old French *seignor*, *seignior*, from Latin *senior*.

senses.definition: The bodily and mental deterioration associated with old age: Synonym of senescence.
senses.example: Her grandfather's senility made him forget names, but he still loved music.

senses.definition: The losing of memory and reason due to senescence.
senses.example: He was entering his years of senility and not liking it a bit.

core.definition: Mental and physical decline associated with old age, especially memory loss and reduced reasoning ability.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NIL, the second syllable. The first syllable is a weak 'suh', and the final -ity is a light 'ih-tee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative and often hurtful; applied to a living person, it sounds dismissive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use senility mainly in medicine and in news reports about dementia. In everyday talk, calling someone senile is rude. Say 'he's getting forgetful' or 'she has dementia' instead, and doctors now prefer terms like dementia or cognitive decline.

distinctions.note: Senescence is the neutral biological process of aging; senility is the mental impairment often associated with it.
Dementia is the modern medical term for significant cognitive decline; senility is older and less precise.

examples.everyday: My uncle keeps forgetting names, but I wouldn't call it senility; he just needs his glasses.
examples.professional: The clinic note mentions senility, but we should use the more specific term dementia in the chart.
examples.analytical: Cicero's essay on old age challenges the assumption that growing old must mean senility, though he does not deny decline.

nuance.analogy: Like a house whose lights flicker: the structure is still there, but the connections no longer hold.
nuance.etymology: From Latin senilis, 'of old men', from senex, 'old man'.
common_mistakes: Calling people senile casually; it sounds rude and hurtful.
Mixing it up with senescence, which is neutral and biological.

senses.definition: A device or organ that detects certain external stimuli and responds in a distinctive manner.
senses.example: The smoke sensor triggered the alarm.

core.definition: A device that detects a physical condition such as heat, light, motion, or pressure and responds by sending a signal or reading.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SEN. The final syllable is the American r-colored schwa, so it sounds like 'SEN-ser', not 'sen-sore' and not 'censor'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, technical term without emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'sensor' every day for devices in phones, cars, thermostats, and home security systems, such as a motion sensor or smoke sensor. In biology and robotics it can also mean the part of an organism or machine that detects stimuli. A sensor usually measures or reports a quantity, while a detector may only signal that something is present.

distinctions.note: A detector signals whether something is present, while a sensor typically measures or reports a level or change.
A transducer converts energy from one form to another, and many sensors are transducers, but the word emphasizes conversion rather than detection.

examples.everyday: The porch light turns on by itself because it has a motion sensor.
examples.professional: The temperature sensor on the server is reporting readings that drift overnight.
examples.analytical: Whether a thermostat truly perceives heat or merely registers a voltage change is a question about what counts as sensing.

nuance.analogy: A sensor is like a thermometer in a car: it notices a change in the environment and reports it so the system can respond.
nuance.etymology: Formed from sense, with the agent suffix -or, in the sense 'something that senses'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'sensor' with 'censor', which means to remove or suppress material.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'sore' instead of the reduced American 'ser'.

sensor.etymology: Originated 1925–30, formed as a Latin loanword from *sentiō* + *-tor*.

senses.definition: Using as few words as possible; pithy and concise.
Tending to the frequent use aphorisms or maxims; especially, in a manner that is affected, trite or self-righteous.
senses.example: His sententious remarks quickly bored the audience.

core.definition: Using pompous, preachy moral statements or maxims in a self-important way. Less commonly, meaning pithy and concise.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, TEN. Say the middle syllable clearly and do not add an extra vowel in the final -ous, which is a reduced syllable like 'shus'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests someone who sounds wise but is actually preachy, self-righteous, or annoyingly moralizing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in writing, book reviews, and thoughtful commentary about a speaker or writer. It is a criticism, so use it carefully, since calling someone sententious in conversation sounds sharp. Plain words like preachy or moralistic are more common in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Pithy is a neutral or positive compliment for saying a lot in few words. Sententious can describe the same style but adds the sense that the speaker is pompous.
Moralistic describes a tendency to judge others by morals. Sententious focuses on the pompous tone of the pronouncements themselves.
Preachy is casual and common in speech. Sententious is more formal and literary, and suggests a fondness for weighty-sounding maxims.

examples.everyday: My uncle gets sententious every time he talks about money, as if every purchase were a moral test.
examples.professional: The manager's email was so sententious about teamwork that nobody could tell what actually needed to change.
examples.analytical: Montaigne's essays avoid the sententious posture of the moralist, preferring to test ideas through personal experience rather than pronouncing them as settled truths.

nuance.analogy: A sententious speaker is like a fortune cookie that has learned to lecture you.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sententiosus, from sententia meaning opinion or maxim.
common_mistakes: Confusing sententious with sentient, which has to do with feeling or awareness.
Using it as a simple compliment for wise, when it usually carries a sense of pompousness.

senses.definition: The property of being separate.

core.definition: The quality or state of being separate, distinct and apart from other people or things.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the middle syllable with an American r-colored vowel ('ur'). The ending '-ness' is short and unstressed, so do not stretch it into 'nes'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can be positive when it means independence or distinct identity, and slightly negative when it means emotional distance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'separateness' in casual speech; they would say 'being apart' or 'feeling cut off.' It appears more often in writing about identity, philosophy, or relationships, such as 'a sense of separateness.' In conversation, a simpler word like 'separation' or 'independence' usually sounds more natural.

distinctions.note: 'Separation' can be an act or process of parting, while 'separateness' names the state or quality of being distinct.
'Isolation' usually sounds negative and lonely, while 'separateness' can be neutral or descriptive.
'Independence' emphasizes self-government or self-reliance, while 'separateness' emphasizes being distinct from others.

examples.everyday: Some days I feel a kind of separateness from my friends back home, even when we talk every week.
examples.professional: Our team wants to keep its separateness from the platform group, so the two teams have separate roadmaps.
examples.analytical: Rawls insists on the separateness of persons, the claim that each individual has a distinct life that cannot be merged into a single social total.

nuance.analogy: Like islands in a lake: each one has its own shape and ground, even though the same water surrounds them.
nuance.etymology: From separate (Latin separatus, 'set apart') plus the noun suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Using it as a verb or as a casual synonym for 'separation'; 'separateness' describes a quality, not an event.
Misplacing the stress as 'sep-ur-uht-NESS'; the stress belongs on the first syllable.

senses.definition: Succeeding or following in order.
Expressing succession of events.
senses.example: The instructions list sequential steps, so each task must finish before the next begins.

senses.definition: Executed as a sequence of instructions, without concurrency or parallelism.
senses.example: The sequential processing of the data avoids race conditions because only one task runs at a time.
